paragraphs: This paper proposes a probabilistic interpretation of supervised neural-network learning. It treats the values of both input and output neurons as probabilities. That interpretation makes uncertain information part of the model’s basic meaning, which is useful when observations or desired responses are imperfect.

The proposed learning objective is log likelihood. Connection weights change in the gradient direction that makes the supervised information more probable under the network. This reframes back-propagation around a statistical objective and connects the interpretation of neural values directly to the quantity optimized during learning.

The authors argue that this perspective generalizes back-propagation and gives it a stronger conceptual foundation. They also suggest that it could improve efficiency, presenting that benefit as a possibility. The motivation includes applications such as text-to-phoneme mapping, illness diagnosis, and sonar-target classification, where probabilistic information can be natural. The contribution described is the proposed learning formulation: probabilities define what neural values mean, and likelihood defines how the network should adjust its connections to fit supervised evidence.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes probabilistic inputs and outputs with log-likelihood learning as a principled generalization of back-propagation.

title: Supervised Learning of Probability Distributions by Neural Networks

paragraphs: Understanding language requires keeping track of which concepts fill which roles in a larger interpretation. This paper addresses how a localist spreading-activation network can maintain those assignments when the relevant information must travel across many intervening nodes. The challenge is to preserve a concept's identity while using it in reasoning elsewhere in the network.

The proposed mechanism gives every conceptual node a stable, distinctive activation pattern called a signature. A role becomes bound to a concept when the role's binding node carries the matching signature. Because signatures can propagate along long paths, a binding can remain available beyond the immediate neighborhood of its original concept.

The resulting model, ROBIN, uses these signatures to represent role assignments within schemata and support inference. Its stated capabilities include analyzing plans and goals, instantiating schemata, resolving word meanings, and revising interpretations dynamically. The approach matters because it gives activation a way to carry both activity and identifying information, supporting reasoning that depends on maintaining the correct assignments across a network.
summary.tldr: ROBIN propagates distinctive activation signatures to preserve concept-role assignments across a network during language understanding.

title: Dynamic, Non-Local Role Bindings and Inferencing in a Localist Network for Natural Language Understanding

abstract: For a simple linear case, a mathematical analysis of the training and gener(cid:173) alization (validation) performance of networks trained by gradient descent on a Least Mean Square cost function is provided as a function of the learn(cid:173) ing parameters and of the statistics of the training data base. The analysis predicts that generalization error dynamics are very dependent on a pri(cid:173) ori initial weights. In particular, the generalization error might sometimes weave within a computable range during extended training. In some cases, the analysis provides bounds on the optimal number of training cycles for minimal validation error. For a speech labeling task, predicted weaving effects were qualitatively tested and observed by computer simulations in networks trained by the linear and non-linear back-propagation algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper mathematically analyzes how training and validation performance change during gradient descent on a least mean square objective. It focuses on a simple linear network, relating learning behavior to the learning parameters and the statistical properties of the training data. The aim is to understand the course of generalization throughout training.

A central prediction is that initial weights strongly affect validation-error dynamics. With some starting weights, validation error can weave within a calculable range during extended training rather than improve steadily. In certain cases, the analysis also bounds the number of training cycles that yields the lowest validation error, connecting the dynamics to the question of when training should stop.

The authors investigate the predicted weaving behavior in simulations of a speech-labeling task. They observe it qualitatively in networks trained with both linear and nonlinear back-propagation. The formal analysis belongs to the linear case, while the simulations show that the predicted pattern also appears in the nonlinear networks examined.
summary.tldr: Initial weights can make validation error weave during training, and linear analysis can sometimes bound the best stopping time.

title: Generalization Dynamics in LMS Trained Linear Networks

The proposed network is a two-dimensional sheet of neurons forming a distributed representation of the robot's workspace. Lateral interconnections between neurons are "cooperative", so that the network exhibits oscillatory behaviour. These oscillations are used to gen(cid:173) erate solutions of Bellman's dynamic programming equation in the context of path planning. Simulation experiments imply that these networks locate global optimal paths even in the presence of substantial levels of circuit nOlse. 1 Dynamic Programming and Path Planning Consider a 2-DOF robot moving about in a 2-dimensional world. A robot's location is denoted by the real vector, p. The collection of all locations forms a set called the workspace. An admissible point in the workspace is any location which the robot may occupy. The set of all admissible points is called the free workspace. The free workspace's complement represents a collection of obstacles. The robot moves through the workspace along a path which is denoted by the parameterized curve, p(t). An admissible path is one which lies wholly in the robot's free workspace. paragraphs: This paper proposes a neural network for planning mobile-robot paths through a two-dimensional workspace. A valid path must connect the initial and final positions while remaining in the region the robot can occupy. The goal is to find a valid path that also satisfies an optimality criterion, so avoiding obstacles is only part of the planning problem.

The network is arranged as a two-dimensional sheet of neurons that collectively represents the workspace. Cooperative lateral connections cause the sheet to oscillate. The authors use those oscillations to generate solutions of Bellman’s dynamic programming equation for path planning, linking the network’s evolving activity to a mathematical formulation of optimal routes.

Simulation experiments suggest that the networks find globally optimal paths even with substantial circuit noise. The stated evidence therefore supports both the planning mechanism and its tolerance of noisy circuit behavior in simulation. The distinctive contribution is the use of oscillatory distributed computation to solve the planning equation, giving the network’s dynamics a direct role in determining a route.
summary.tldr: An oscillating neural sheet solves a dynamic-programming path-planning equation and finds globally optimal routes in noisy simulations.

title: Oscillatory Neural Fields for Globally Optimal Path Planning

paragraphs: This paper analyzes stochastic learning by treating network weights as random variables. Instead of describing just one sequence of weight updates, it follows a probability density over possible weight configurations. The density evolves through a Markov process, providing a way to study the changing distribution of learning outcomes over time.

The authors summarize the evolution theory and illustrate how stochastic learning differs from batch gradient descent. This perspective addresses the search process itself, including transient behavior before settling near an optimum. It also makes it possible to examine movement between basins, the regions associated with different optima in weight space.

Using the formalism, the paper predicts how long noise takes to drive a network from one basin to another. Those predictions are compared with simulations of large ensembles of networks on simple supervised and unsupervised problems. The contribution is a framework for studying where learning travels and how long transitions take, extending the analysis beyond whether a learning procedure eventually converges.
summary.tldr: A probability-density view of stochastic learning predicts transient behavior and noise-driven transition times between different optima.

title: Weight Space Probability Densities in Stochastic Learning: II. Transients and Basin Hopping Times

abstract: Learning to recognize or predict sequences using long-term con(cid:173) text has many applications. However, practical and theoretical problems are found in training recurrent neural networks to per(cid:173) form tasks in which input/output dependencies span long intervals. Starting from a mathematical analysis of the problem, we consider and compare alternative algorithms and architectures on tasks for which the span of the input/output dependencies can be controlled. Results on the new algorithms show performance qualitatively su(cid:173) perior to that obtained with backpropagation.

paragraphs: The paper investigates learning from sequences when an output depends on information received much earlier. Such tasks require long-term context, but training recurrent networks to use that context presents both practical and theoretical difficulties. The central issue is assigning learning credit across the interval separating relevant inputs and outputs.

The authors begin with a mathematical analysis and then consider alternative learning algorithms and architectures. They compare these alternatives on tasks where the length of the input-output dependency can be controlled. Making that interval adjustable lets the study examine the specific challenge of learning across time, rather than treating sequence learning as a single undifferentiated capability.

The new algorithms show qualitatively better performance than backpropagation in the reported comparisons. This finding supports investigating changes to both learning procedures and network structure when distant context is necessary. The contribution combines an analysis of the training difficulty with controlled comparisons of alternatives, linking the theoretical problem of temporal credit assignment to observed differences in sequence-learning behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes long-term temporal credit assignment and reports alternatives that perform qualitatively better than backpropagation on controlled sequence tasks.

title: Credit Assignment through Time: Alternatives to Backpropagation

abstract: This paper investigates the stationary points of a Hebb learning rule with a sigmoid nonlinearity in it. We show mathematically that when the input has a low information content, as measured by the input's variance, this learning rule suppresses learning, that is, forces the weight vector to converge to the zero vector. When the information content exceeds a certain value, the rule will automatically begin to learn a feature in the input. Our analysis suggests that under certain conditions it is the first principal component that is learned. The weight vector length remains bounded, provided the variance of the input is finite. Simulations confirm the theoretical results derived.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a Hebbian learning rule that includes a sigmoid nonlinearity. It studies the rule's stationary points to understand when learning develops a feature and when it suppresses weights. The analysis uses input variance as the measure of information content, making the strength of input variation central to the result.

When that variance is low, the weight vector converges to zero. Once the variance passes a threshold, the same rule begins learning a feature from the input automatically. This creates a transition between suppressing learning and extracting structure, governed by the input rather than a separate decision to activate learning.

Under certain conditions, the analysis suggests that the learned feature is the first principal component. The authors also show that the weight vector's length stays bounded when input variance is finite, and simulations confirm their theoretical results. Together, these findings describe both what the rule can learn and how its weights remain controlled as learning proceeds.
summary.tldr: A sigmoid Hebbian rule suppresses weights for low-variance inputs and automatically learns a feature above a variance threshold.

title: Hebb Learning of Features based on their Information Content

abstract: The way groups of auditory neurons interact to code acoustic in(cid:173) formation is investigated using an information theoretic approach. We develop measures of redundancy among groups of neurons, and apply them to the study of collaborative coding efficiency in two processing stations in the auditory pathway: the inferior colliculus (IC) and the primary auditory cortex (AI). Under two schemes for the coding of the acoustic content, acoustic segments coding and stimulus identity coding, we show differences both in information content and group redundancies between IC and AI neurons. These results provide for the first time a direct evidence for redundancy reduction along the ascending auditory pathway, as has been hy(cid:173) pothesized for theoretical considerations [Barlow 1959,2001]. The redundancy effects under the single-spikes coding scheme are signif(cid:173) icant only for groups larger than ten cells, and cannot be revealed with the redundancy measures that use only pairs of cells. The results suggest that the auditory system transforms low level rep(cid:173) resentations that contain redundancies due to the statistical struc(cid:173) ture of natural stimuli, into a representation in which cortical neu(cid:173) rons extract rare and independent component of complex acoustic signals, that are useful for auditory scene analysis.

paragraphs: The paper asks how groups of auditory neurons share information about sounds. The authors develop information-theoretic measures of group redundancy and apply them to two processing stations: the inferior colliculus and primary auditory cortex. Redundancy concerns how much information carried by neurons overlaps within a group.

They examine coding of acoustic segments and stimulus identity, finding differences between the two stations in both information content and group redundancy. The results provide direct evidence for reduced redundancy along the ascending auditory pathway. Under the single-spike coding scheme, significant redundancy effects occur only in groups containing more than ten cells, so measures restricted to pairs cannot reveal them.

This group-size result matters for how population coding is assessed: interactions visible across larger collections may escape pairwise analysis. The authors interpret the broader findings as suggesting a transformation from redundant lower-level representations toward cortical representations of rare, independent acoustic components. They propose that these components are useful for auditory scene analysis.
summary.tldr: Group-level information measures reveal auditory redundancy reduction and effects that pairwise neuron comparisons cannot detect.

title: Group Redundancy Measures Reveal Redundancy Reduction in the Auditory Pathway

abstract: Asymmetric lateral connections are one possible mechanism that can ac- count for the direction selectivity of cortical neurons. We present a math- ematical analysis for a class of these models. Contrasting with earlier theoretical work that has relied on methods from linear systems theory, we study the network’s nonlinear dynamic properties that arise when the threshold nonlinearity of the neurons is taken into account. We show that such networks have stimulus-locked traveling pulse solutions that are appropriate for modeling the responses of direction selective cortical neurons. In addition, our analysis shows that outside a certain regime of stimulus speeds the stability of this solutions breaks down giving rise to another class of solutions that are characterized by speciﬁc spatio- temporal periodicity. This predicts that if direction selectivity in the cor- tex is mainly achieved by asymmetric lateral connections lurching activ- ity waves might be observable in ensembles of direction selective cortical neurons within appropriate regimes of the stimulus speed.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes asymmetric lateral connections as a possible explanation for cortical neurons that prefer particular directions of motion. It studies a class of recurrent networks while explicitly accounting for neuronal thresholds. This allows the analysis to address nonlinear dynamics that earlier treatments based on linear systems methods did not capture.

The authors show that these networks support traveling pulses of activity that remain locked to a moving stimulus. Such solutions are appropriate for modeling direction-selective responses. However, their stability holds only within a certain range of stimulus speeds. Outside that range, the stable behavior gives way to another class of solutions with specific repeating patterns in space and time.

The resulting prediction is conditional: if asymmetric lateral connections are the main source of cortical direction selectivity, suitable stimulus speeds might produce observable lurching activity waves. The analysis therefore connects a proposed circuit mechanism to a distinctive population-level pattern, providing more than a description of a single neuron's preferred direction.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear analysis of asymmetric recurrent networks predicts stimulus-locked pulses and, conditionally, lurching activity waves outside a stable speed range.

title: Generating velocity tuning by asymmetric recurrent connections

abstract: We consider the use of two additive control variate methods to reduce the variance of performance gradient estimates in reinforcement learning problems. The first approach we consider is the baseline method, in which a function of the current state is added to the discounted value estimate. We relate the performance of these methods, which use sample paths, to the variance of estimates based on iid data. We derive the baseline function that minimizes this variance, and we show that the variance for any baseline is the sum of the optimal variance and a weighted squared distance to the optimal baseline. We show that the widely used average discounted value baseline (where the reward is replaced by the difference between the reward and its expectation) is suboptimal. The second approach we consider is the actor-critic method, which uses an approximate value function. We give bounds on the expected squared error of its estimates. We show that minimizing distance to the true value function is suboptimal in general; we provide an example for which the true value function gives an estimate with positive variance, but the optimal value function gives an unbiased estimate with zero variance. Our bounds suggest algorithms to estimate the gradient of the performance of parameterized baseline or value functions. We present preliminary experiments that illustrate the performance improvements on a simple control problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies two ways to reduce variability in reinforcement-learning performance-gradient estimates. Such estimates guide changes to a policy, so their statistical quality matters for learning. The first method adds a state-dependent baseline to a discounted value estimate. The authors relate estimates from sampled trajectories to variance calculations for independent, identically distributed data.

They derive the variance-minimizing baseline and show that any other baseline's variance equals the optimum plus a weighted squared distance from it. The commonly used average discounted value baseline is suboptimal. This gives a precise account of how baseline choice affects gradient estimation, beyond whether the baseline seems like a sensible value prediction.

For actor-critic methods, the authors bound expected squared estimation error and show that approximating the true value function as closely as possible is generally suboptimal. In one example, the true value function produces positive variance, while an optimal alternative gives an unbiased, zero-variance estimate. The bounds suggest algorithms for optimizing parameterized baselines or value functions. Preliminary experiments on a simple control problem illustrate performance improvements.
summary.tldr: The best baseline or critic for gradient estimation need not be the one that most accurately predicts value.

title: Variance Reduction Techniques for Gradient Estimates in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Re-mapping patterns in order to equalize their distribution may greatly simplify both the structure and the training of classifiers. Here, the properties of one such map obtained by running a few steps of discrete-time dynamical system are explored. The system is called 'Digital Antennal Lobe' (DAL) because it is inspired by recent studies of the antennallobe, a structure in the olfactory sys(cid:173) tem of the grasshopper. The pattern-spreading properties of the DAL as well as its average behavior as a function of its (few) de(cid:173) sign parameters are analyzed by extending previous results of Van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky. Furthermore, a technique for adapting the parameters of the initial design in order to obtain opportune noise-rejection behavior is suggested. Our results are demonstrated with a number of simulations.

paragraphs: A classifier may be easier to design and train if its input patterns are spread more evenly through their representation space. This paper investigates a transformation intended to produce that spreading. Called the Digital Antennal Lobe, it takes inspiration from a structure involved in the grasshopper's sense of smell.

The transformation runs a discrete-time dynamical system for a few steps. The authors analyze how it redistributes patterns and how its average behavior depends on a small number of design parameters. This connects the system's adjustable settings to the behavior of the resulting map, making parameter choice an explicit design question.

The paper also suggests adapting the initial parameters to obtain suitable rejection of noise. That matters because redistributing patterns is useful only insofar as the transformation also handles unwanted input variation appropriately. Simulations demonstrate the reported properties. The broader motivation is that distribution equalization may simplify classification; the abstract does not claim that every classifier or dataset necessarily benefits.
summary.tldr: A biologically inspired dynamical map spreads input patterns, with analysis and simulations connecting its parameters to equalization and noise rejection.

title: A Digital Antennal Lobe for Pattern Equalization: Analysis and Design

abstract: New feature selection algorithms for linear threshold functions are de- scribed which combine backward elimination with an adaptive regular- ization method. This makes them particularly suitable to the classiﬁca- tion of microarray expression data, where the goal is to obtain accurate rules depending on few genes only. Our algorithms are fast and easy to implement, since they center on an incremental (large margin) algorithm which allows us to avoid linear, quadratic or higher-order programming methods. We report on preliminary experiments with ﬁve known DNA microarray datasets. These experiments suggest that multiplicative large margin algorithms tend to outperform additive algorithms (such as SVM) on feature selection tasks.

This makes them particularly suitable to the classiﬁca- tion of microarray expression data, where the goal is to obtain accurate rules depending on few genes only. Our algorithms are fast and easy to implement, since they center on an incremental (large margin) algorithm which allows us to avoid linear, quadratic or higher-order programming methods. paragraphs: Microarray classification seeks accurate decision rules that depend on only a small number of genes. This paper develops feature-selection algorithms for linear threshold functions with that objective in mind. Selecting genes is part of building a compact classifier, so the method must balance predictive usefulness with reducing how many features the rule uses.

The algorithms combine backward elimination with adaptive regularization. Features are removed through the elimination process, while regularization adapts as part of the procedure. An incremental large-margin algorithm supplies the computational core. The authors describe the resulting methods as fast and straightforward to implement because they avoid linear, quadratic, and higher-order programming methods.

Preliminary experiments use five established DNA microarray datasets. Their results suggest that multiplicative large-margin algorithms tend to outperform additive algorithms, including SVMs, on feature-selection tasks. The finding is a qualified empirical tendency from those experiments. It supports further interest in multiplicative updates when the goal is an accurate classifier using few genes, alongside the proposed method's computational simplicity.
summary.tldr: Fast feature-selection methods combine backward elimination and adaptive regularization, with preliminary microarray results favoring multiplicative large-margin algorithms.

title: Fast Feature Selection from Microarray Expression Data via Multiplicative Large Margin Algorithms

abstract: Belief propagation (BP) is an increasingly popular method of perform- ing approximate inference on arbitrary graphical models. At times, even further approximations are required, whether from quantization or other simplified message representations or from stochastic approxima- tion methods. Introducing such errors into the BP message computations has the potential to adversely affect the solution obtained. We analyze this effect with respect to a particular measure of message error, and show bounds on the accumulation of errors in the system. This leads both to convergence conditions and error bounds in traditional and approximate BP message passing.

paragraphs: Belief propagation performs inference in graphical models by passing messages between parts of the model. In practical implementations, those messages may themselves be approximated. Quantization, simplified representations, and stochastic computation can all introduce errors into the message calculations, creating uncertainty about how much the resulting inference will change.

The paper analyzes these effects using a particular measure of message error. Its central question is how errors accumulate throughout the message-passing system, rather than merely how inaccurate one isolated message is. The authors derive bounds on that accumulation, providing a mathematical connection between imperfect message computations and the behavior of the overall procedure.

The analysis yields convergence conditions and error bounds for both traditional belief propagation and versions that further approximate messages. These are conditional guarantees tied to the analysis, not a statement that every graphical model or approximation scheme converges. The contribution matters when message simplification is needed: it provides a way to reason about the consequences of computational approximation within the inference process.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds how message errors accumulate in belief propagation, yielding convergence conditions and error guarantees for exact-message and approximate-message procedures.

title: Message Errors in Belief Propagation

abstract: The category of visual stimuli has been reliably decoded from patterns of neural activity in extrastriate visual cortex [1]. It has yet to be seen whether object identity can be inferred from this activity. We present fMRI data measuring responses in human extrastriate cortex to a set of 12 distinct object images. We use a simple winner-take-all classifier, using half the data from each recording session as a training set, to evaluate encoding of object identity across fMRI voxels. Since this approach is sensitive to the inclusion of noisy voxels, we describe two methods for identifying subsets of voxels in the data which optimally distinguish object identity. One method characterizes the reliability of each voxel within subsets of the data, while another estimates the mutual information of each voxel with the stimulus set. We find that both metrics can identify subsets of the data which reliably encode object identity, even when noisy measurements are artificially added to the data. The mutual information metric is less efficient at this task, likely due to constraints in fMRI data.

paragraphs: The study asks whether activity in human extrastriate visual cortex distinguishes individual object images, extending beyond the previously demonstrated decoding of object categories. The authors collect fMRI responses to 12 distinct images and examine information distributed across voxels, the spatial measurement units in the scans.

A simple winner-take-all classifier uses half of each recording session's data for training. Because noisy voxels can interfere with this approach, the authors compare two ways to select informative subsets. One measures how reliably a voxel responds across subsets of the data. The other estimates its mutual information with the stimulus set, assessing how informative its response is about the presented image.

Both selection criteria identify subsets that reliably encode object identity, including when artificial noisy measurements are added. Mutual information is less efficient for this task, which the authors suggest is likely related to constraints of fMRI data. The results support the presence of decodable information about these individual images and show why choosing useful measurements matters for recovering it.
summary.tldr: Two voxel-selection methods recover reliable information about 12 individual object images from extrastriate fMRI activity, even with added noisy measurements.

title: Identifying Distributed Object Representations in Human Extrastriate Visual Cortex

abstract: Discriminatively trained undirected graphical models have had wide empirical success, and there has been increasing interest in toolkits that ease their application to complex relational data. The power in relational models is in their repeated structure and tied parameters; at issue is how to define these structures in a powerful and flexible way. Rather than using a declarative language, such as SQL or first-order logic, we advocate using an imperative language to express various aspects of model structure, inference, and learning. By combining the traditional, declarative, statistical semantics of factor graphs with imperative definitions of their construction and operation, we allow the user to mix declarative and procedural domain knowledge, and also gain significant efficiencies. We have implemented such imperatively defined factor graphs in a system we call Factorie, a software library for an object-oriented, strongly-typed, functional language. In experimental comparisons to Markov Logic Networks on joint segmentation and coreference, we find our approach to be 3-15 times faster while reducing error by 20-25%-achieving a new state of the art.

paragraphs: FACTORIE addresses how to express probabilistic models for complex relational data. Such models gain power from repeated structures and shared parameters, but defining those structures flexibly can be difficult. The paper advocates using imperative programming to describe model construction, inference, and learning while retaining the statistical meaning of an undirected factor graph.

This combination lets users express domain knowledge both as relationships in a probabilistic model and as procedures that construct or operate on that model. The authors implement the approach as a library in an object-oriented, strongly typed, functional language. The design links flexible model specification with opportunities for computational efficiency.

In experiments on joint segmentation and coreference, FACTORIE is compared with Markov Logic Networks. The authors report speedups of 3–15 times and error reductions of 20–25%, achieving the leading results reported for that setting. These findings support the practical value of imperative model definitions alongside declarative statistical semantics, particularly for the relational task evaluated.
summary.tldr: FACTORIE combines factor-graph semantics with imperative programming, improving speed and accuracy in experiments on joint segmentation and coreference.

title: FACTORIE: Probabilistic Programming via Imperatively Defined Factor Graphs

abstract: With the advent of crowdsourcing services it has become quite cheap and reasonably effective to get a dataset labeled by multiple annotators in a short amount of time. Various methods have been proposed to estimate the consensus labels by correcting for the bias of annotators with different kinds of expertise. Often we have low quality annotators or spammers--annotators who assign labels randomly (e.g., without actually looking at the instance). Spammers can make the cost of acquiring labels very expensive and can potentially degrade the quality of the consensus labels. In this paper we formalize the notion of a spammer and define a score which can be used to rank the annotators---with the spammers having a score close to zero and the good annotators having a high score close to one.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing makes it possible to collect multiple labels for a dataset quickly and cheaply, but annotators differ in quality and expertise. Some assign labels randomly, potentially without examining the example. Such contributions can increase the cost of obtaining useful labels and degrade the consensus formed from several annotators' responses.

This paper focuses on ranking annotators by formalizing the notion of a spammer and defining an associated score. In the proposed scoring scheme, spammers receive values close to zero, while good annotators receive values close to one. The result is an ordered measure of annotator quality, rather than merely a final label for each data item.

That focus complements methods that estimate consensus labels while correcting for annotator bias. A consensus concerns what label an example should receive; the proposed ranking concerns the people supplying those labels. By making the distinction between useful and random labeling explicit, the paper provides a way to characterize contributors in a setting where annotation quality directly affects the value of collected data.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes random-labeling spammers and defines an annotator score that places them near zero and good annotators near one.

title: Ranking annotators for crowdsourced labeling tasks

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of policy evaluation for continuous-state systems. We present a non-parametric approach to policy evaluation, which uses kernel density estimation to represent the system. The true form of the value function for this model can be determined, and can be computed using Galerkin's method. Furthermore, we also present a unified view of several well-known policy evaluation methods. In particular, we show that the same Galerkin method can be used to derive Least-Squares Temporal Difference learning, Kernelized Temporal Difference learning, and a discrete-state Dynamic Programming solution, as well as our proposed method. In a numerical evaluation of these algorithms, the proposed approach performed better than the other methods.

Furthermore, we also present a unified view of several well-known policy evaluation methods. paragraphs: Policy evaluation asks how valuable it is to follow a given policy from different states. This paper addresses systems with continuous states, where evaluation must account for a space of possible states rather than just a finite list. It proposes a nonparametric representation of the system built using kernel density estimation.

For this estimated model, the authors determine the form of the value function and compute it using Galerkin’s method. The distinction between the modeled system and the original system matters: the stated characterization concerns the value function associated with the kernel-based model. This provides a concrete route from a statistical system representation to policy evaluation.

The paper also uses Galerkin’s method to connect several existing approaches. Least-Squares Temporal Difference learning, Kernelized Temporal Difference learning, discrete-state dynamic programming, and the proposed method can all be derived through this common framework. In the reported numerical evaluation, the new approach performs better than the others. Its contribution combines an evaluation algorithm with a unified view of related methods.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based system model enables continuous-state policy evaluation and connects several established evaluation methods through Galerkin’s method.

title: A Non-Parametric Approach to Dynamic Programming

abstract: Recent work in unsupervised feature learning and deep learning has shown that being able to train large models can dramatically improve performance. In this paper, we consider the problem of training a deep network with billions of parameters using tens of thousands of CPU cores. We have developed a software framework called DistBelief that can utilize computing clusters with thousands of machines to train large models. Within this framework, we have developed two algorithms for large-scale distributed training: (i) Downpour SGD, an asynchronous stochastic gradient descent procedure supporting a large number of model replicas, and (ii) Sandblaster, a framework that supports for a variety of distributed batch optimization procedures, including a distributed implementation of L-BFGS. Downpour SGD and Sandblaster L-BFGS both increase the scale and speed of deep network training. We have successfully used our system to train a deep network 100x larger than previously reported in the literature, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet, a visual object recognition task with 16 million images and 21k categories. We show that these same techniques dramatically accelerate the training of a more modestly sized deep network for a commercial speech recognition service. Although we focus on and report performance of these methods as applied to training large neural networks, the underlying algorithms are applicable to any gradient-based machine learning algorithm.

paragraphs: Training very large neural networks requires methods that can use substantial computing resources effectively. This paper introduces DistBelief, a software framework designed to train models with billions of parameters across clusters containing thousands of machines and tens of thousands of CPU cores. It addresses both the scale of trainable models and the speed of training.

The framework includes two distributed optimization approaches. Downpour SGD uses asynchronous stochastic gradient descent with many model replicas. Sandblaster supports distributed batch optimization, including an implementation of L-BFGS. These provide different ways to distribute the work of updating model parameters, and the authors report that both Downpour SGD and Sandblaster L-BFGS improve training scale and speed.

The system trains a network reported as 100 times larger than previously described in the literature and achieves state-of-the-art ImageNet performance on a task containing 16 million images and 21,000 categories. The same techniques also substantially accelerate a smaller network used for commercial speech recognition. Although the reported applications concern neural networks, the authors describe the underlying algorithms as applicable to gradient-based machine learning more broadly.
summary.tldr: DistBelief distributes neural-network optimization across large computing clusters, enabling much larger models and faster training.

title: Large Scale Distributed Deep Networks

abstract: Probabilistic graphical models are powerful tools for analyzing constrained, continuous domains. However, finding most-probable explanations (MPEs) in these models can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we improve the scalability of MPE inference in a class of graphical models with piecewise-linear and piecewise-quadratic dependencies and linear constraints over continuous domains. We derive algorithms based on a consensus-optimization framework and demonstrate their superior performance over state of the art. We show empirically that in a large-scale voter-preference modeling problem our algorithms scale linearly in the number of dependencies and constraints.

However, finding most-probable explanations (MPEs) in these models can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we improve the scalability of MPE inference in a class of graphical models with piecewise-linear and piecewise-quadratic dependencies and linear constraints over continuous domains. We derive algorithms based on a consensus-optimization framework and demonstrate their superior performance over state of the art. We show empirically that in a large-scale voter-preference modeling problem our algorithms scale linearly in the number of dependencies and constraints.

paragraphs: Finding a most-probable explanation means choosing the joint assignment favored most strongly by a probabilistic model. In continuous domains, that search can also have to satisfy constraints, making inference computationally expensive. This paper targets the scalability of this task in a particular class of constrained continuous graphical models.

The supported models contain piecewise-linear and piecewise-quadratic dependencies together with linear constraints. The authors derive inference algorithms using a consensus-optimization framework. These structural requirements define the scope of the contribution: the approach takes advantage of a specified mathematical form for both dependencies and restrictions on valid assignments.

The experiments demonstrate better performance than state-of-the-art methods. On a large-scale voter-preference modeling problem, the algorithms empirically scale linearly with the number of dependencies and constraints. That finding suggests that adding more modeled relationships and restrictions can remain manageable in this application. The linear scaling is an experimental observation from the reported problem, while the broader contribution is the consensus-based approach to MPE inference for the stated model class.
summary.tldr: Consensus optimization accelerates MPE inference for a specified class of constrained continuous graphical models, with empirical linear scaling in voter-preference modeling.

title: Scaling MPE Inference for Constrained Continuous Markov Random Fields with Consensus Optimization

abstract: In this paper, we provide a new framework to study the generalization bound of the learning process for domain adaptation. Without loss of generality, we consider two kinds of representative domain adaptation settings: one is domain adaptation with multiple sources and the other is domain adaptation combining source and target data. In particular, we introduce two quantities that capture the inherent characteristics of domains. For either kind of domain adaptation, based on the two quantities, we then develop the specific Hoeffding-type deviation inequality and symmetrization inequality to achieve the corresponding generalization bound based on the uniform entropy number. By using the resultant generalization bound, we analyze the asymptotic convergence and the rate of convergence of the learning process for such kind of domain adaptation. Meanwhile, we discuss the factors that affect the asymptotic behavior of the learning process. The numerical experiments support our results.

In particular, we introduce two quantities that capture the inherent characteristics of domains. For either kind of domain adaptation, based on the two quantities, we then develop the specific Hoeffding-type deviation inequality and symmetrization inequality to achieve the corresponding generalization bound based on the uniform entropy number. Meanwhile, we discuss the factors that affect the asymptotic behavior of the learning process. The numerical experiments support our results.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation studies learning when the data used for training and the domain of interest differ. This paper develops a framework for analyzing generalization in two representative settings: learning from multiple source domains, and learning with a combination of source and target data. The goal is to characterize how the learning process behaves as more data become available.

The framework introduces two quantities that describe inherent characteristics of the domains. Using these quantities, the authors derive deviation and symmetrization inequalities tailored to each setting. These lead to generalization bounds based on the uniform entropy number, which serves as a way to account for the complexity of the functions being learned.

The resulting bounds are then used to analyze asymptotic convergence and convergence rates, as well as factors that influence long-run behavior. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results. The contribution is an analytical framework connecting domain characteristics and learning complexity to generalization, giving a way to study both multiple-source adaptation and the use of target data within a common approach.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework derives generalization and convergence bounds for adaptation from multiple sources or combined source and target data.

title: Generalization Bounds for Domain Adaptation

abstract: We focus on the problem of maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference in Markov random fields with binary variables and pairwise interactions. For this common subclass of inference tasks, we consider low-rank relaxations that interpolate between the discrete problem and its full-rank semidefinite relaxation, followed by randomized rounding. We develop new theoretical bounds studying the effect of rank, showing that as the rank grows, the relaxed objective increases but saturates, and that the fraction in objective value retained by the rounded discrete solution decreases. In practice, we show two algorithms for optimizing the low-rank objectives which are simple to implement, enjoy ties to the underlying theory, and outperform existing approaches on benchmark MAP inference tasks.

For this common subclass of inference tasks, we consider low-rank relaxations that interpolate between the discrete problem and its full-rank semidefinite relaxation, followed by randomized rounding. We develop new theoretical bounds studying the effect of rank, showing that as the rank grows, the relaxed objective increases but saturates, and that the fraction in objective value retained by the rounded discrete solution decreases. paragraphs: The paper studies how to find the most probable assignment in a Markov random field with binary variables and pairwise interactions. This maximum a posteriori inference task is discrete. The authors approach it through low-rank relaxations that lie between the original problem and a full-rank semidefinite relaxation.

After optimizing a relaxed problem, randomized rounding converts its solution back into a discrete assignment. The analysis examines how the chosen rank affects both stages. As rank grows, the relaxed objective increases but eventually saturates. Meanwhile, the fraction of objective value retained by the rounded discrete solution decreases, exposing a tradeoff between the relaxed objective and what rounding preserves.

The authors develop two algorithms for optimizing these low-rank objectives. They describe both as simple to implement, connected to the theoretical analysis, and better than existing approaches on benchmark MAP inference tasks. The contribution combines practical optimization methods with bounds that explain why rank is a meaningful design choice. A larger relaxed objective alone does not describe the full behavior of the final rounded solution.
summary.tldr: Low-rank relaxations and randomized rounding provide simple MAP inference algorithms, with theory exposing tradeoffs as relaxation rank increases.

title: Simple MAP Inference via Low-Rank Relaxations

abstract: To capture the interdependencies between labels in multi-label classification problems, classifier chain (CC) tries to take the multiple labels of each instance into account under a deterministic high-order Markov Chain model. Since its performance is sensitive to the choice of label order, the key issue is how to determine the optimal label order for CC. In this work, we first generalize the CC model over a random label order. Then, we present a theoretical analysis of the generalization error for the proposed generalized model. Based on our results, we propose a dynamic programming based classifier chain (CC-DP) algorithm to search the globally optimal label order for CC and a greedy classifier chain (CC-Greedy) algorithm to find a locally optimal CC. Comprehensive experiments on a number of real-world multi-label data sets from various domains demonstrate that our proposed CC-DP algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art approaches and the CC-Greedy algorithm achieves comparable prediction performance with CC-DP.

paragraphs: Classifier chains model dependencies among the labels assigned to one instance by arranging label predictions in an ordered chain. Their performance can depend strongly on that ordering. This paper addresses how to select the order systematically, rather than leaving a consequential modeling choice unspecified or treating all orders as equivalent.

The authors first generalize the classifier-chain model to allow a random label order and analyze its generalization error. That theoretical treatment motivates two search algorithms. CC-DP uses dynamic programming to search for a globally optimal label order for the chain, while CC-Greedy seeks a locally optimal classifier chain.

Experiments on real-world multilabel datasets from several domains show CC-DP outperforming the compared state-of-the-art approaches. CC-Greedy achieves prediction performance comparable to CC-DP in those evaluations. The results give label ordering both a theoretical treatment and practical algorithms, while distinguishing the global and local search objectives. The empirical similarity of the two methods concerns predictive performance; it does not make their optimization guarantees identical.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis of classifier-chain ordering motivates globally optimal dynamic-programming search and a greedy alternative with comparable reported prediction performance.

title: On the Optimality of Classifier Chain for Multi-label Classification

abstract: The completion of low rank matrices from few entries is a task with many practical applications. We consider here two aspects of this problem: detectability, i.e. the ability to estimate the rank $r$ reliably from the fewest possible random entries, and performance in achieving small reconstruction error. We propose a spectral algorithm for these two tasks called MaCBetH (for Matrix Completion with the Bethe Hessian). The rank is estimated as the number of negative eigenvalues of the Bethe Hessian matrix, and the corresponding eigenvectors are used as initial condition for the minimization of the discrepancy between the estimated matrix and the revealed entries. We analyze the performance in a random matrix setting using results from the statistical mechanics of the Hopfield neural network, and show in particular that MaCBetH efficiently detects the rank $r$ of a large $n\times m$ matrix from $C(r)r\sqrt{nm}$ entries, where $C(r)$ is a constant close to $1$. We also evaluate the corresponding root-mean-square error empirically and show that MaCBetH compares favorably to other existing approaches.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix completion reconstructs a matrix from a limited set of observed entries. This paper addresses two linked problems: determining the rank from few randomly revealed entries and obtaining a reconstruction with small error. Knowing the rank matters because it describes the size of the low-rank structure being recovered.

The proposed MaCBetH algorithm uses the Bethe Hessian matrix. It estimates rank by counting negative eigenvalues, then uses the corresponding eigenvectors to initialize a procedure that minimizes disagreement with observed entries. The spectral calculation thus supplies both a structural estimate and a starting point for fitting the missing-data reconstruction.

In a random-matrix setting, the authors use results from the statistical mechanics of Hopfield networks to analyze detection. They show efficient rank detection for a large n-by-m matrix from C(r)r sqrt(nm) entries, with C(r) close to one. Empirical root-mean-square reconstruction errors compare favorably with existing approaches. The theoretical detection result and empirical reconstruction assessment support different parts of the algorithm's purpose.
summary.tldr: MaCBetH uses Bethe Hessian eigenvalues to estimate matrix rank and eigenvectors to initialize accurate low-rank completion.

title: Matrix Completion from Fewer Entries: Spectral Detectability and Rank Estimation

abstract: Bidirectional recurrent neural networks (RNN) are trained to predict both in the positive and negative time directions simultaneously. They have not been used commonly in unsupervised tasks, because a probabilistic interpretation of the model has been difficult. Recently, two different frameworks, GSN and NADE, provide a connection between reconstruction and probabilistic modeling, which makes the interpretation possible. As far as we know, neither GSN or NADE have been studied in the context of time series before.As an example of an unsupervised task, we study the problem of filling in gaps in high-dimensional time series with complex dynamics. Although unidirectional RNNs have recently been trained successfully to model such time series, inference in the negative time direction is non-trivial. We propose two probabilistic interpretations of bidirectional RNNs that can be used to reconstruct missing gaps efficiently. Our experiments on text data show that both proposed methods are much more accurate than unidirectional reconstructions, although a bit less accurate than a computationally complex bidirectional Bayesian inference on the unidirectional RNN. We also provide results on music data for which the Bayesian inference is computationally infeasible, demonstrating the scalability of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: The paper develops probabilistic interpretations of bidirectional recurrent neural networks for reconstructing gaps in time series. These networks predict in both temporal directions, but their use in unsupervised tasks has been hindered by the difficulty of giving them a probabilistic interpretation. The authors build on the GSN and NADE frameworks to address this obstacle.

Their two proposed interpretations connect reconstruction with probabilistic modeling and enable efficient filling of missing stretches in high-dimensional sequences. This matters because a gap can depend on context on either side. A unidirectional recurrent model can represent complex dynamics, but using it to infer backward through time is not straightforward.

On text, both methods reconstruct missing data much more accurately than unidirectional approaches. They are slightly less accurate than a more computationally demanding bidirectional Bayesian inference procedure applied to a unidirectional RNN. Results on music demonstrate scalability in a setting where that Bayesian procedure is computationally infeasible, illustrating the practical value of efficient bidirectional reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Two probabilistic interpretations make bidirectional RNNs practical for reconstructing missing segments in complex sequences.

title: Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks as Generative Models

abstract: We consider control problems for multi-stage campaigning over social networks. The dynamic programming framework is employed to balance the high present reward and large penalty on low future outcome in the presence of extensive uncertainties. In particular, we establish theoretical foundations of optimal campaigning over social networks where the user activities are modeled as a multivariate Hawkes process, and we derive a time dependent linear relation between the intensity of exogenous events and several commonly used objective functions of campaigning. We further develop a convex dynamic programming framework for determining the optimal intervention policy that prescribes the required level of external drive at each stage for the desired campaigning result. Experiments on both synthetic data and the real-world MemeTracker dataset show that our algorithm can steer the user activities for optimal campaigning much more accurately than baselines.
originalAbstract: We consider control problems for multi-stage campaigning over social networks. The dynamic programming framework is employed to balance the high present reward and large penalty on low future outcome in the presence of extensive uncertainties. In particular, we establish theoretical foundations of optimal campaigning over social networks where the user activities are modeled as a multivariate Hawkes process, and we derive a time dependent linear relation between the intensity of exogenous events and several commonly used objective functions of campaigning. We further develop a convex dynamic programming framework for determining the optimal intervention policy that prescribes the required level of external drive at each stage for the desired campaigning result. Experiments on both synthetic data and the real-world MemeTracker dataset show that our algorithm can steer the user activities for optimal campaigning much more accurately than baselines.

paragraphs: Campaigning over a social network involves choices across multiple stages, with uncertain responses and consequences that extend beyond the present. This paper frames those choices as a control problem. Its objective balances attractive immediate rewards against substantial penalties for poor future outcomes, making the timing of interventions part of the decision.

The authors model user activity with a multivariate Hawkes process, which represents interactions among event streams. Within that model, they derive a time-dependent linear relationship between the intensity of externally driven events and several common campaign objectives. This relationship connects the intervention being chosen to the outcomes the campaign seeks to influence.

They then develop a convex dynamic programming framework that determines the external drive required at each stage. The resulting policy is optimal within the formulated control problem. Experiments using synthetic data and the MemeTracker dataset show more accurate steering of user activity than the evaluated baselines. The contribution combines a model of network activity with a tractable method for planning interventions over time.
summary.tldr: A Hawkes-process model and convex dynamic programming choose staged social-network interventions while balancing immediate and future campaign outcomes.

title: Multistage Campaigning in Social Networks

abstract: Binary classifiers are employed as discriminators in GAN-based unsupervised style transfer models to ensure that transferred sentences are similar to sentences in the target domain. One difficulty with the binary discriminator is that error signal is sometimes insufficient to train the model to produce rich-structured language. In this paper, we propose a technique of using a target domain language model as the discriminator to provide richer, token-level feedback during the learning process. Because our language model scores sentences directly using a product of locally normalized probabilities, it offers more stable and more useful training signal to the generator. We train the generator to minimize the negative log likelihood (NLL) of generated sentences evaluated by a language model. By using continuous approximation of the discrete samples, our model can be trained using back-propagation in an end-to-end way. Moreover, we find empirically with a language model as a structured discriminator, it is possible to eliminate the adversarial training steps using negative samples, thus making training more stable. We compare our model with previous work using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as discriminators and show our model outperforms them significantly in three tasks including word substitution decipherment, sentiment modification and related language translation.

This paper replaces that discriminator with a target-domain language model, which supplies feedback at the level of individual tokens.

The results support richer language-model feedback as both a useful learning signal and a way to simplify training in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Using a language model as a discriminator gives token-level feedback that improves unsupervised text transfer and can simplify adversarial training.

title: Unsupervised Text Style Transfer using Language Models as Discriminators

abstract: Distributed learning allows a group of independent data owners to collaboratively learn a model over their data sets without exposing their private data. We present a distributed learning approach that combines differential privacy with secure multi-party computation. We explore two popular methods of differential privacy, output perturbation and gradient perturbation, and advance the state-of-the-art for both methods in the distributed learning setting. In our output perturbation method, the parties combine local models within a secure computation and then add the required differential privacy noise before revealing the model. In our gradient perturbation method, the data owners collaboratively train a global model via an iterative learning algorithm. At each iteration, the parties aggregate their local gradients within a secure computation, adding sufficient noise to ensure privacy before the gradient updates are revealed. For both methods, we show that the noise can be reduced in the multi-party setting by adding the noise inside the secure computation after aggregation, asymptotically improving upon the best previous results. Experiments on real world data sets demonstrate that our methods provide substantial utility gains for typical privacy requirements.

This paper combines secure multi-party computation with differential privacy. Secure computation supports combining information without exposing the underlying private inputs, while differential privacy adds noise to the results that are released.

The authors develop two approaches. In output perturbation, the participants combine locally trained models inside a secure computation and add noise before releasing the combined model. In gradient perturbation, they jointly train a global model over multiple iterations, securely aggregate local gradients, and add noise before revealing each update.

The central result is that adding noise after aggregation, while still inside the secure computation, can reduce the noise required in the multi-party setting. Both approaches asymptotically improve on the best previous results described by the paper. Experiments on real-world datasets show substantial gains in model utility for typical privacy requirements, linking the improved noise treatment to more useful collaborative learning.
summary.tldr: Securely aggregating models or gradients before adding differential-privacy noise improves the utility of distributed learning.

title: Distributed Learning without Distress: Privacy-Preserving Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: An agent facing sequential decisions that are characterized by partial feedback needs to strike a balance between maximizing immediate payoffs based on available information, and acquiring new information that may be essential for maximizing future payoffs. This trade-off is captured by the multi-armed bandit (MAB) framework that has been studied and applied when at each time epoch payoff observations are collected on the actions that are selected at that epoch. In this paper we introduce a new, generalized MAB formulation in which additional information on each arm may appear arbitrarily throughout the decision horizon, and study the impact of such information flows on the achievable performance and the design of efficient decision-making policies. By obtaining matching lower and upper bounds, we characterize the (regret) complexity of this family of MAB problems as a function of the information flows. We introduce an adaptive exploration policy that, without any prior knowledge of the information arrival process, attains the best performance (in terms of regret rate) that is achievable when the information arrival process is a priori known. Our policy uses dynamically customized virtual time indexes to endogenously control the exploration rate based on the realized information arrival process.

paragraphs: An agent making repeated decisions must balance choosing actions that currently look rewarding against exploring actions that could prove better. The standard multi-armed bandit setting ties new payoff observations to the actions the agent selects. This paper studies a broader setting where extra information about any action can arrive throughout the decision process, without a previously known arrival pattern.

The authors characterize how these information flows affect regret, the performance loss associated with learning which actions to choose. They establish matching lower and upper bounds, connecting the best achievable regret rate to the information available over time. This makes the arrival of information part of the problem's difficulty rather than merely an incidental benefit.

Their adaptive policy adjusts exploration using dynamically customized virtual time indexes. These indexes respond to information that has actually arrived. Without knowing the arrival process beforehand, the policy attains the regret rate achievable with that advance knowledge. The result concerns matching rates of performance, rather than claiming identical decisions or payoffs at every step.
summary.tldr: An adaptive bandit policy uses arriving side information to match the regret rate achievable when information flows are known beforehand.

title: Adaptive Learning with Unknown Information Flows

abstract: We consider the estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects with arbitrary machine learning methods in the presence of unobserved confounders with the aid of a valid instrument. Such settings arise in A/B tests with an intent-to-treat structure, where the experimenter randomizes over which user will receive a recommendation to take an action, and we are interested in the effect of the downstream action. We develop a statistical learning approach to the estimation of heterogeneous effects, reducing the problem to the minimization of an appropriate loss function that depends on a set of auxiliary models (each corresponding to a separate prediction task). The reduction enables the use of all recent algorithmic advances (e.g. neural nets, forests). We show that the estimated effect model is robust to estimation errors in the auxiliary models, by showing that the loss satisfies a Neyman orthogonality criterion. Our approach can be used to estimate projections of the true effect model on simpler hypothesis spaces. When these spaces are parametric, then the parameter estimates are asymptotically normal, which enables construction of confidence sets. We applied our method to estimate the effect of membership on downstream webpage engagement for a major travel webpage, using as an instrument an intent-to-treat A/B test among 4 million users, where some users received an easier membership sign-up process. We also validate our method on synthetic data and on public datasets for the effects of schooling on income.

paragraphs: This paper estimates treatment effects that vary across individuals when unobserved confounders are present, using a valid instrument. One motivating setting randomizes a recommendation or opportunity to act, while the desired effect concerns the action itself. The randomized intervention and the downstream treatment therefore play different roles in the estimation problem.

The authors reduce effect estimation to minimizing a loss that depends on auxiliary prediction models. This allows flexible machine-learning methods, including neural networks and forests, to fit the effect model. The loss satisfies Neyman orthogonality, providing robustness to errors in estimating those auxiliary models.

The framework can also estimate projections of the true effect onto simpler model classes. For parametric classes, the parameter estimates are asymptotically normal, enabling confidence sets. Applications include estimating membership's effect on webpage engagement using an intent-to-treat experiment involving four million travel-site users. Synthetic data and public schooling-and-income datasets provide additional validation. The contribution connects flexible prediction tools to causal estimation with explicit robustness and inference properties, with a valid instrument remaining central to the setting.
summary.tldr: An orthogonal learning objective enables flexible estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects with valid instruments and robustness to auxiliary-model errors.

title: Machine Learning Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Instruments

abstract: We envision Artificial Intelligence marketplaces to be platforms where consumers, with very less data for a target task, can obtain a relevant model by accessing many private data sources with vast number of data samples. One of the key challenges is to construct a training dataset that matches a target task without compromising on privacy of the data sources. To this end, we consider the following distributed data summarizataion problem. Given K private source datasets denoted by $[D_i]_{i\in [K]}$ and a small target validation set $D_v$, which may involve a considerable covariate shift with respect to the sources, compute a summary dataset $D_s\subseteq \bigcup_{i\in [K]} D_i$ such that its statistical distance from the validation dataset $D_v$ is minimized. We use the popular Maximum Mean Discrepancy as the measure of statistical distance. The non-private problem has received considerable attention in prior art, for example in prototype selection (Kim et al., NIPS 2016). Our work is the first to obtain strong differential privacy guarantees while ensuring the quality guarantees of the non-private version. We study this problem in a Parsimonious Curator Privacy Model, where a trusted curator coordinates the summarization process while minimizing the amount of private information accessed. Our central result is a novel protocol that (a) ensures the curator does not access more than $O(K^{\frac{1}{3}}|D_s| + |D_v|)$ points (b) has formal privacy guarantees on the leakage of information between the data owners and (c) closely matches the best known non-private greedy algorithm. Our protocol uses two hash functions, one inspired by the Rahimi-Recht random features method and the second leverages state of the art differential privacy mechanisms. We introduce a novel ``noiseless'' differentially private auctioning protocol, which may be of independent interest. Apart from theoretical guarantees, we demonstrate the efficacy of our protocol using real-world datasets.

paragraphs: This paper considers selecting training examples from multiple private datasets to match a target task represented by a small validation set. The source and target data may have substantially different input distributions. The selection objective minimizes Maximum Mean Discrepancy, a measure of statistical distance, between the chosen summary and the target validation data.

The authors work in a privacy model where a trusted curator coordinates selection while accessing as little private information as possible. Their protocol limits curator access to O(K^(1/3)|D_s| + |D_v|) points, where K is the number of sources and the two set sizes describe the summary and validation data. It also provides formal privacy guarantees for information leakage between data owners.

The protocol combines two hash functions, drawing on random features and differential privacy mechanisms, and introduces a differentially private auctioning procedure described as noiseless. Its quality closely matches the best known non-private greedy method while adding strong privacy guarantees. Experiments on real-world datasets support the protocol's effectiveness, connecting the theoretical guarantees to the proposed distributed summarization task.
summary.tldr: A distributed protocol selects target-relevant data summaries with strong privacy guarantees and limited access by a trusted curator.

title: Differentially Private Distributed Data Summarization under Covariate Shift

abstract: The application of stochastic variance reduction to optimization has shown remarkable recent theoretical and practical success. The applicability of these techniques to the hard non-convex optimization problems encountered during training of modern deep neural networks is an open problem. We show that naive application of the SVRG technique and related approaches fail, and explore why.
originalAbstract: The application of stochastic variance reduction to optimization has shown remarkable recent theoretical and practical success. The applicability of these techniques to the hard non-convex optimization problems encountered during training of modern deep neural networks is an open problem. We show that naive application of the SVRG technique and related approaches fail, and explore why.

paragraphs: Stochastic variance reduction has achieved strong theoretical and practical results in optimization. This paper examines whether that success carries over to training modern deep neural networks. The relevant setting involves difficult non-convex optimization, so the applicability of these techniques remains a question rather than a consequence of their success elsewhere.

The authors focus on straightforward applications of SVRG and related approaches. Their stated finding is that these naive applications fail, and the paper investigates why. The contribution is therefore an examination of a transfer problem: whether an established family of optimization techniques remains effective when applied to the training problems encountered in modern deep learning.

The scope of the conclusion matters. The finding concerns naive application of the studied methods, rather than establishing that every possible variance-reduction method must fail for neural networks. It challenges the expectation that prior optimization successes alone justify direct adoption in this setting and motivates understanding the source of the failure before treating these techniques as effective deep-learning optimizers.
summary.tldr: The paper finds that naive applications of SVRG and related variance-reduction methods fail in modern deep-network training and investigates why.

title: On the Ineffectiveness of Variance Reduced Optimization for Deep Learning

abstract: For embodied agents to infer representations of the underlying 3D physical world they inhabit, they should efficiently combine multisensory cues from numerous trials, e.g., by looking at and touching objects. Despite its importance, multisensory 3D scene representation learning has received less attention compared to the unimodal setting. In this paper, we propose the Generative Multisensory Network (GMN) for learning latent representations of 3D scenes which are partially observable through multiple sensory modalities. We also introduce a novel method, called the Amortized Product-of-Experts, to improve the computational efficiency and the robustness to unseen combinations of modalities at test time. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model can efficiently infer robust modality-invariant 3D-scene representations from arbitrary combinations of modalities and perform accurate cross-modal generation. To perform this exploration we have also developed a novel multi-sensory simulation environment for embodied agents.
