paragraphs: An embodied agent receives incomplete information about a three-dimensional scene through different senses and repeated observations. Looking at an object and touching it provide different views of the same physical world. The paper introduces the Generative Multisensory Network to combine such partial observations into a shared latent representation of a scene.

A central component is the Amortized Product-of-Experts, a method designed to make this combination more computationally efficient and robust to sensory combinations not seen during training. This addresses the need to infer a scene when the available modalities vary, rather than requiring a single fixed collection of sensory inputs at test time.

The experimental results show efficient inference of robust representations that are invariant to modality, together with accurate generation across modalities. The model can use different combinations of sensory evidence to represent the underlying scene and generate observations in another modality. The authors also develop a multisensory simulation environment for embodied agents to support this investigation.
summary.tldr: The Generative Multisensory Network combines partial sensory observations into shared 3D scene representations and supports cross-modal generation.

title: Neural Multisensory Scene Inference

abstract: We propose a novel spectral convolutional neural network (CNN) model on graph structured data, namely Distributed Feedback-Looped Networks (DFNets). This model is incorporated with a robust class of spectral graph filters, called feedback-looped filters, to provide better localization on vertices, while still attaining fast convergence and linear memory requirements. Theoretically, feedback-looped filters can guarantee convergence w.r.t. a specified error bound, and be applied universally to any graph without knowing its structure. Furthermore, the propagation rule of this model can diversify features from the preceding layers to produce strong gradient flows. We have evaluated our model using two benchmark tasks: semi-supervised document classification on citation networks and semi-supervised entity classification on a knowledge graph. The experimental results show that our model considerably outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in both benchmark tasks over all datasets.
authors: W. O. K. Asiri Suranga Wijesinghe

paragraphs: DFNets is a convolutional neural-network model for data organized as a graph. Its central component is a class of spectral graph filters with feedback loops. These filters aim to localize processing more effectively around graph vertices while retaining fast convergence and memory requirements that grow linearly.

The paper supplies theoretical support for the filtering procedure. Feedback-looped filters can converge to a specified error bound and can be applied to any graph without advance knowledge of its structure. The model’s propagation rule also diversifies features inherited from earlier layers, which the authors connect to strong gradient flows. Together, these properties address how graph information is processed and how the network can be trained.

The evaluation covers semi-supervised document classification on citation networks and entity classification on a knowledge graph. Across all datasets in those two benchmark tasks, the authors report considerable improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The results support feedback-looped filtering as an effective design in these settings, alongside the separate theoretical guarantees about filter convergence and applicability.
summary.tldr: DFNets uses feedback-looped graph filters to improve feature localization and training, with strong reported results on two classification benchmarks.

title: DFNets: Spectral CNNs for Graphs with Feedback-Looped Filters

abstract: Playing text-based games requires skills in processing natural language and sequential decision making. Achieving human-level performance on text-based games remains an open challenge, and prior research has largely relied on hand-crafted structured representations and heuristics. In this work, we investigate how an agent can plan and generalize in text-based games using graph-structured representations learned end-to-end from raw text. We propose a novel graph-aided transformer agent (GATA) that infers and updates latent belief graphs during planning to enable effective action selection by capturing the underlying game dynamics. GATA is trained using a combination of reinforcement and self-supervised learning. Our work demonstrates that the learned graph-based representations help agents converge to better policies than their text-only counterparts and facilitate effective generalization across game configurations. Experiments on 500+ unique games from the TextWorld suite show that our best agent outperforms text-based baselines by an average of 24.2%.

paragraphs: Text-based games require an agent to interpret language and make decisions over time. Earlier work often supplied handcrafted structures or heuristics to support these abilities. This paper investigates whether an agent can instead learn graph-based representations directly from game text and use them to plan and generalize across different game configurations.

The proposed graph-aided transformer agent, GATA, infers a latent belief graph and updates it during planning. This graph represents learned information about the game’s underlying dynamics and helps guide action selection. Training combines reinforcement learning with self-supervised learning, allowing the structured representation and decision-making system to be learned together from raw text.

Experiments cover more than 500 distinct games in the TextWorld suite. The learned graphs help agents converge to better policies than text-only counterparts and support generalization between configurations. The best agent exceeds text-based baselines by an average of 24.2%. These results support learned, dynamically updated structure as a useful component of text-game agents, while human-level performance remains an open challenge in the abstract’s framing.
summary.tldr: GATA learns and updates belief graphs from raw game text, improving policies and generalization across hundreds of TextWorld games.

title: Learning Dynamic Belief Graphs to Generalize on Text-Based Games

abstract: We study the fundamental task of estimating the median of an underlying distribution from a finite number of samples, under pure differential privacy constraints. We focus on distributions satisfying the minimal assumption that they have a positive density at a small neighborhood around the median. In particular, the distribution is allowed to output unbounded values and is not required to have finite moments. We compute the exact, up-to-constant terms, statistical rate of estimation for the median by providing nearly-tight upper and lower bounds. Furthermore, we design a polynomial-time differentially private algorithm which provably achieves the optimal performance. At a technical level, our results leverage a Lipschitz Extension Lemma which allows us to design and analyze differentially private algorithms solely on appropriately defined ``typical" instances of the samples.

paragraphs: The paper asks how accurately a distribution's median can be estimated from finitely many samples while satisfying pure differential privacy. Its distributional assumption is local: the distribution has positive density in a small neighborhood around the median. Values may be unbounded, and finite moments are not required, allowing the analysis to cover distributions without restrictive tail conditions.

The authors establish the statistical estimation rate up to constant factors through nearly matching upper and lower bounds. The upper bound describes achievable accuracy, while the lower bound limits what any qualifying estimator can achieve. They also design a polynomial-time private algorithm with provably optimal performance, connecting the statistical result to an efficient computational procedure.

A Lipschitz Extension Lemma supplies the technical bridge. It lets the authors design and analyze the private algorithm on appropriately defined typical sample instances. This supports an estimator whose accuracy is governed by the stated behavior near the median, while the overall algorithm still satisfies the required pure differential privacy constraint.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time, purely differentially private median estimator achieves optimal accuracy rates under a local positive-density assumption, even with unbounded values and no finite moments.

title: Optimal Private Median Estimation under Minimal Distributional Assumptions

abstract: The actor-critic (AC) algorithm is a popular method to find an optimal policy in reinforcement learning. In the infinite horizon scenario, the finite-sample convergence rate for the AC and natural actor-critic (NAC) algorithms has been established recently, but under independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sampling and single-sample update at each iteration. In contrast, this paper characterizes the convergence rate and sample complexity of AC and NAC under Markovian sampling, with mini-batch data for each iteration, and with actor having general policy class approximation. We show that the overall sample complexity for a mini-batch AC to attain an $\epsilon$-accurate stationary point improves the best known sample complexity of AC by an order of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}\log(1/\epsilon))$, and the overall sample complexity for a mini-batch NAC to attain an $\epsilon$-accurate globally optimal point improves the existing sample complexity of NAC by an order of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}/\log(1/\epsilon))$. Moreover, the sample complexity of AC and NAC characterized in this work outperforms that of policy gradient (PG) and natural policy gradient (NPG) by a factor of $\mathcal{O}((1-\gamma)^{-3})$ and $\mathcal{O}((1-\gamma)^{-4}\epsilon^{-2}/\log(1/\epsilon))$, respectively. This is the first theoretical study establishing that AC and NAC attain orderwise performance improvement over PG and NPG under infinite horizon due to the incorporation of critic.
originalAbstract: The actor-critic (AC) algorithm is a popular method to find an optimal policy in reinforcement learning. In the infinite horizon scenario, the finite-sample convergence rate for the AC and natural actor-critic (NAC) algorithms has been established recently, but under independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sampling and single-sample update at each iteration. In contrast, this paper characterizes the convergence rate and sample complexity of AC and NAC under Markovian sampling, with mini-batch data for each iteration, and with actor having general policy class approximation. We show that the overall sample complexity for a mini-batch AC to attain an $\epsilon$-accurate stationary point improves the best known sample complexity of AC by an order of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}\log(1/\epsilon))$, and the overall sample complexity for a mini-batch NAC to attain an $\epsilon$-accurate globally optimal point improves the existing sample complexity of NAC by an order of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}/\log(1/\epsilon))$. Moreover, the sample complexity of AC and NAC characterized in this work outperforms that of policy gradient (PG) and natural policy gradient (NPG) by a factor of $\mathcal{O}((1-\gamma)^{-3})$ and $\mathcal{O}((1-\gamma)^{-4}\epsilon^{-2}/\log(1/\epsilon))$, respectively. This is the first theoretical study establishing that AC and NAC attain orderwise performance improvement over PG and NPG under infinite horizon due to the incorporation of critic.

paragraphs: Actor-critic methods combine a policy-learning actor with a critic that helps evaluate behavior. This paper studies how much sampled experience actor-critic and natural actor-critic algorithms need in infinite-horizon reinforcement learning. Earlier finite-sample analyses considered independent samples and one sample per update; this analysis instead handles Markovian sampling and minibatch updates.

Markovian sampling allows the dependence that arises when data are collected along an evolving process. The analysis also accommodates a general approximating policy class for the actor. It establishes improved sample complexity bounds for two distinct targets: an approximately stationary point for actor-critic and an approximately globally optimal point for natural actor-critic.

The bounds improve previously known results for both algorithms and also improve on corresponding policy gradient and natural policy gradient bounds. These are theoretical comparisons of required sample counts, with improvements depending on the accuracy target and discount factor. The stated significance is that the critic yields an orderwise advantage in the infinite-horizon analysis, giving a formal account of its benefit beyond changing the algorithm's structure.
summary.tldr: New finite-sample analyses show improved actor-critic guarantees with dependent sampling and minibatches, including theoretical advantages over policy gradient methods.

title: Improving Sample Complexity Bounds for (Natural) Actor-Critic Algorithms

abstract: Understanding of GAN training is still very limited. One major challenge is its non-convex-non-concave min-max objective, which may lead to sub-optimal local minima. In this work, we perform a global landscape analysis of the empirical loss of GANs. We prove that a class of separable-GAN, including the original JS-GAN, has exponentially many bad basins which are perceived as mode-collapse. We also study the relativistic pairing GAN (RpGAN) loss which couples the generated samples and the true samples. We prove that RpGAN has no bad basins. Experiments on synthetic data show that the predicted bad basin can indeed appear in training. We also perform experiments to support our theory that RpGAN has a better landscape than separable-GAN. For instance, we empirically show that RpGAN performs better than separable-GAN with relatively narrow neural nets. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/AilsaF/RS-GAN}.

paragraphs: GAN training involves a minimax objective with a difficult global shape, creating opportunities for optimization to reach poor solutions. This paper studies the empirical loss landscape to understand how the choice of objective contributes to that difficulty. It focuses on whether the landscape contains bad basins associated with mode collapse.

The authors prove that a class of separable GAN objectives, including the original JS-GAN, contains exponentially many such basins. They then analyze relativistic pairing GAN loss, which couples generated samples with real samples, and prove that it has no bad basins in their landscape analysis. This identifies a consequential structural difference between the objectives.

Synthetic experiments show that a predicted bad basin can occur during training. Further experiments support the proposed landscape advantage, including better performance for the pairing objective with relatively narrow neural networks. The theoretical and empirical findings together motivate changing the loss to improve training geometry. The absence of bad basins is the specific proved property, rather than a blanket claim that every aspect of GAN optimization is solved.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a bad-basin advantage for relativistic pairing GAN loss over a class of separable objectives and supports it experimentally.

title: Towards a Better Global Loss Landscape of GANs

abstract: Machine learning with missing data has been approached in many different ways, including feature imputation where missing feature values are estimated based on observed values and label prediction where downstream labels are learned directly from incomplete data. However, existing imputation models tend to have strong prior assumptions and cannot learn from downstream tasks, while models targeting label predictions often involve heuristics and can encounter scalability issues. Here we propose GRAPE, a framework for feature imputation as well as label prediction. GRAPE tackles the missing data problem using graph representation, where the observations and features are viewed as two types of nodes in a bipartite graph, and the observed feature values as edges. Under the GRAPE framework, the feature imputation is formulated as an edge-level prediction task and the label prediction as a node-level prediction task. These tasks are then solved with Graph Neural Networks. Experimental results on nine benchmark datasets show that GRAPE yields 20% lower mean absolute error for imputation tasks and 10% lower for label prediction tasks, compared with existing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: GRAPE addresses two related problems with incomplete data: estimating missing feature values and predicting labels from partially observed examples. Existing approaches often handle these separately, with imputation methods relying on strong prior assumptions and label-prediction methods using heuristics or facing scaling difficulties. The paper proposes a shared graph-based framework for both tasks.

It represents observations and features as two different kinds of nodes in a bipartite graph. An observed feature value becomes an edge connecting its observation to its feature. Under this representation, filling in a missing value becomes an edge-level prediction problem, while predicting an observation's label becomes a node-level prediction problem. Graph neural networks solve both types of prediction.

Across nine benchmark datasets, the authors report 20% lower mean absolute error for imputation and 10% lower error for label prediction compared with existing state-of-the-art methods. These results support organizing incomplete data around relationships between observations and features. The representation supplies a common learning structure for reconstructing missing entries and making downstream predictions.
summary.tldr: GRAPE turns incomplete data into a bipartite graph so graph neural networks can predict both missing values and labels.

title: Handling Missing Data with Graph Representation Learning

abstract: The softmax is the standard transformation used in machine learning to map real-valued vectors to categorical distributions. Unfortunately, this transform poses serious drawbacks for gradient descent (ascent) optimization. We reveal this difficulty by establishing two negative results: (1) optimizing any expectation with respect to the softmax must exhibit sensitivity to parameter initialization (``softmax gravity well''), and (2) optimizing log-probabilities under the softmax must exhibit slow convergence (``softmax damping''). Both findings are based on an analysis of convergence rates using the Non-uniform \L{}ojasiewicz (N\L{}) inequalities. To circumvent these shortcomings we investigate an alternative transformation, the \emph{escort} mapping, that demonstrates better optimization properties. The disadvantages of the softmax and the effectiveness of the escort transformation are further explained using the concept of N\L{} coefficient. In addition to proving bounds on convergence rates to firmly establish these results, we also provide experimental evidence for the superiority of the escort transformation.

paragraphs: Softmax converts a vector of real numbers into probabilities over categories. This paper examines how that transformation affects gradient-based optimization. The question is about the optimization behavior induced by the mapping itself: representing probabilities with softmax can create difficulties even before considering the rest of a learning system.

The authors establish two negative results. Optimizing an expectation through softmax must be sensitive to parameter initialization, a phenomenon they call the softmax gravity well. Their analysis uses non-uniform Łojasiewicz inequalities to derive convergence-rate bounds and explain these difficulties through the associated coefficient.

The paper then studies an alternative probability transformation called the escort mapping. It proves bounds establishing better optimization properties and supplies experimental evidence favoring the alternative. The findings make probability parameterization an explicit part of optimization design: the way numerical parameters become probabilities affects both sensitivity to starting values and the speed at which gradient-based updates make progress.
summary.tldr: The paper proves optimization drawbacks of softmax and investigates an escort mapping with better convergence properties.

title: Escaping the Gravitational Pull of Softmax

abstract: The lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) states that learning on a properly pruned network (the winning ticket) has improved test accuracy over the original unpruned network. Although LTH has been justified empirically in a broad range of deep neural network (DNN) involved applications like computer vision and natural language processing, the theoretical validation of the improved generalization of a winning ticket remains elusive. To the best of our knowledge, our work, for the first time, characterizes the performance of training a pruned neural network by analyzing the geometric structure of the objective function and the sample complexity to achieve zero generalization error. We show that the convex region near a desirable model with guaranteed generalization enlarges as the neural network model is pruned, indicating the structural importance of a winning ticket. Moreover, as the algorithm for training a pruned neural network is specified as an (accelerated) stochastic gradient descent algorithm, we theoretically show that the number of samples required for achieving zero generalization error is proportional to the number of the non-pruned weights in the hidden layer. With a fixed number of samples, training a pruned neural network enjoys a faster convergence rate to the desired model than training the original unpruned one, providing a formal justification of the improved generalization of the winning ticket. Our theoretical results are acquired from learning a pruned neural network of one hidden layer, while experimental results are further provided to justify the implications in pruning multi-layer neural networks.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis motivates studying why a properly pruned neural network can generalize better than its original dense version. This paper analyzes that question through the geometry of the training objective and the number of samples needed to reach zero generalization error. Its theoretical setting is a neural network with one hidden layer.

Within that setting, pruning enlarges the convex region around a desirable model with guaranteed generalization. For training by stochastic gradient descent or its accelerated form, the required sample count is proportional to the number of retained hidden-layer weights. These results connect the network’s sparse structure to both the surrounding optimization landscape and its data requirements.

With a fixed number of samples, the analysis also gives faster convergence to the desired model for the pruned network than for the original network. Experiments explore implications for pruning networks with multiple layers. The distinction in scope matters: the formal results concern the one-hidden-layer setting, while the deeper-network evidence is experimental. Together, they provide a theoretical explanation and broader empirical support for benefits associated with winning tickets.
summary.tldr: A one-hidden-layer analysis links pruning to favorable optimization geometry, lower sample requirements, and faster convergence.

title: Why Lottery Ticket Wins? A Theoretical Perspective of Sample Complexity on Sparse Neural Networks

abstract: In this paper, we evaluate the quality of knowledge representations encoded in deep neural networks (DNNs) for 3D point cloud processing. We propose a method to disentangle the overall model vulnerability into the sensitivity to the rotation, the translation, the scale, and local 3D structures. Besides, we also propose metrics to evaluate the spatial smoothness of encoding 3D structures, and the representation complexity of the DNN. Based on such analysis, experiments expose representation problems with classic DNNs, and explain the utility of the adversarial training. The code will be released when this paper is accepted.

paragraphs: This paper studies the quality of the internal representations learned by neural networks that process 3D point clouds. Its focus is on understanding what those representations encode and where they are vulnerable. The proposed analysis breaks an overall assessment into properties tied to different aspects of the input geometry.

The authors introduce a method that separates model vulnerability into sensitivity to rotation, translation, scale, and local 3D structures. This makes it possible to distinguish responses to changes in an object's overall placement or size from responses to its local geometry. They also propose metrics for the spatial smoothness of encoded 3D structures and the complexity of the network's representation.

Experiments using these analyses reveal representation problems in classic point-cloud networks and help explain the usefulness of adversarial training. The contribution is a set of diagnostic perspectives for examining representation quality. Together, the sensitivity breakdown and additional metrics connect observed vulnerability to more specific properties of how a network encodes three-dimensional information.
summary.tldr: The paper diagnoses 3D point-cloud representations by separating geometric sensitivities and measuring representation smoothness and complexity.

title: Interpreting Representation Quality of DNNs for 3D Point Cloud Processing

abstract: Recent advances in computationally efficient non-myopic Bayesian optimization offer improved query efficiency over traditional myopic methods like expected improvement, with only a modest increase in computational cost. These advances have been largely limited to unconstrained BO methods with only a few exceptions which require heavy computation. For instance, one existing multi-step lookahead constrained BO method (Lam & Willcox, 2017) relies on computationally expensive unreliable brute force derivative-free optimization of a Monte Carlo rollout acquisition function. Methods that use the reparameterization trick for more efficient derivative-based optimization of non-myopic acquisition functions in the unconstrained setting, like sample average approximation and infinitesimal perturbation analysis, do not extend: constraints introduce discontinuities in the sampled acquisition function surface. Moreover, we argue here that being non-myopic is even more important in constrained problems because fear of violating constraints pushes myopic methods away from sampling the boundary between feasible and infeasible regions, slowing the discovery of optimal solutions with tight constraints. In this paper, we propose a computationally efficient two-step lookahead constrained Bayesian optimization acquisition function (2-OPT-C) supporting both sequential and batch settings. To enable fast acquisition function optimization, we develop a novel likelihood ratio-based unbiased estimator of the gradient of the two-step optimal acquisition function that does not use the reparameterization trick. In numerical experiments, 2-OPT-C typically improves query efficiency by 2x or more over previous methods, and in some cases by 10x or more.

paragraphs: Constrained Bayesian optimization searches for good solutions while respecting feasibility requirements. A method focused only on immediate improvement may avoid the boundary between feasible and infeasible regions. The authors argue that this caution can delay discovery of excellent solutions near tight constraints, making planning beyond the next evaluation especially valuable.

Their method, 2-OPT-C, evaluates the value of looking two steps ahead and supports both sequential and batch queries. The computational challenge is that constraints create discontinuities in sampled acquisition functions. These discontinuities prevent efficient derivative techniques used for unconstrained lookahead optimization from carrying over directly to this setting.

The paper develops an unbiased gradient estimator based on likelihood ratios, enabling fast optimization without the reparameterization trick. This connects a longer planning horizon with a practical way to choose evaluations. In numerical experiments, the method typically improves query efficiency by at least a factor of two over previous methods, with improvements of tenfold or more in some cases. Those gains are reported experimental outcomes.
summary.tldr: An efficient two-step lookahead method improves constrained Bayesian optimization by accounting for future evaluations and estimating gradients despite constraint discontinuities.

title: Constrained Two-step Look-Ahead Bayesian Optimization

abstract: The process of manually searching for relevant instances in, and extracting information from, clinical databases underpin a multitude of clinical tasks. Such tasks include disease diagnosis, clinical trial recruitment, and continuing medical education. This manual search-and-extract process, however, has been hampered by the growth of large-scale clinical databases and the increased prevalence of unlabelled instances. To address this challenge, we propose a supervised contrastive learning framework, CROCS, where representations of cardiac signals associated with a set of patient-specific attributes (e.g., disease class, sex, age) are attracted to learnable embeddings entitled clinical prototypes. We exploit such prototypes for both the clustering and retrieval of unlabelled cardiac signals based on multiple patient attributes. We show that CROCS outperforms the state-of-the-art method, DTC, when clustering and also retrieves relevant cardiac signals from a large database. We also show that clinical prototypes adopt a semantically meaningful arrangement based on patient attributes and thus confer a high degree of interpretability.

paragraphs: Large clinical databases make finding relevant records increasingly difficult, especially when many instances lack labels. CROCS addresses this problem for cardiac signals by organizing them around patient attributes such as disease class, sex, and age. The intended capabilities are clustering signals and retrieving relevant examples using multiple attributes together.

The method uses supervised contrastive learning to bring signal representations toward learned embeddings called clinical prototypes. Each prototype is associated with a set of patient attributes. These learned reference points then support organizing and searching unlabeled cardiac signals, linking the representation space to clinically meaningful descriptions.

The authors report better clustering than DTC and demonstrate retrieval of relevant signals from a large database. They also find that the prototypes arrange themselves in ways that reflect patient attributes, supporting interpretation of the learned space. The contribution is therefore both a search-and-organization framework and a representation whose structure can be understood through the attributes used to train it.
summary.tldr: CROCS learns patient-attribute prototypes that support interpretable clustering and retrieval of unlabeled cardiac signals.

title: CROCS: Clustering and Retrieval of Cardiac Signals Based on Patient Disease Class, Sex, and Age

abstract: Bootstrapping has been a primary tool for ensemble and uncertainty quantification in machine learning and statistics. However, due to its nature of multiple training and resampling, bootstrapping deep neural networks is computationally burdensome; hence it has difficulties in practical application to the uncertainty estimation and related tasks. To overcome this computational bottleneck, we propose a novel approach called Neural Bootstrapper (NeuBoots), which learns to generate bootstrapped neural networks through single model training. NeuBoots injects the bootstrap weights into the high-level feature layers of the backbone network and outputs the bootstrapped predictions of the target, without additional parameters and the repetitive computations from scratch. We apply NeuBoots to various machine learning tasks related to uncertainty quantification, including prediction calibrations in image classification and semantic segmentation, active learning, and detection of out-of-distribution samples. Our empirical results show that NeuBoots outperforms other bagging based methods under a much lower computational cost without losing the validity of bootstrapping.

paragraphs: Bootstrapping uses variations of the training data to produce multiple fitted models, supporting ensembles and uncertainty estimation. With deep networks, repeatedly resampling and training models can be expensive. Neural Bootstrapper addresses this bottleneck by learning to generate bootstrapped predictions through a single model-training process, making the uncertainty workflow less computationally demanding.

The method, called NeuBoots, injects bootstrap weights into high-level feature layers of a backbone network. Those weights let the model output bootstrapped target predictions without adding parameters or repeatedly recomputing training from scratch. The design moves the variation needed for bootstrap predictions into the network’s feature processing rather than requiring separately trained networks for each variation.

The authors apply NeuBoots to prediction calibration in image classification and semantic segmentation, active learning, and out-of-distribution detection. Their empirical results show better performance than other bagging-based methods at substantially lower computational cost, while preserving the validity of bootstrapping. These findings support the method as a way to make bootstrap-based uncertainty tools more practical across several learning tasks.
summary.tldr: NeuBoots generates bootstrap predictions from one trained network, reducing computation while supporting effective uncertainty estimation.

title: Neural Bootstrapper

abstract: It is a commonly held belief that enforcing invariance improves generalisation. Although this approach enjoys widespread popularity, it is only very recently that a rigorous theoretical demonstration of this benefit has been established. In this work we build on the function space perspective of Elesedy and Zaidi [8] to derive a strictly non-zero generalisation benefit of incorporating invariance in kernel ridge regression when the target is invariant to the action of a compact group. We study invariance enforced by feature averaging and find that generalisation is governed by a notion of effective dimension that arises from the interplay between the kernel and the group. In building towards this result, we find that the action of the group induces an orthogonal decomposition of both the reproducing kernel Hilbert space and its kernel, which may be of interest in its own right.

paragraphs: Enforcing invariance means requiring a model to give the same result under specified transformations of its input. This paper provides a rigorous generalization benefit for doing so in kernel ridge regression. Its key condition is that the target function itself is invariant under the action of a compact group of transformations.

The authors study invariance imposed through feature averaging and derive a strictly nonzero benefit under their analyzed setting. They identify an effective dimension that governs generalization and depends jointly on the kernel and the transformation group. This ties the benefit to the interaction between the chosen representation and the symmetry being enforced.

The analysis also shows that the group action induces an orthogonal decomposition of both the reproducing kernel Hilbert space and its kernel. This supplies mathematical structure for understanding the effect of invariance on the learned function space. The contribution is a conditional theoretical justification for symmetry-aware kernel learning, with the target's invariance central to the stated result.
summary.tldr: For compact-group-invariant targets, the paper proves a strictly nonzero generalization benefit from enforcing invariance in kernel ridge regression.

title: Provably Strict Generalisation Benefit for Invariance in Kernel Methods

abstract: Predicting stable 3D conformations from 2D molecular graphs has been a long-standing challenge in computational chemistry. Recently, machine learning approaches have demonstrated very promising results compared to traditional experimental and physics-based simulation methods. These approaches mainly focus on modeling the local interactions between neighboring atoms on the molecular graphs and overlook the long-range interactions between non-bonded atoms. However, these non-bonded atoms may be proximal to each other in 3D space, and modeling their interactions is of crucial importance to accurately determine molecular conformations, especially for large molecules and multi-molecular complexes. In this paper, we propose a new approach called Dynamic Graph Score Matching (DGSM) for molecular conformation prediction, which models both the local and long-range interactions by dynamically constructing graph structures between atoms according to their spatial proximity during both training and inference. Specifically, the DGSM directly estimates the gradient fields of the logarithm density of atomic coordinates according to the dynamically constructed graphs using score matching methods. The whole framework can be efficiently trained in an end-to-end fashion. Experiments across multiple tasks show that the DGSM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by a large margin, and it is capable of generating conformations for a broader range of systems such as proteins and multi-molecular complexes.

paragraphs: Predicting a molecule's stable three-dimensional shape from its two-dimensional graph requires more than understanding bonded neighbors. Atoms far apart in the molecular graph can sit close together in space and interact. The paper argues that overlooking these non-bonded interactions is particularly consequential for large molecules and systems containing multiple molecules.

Dynamic Graph Score Matching, or DGSM, constructs graphs according to atoms' current spatial proximity during both training and inference. This lets the model represent local interactions and interactions between atoms that are distant along bonds. The key modeling change is to let spatial relationships shape the interaction graph as coordinates change, rather than relying only on fixed molecular connectivity.
summary.tldr: DGSM predicts molecular conformations using dynamically updated spatial graphs that capture both bonded and non-bonded atomic interactions.

title: Predicting Molecular Conformation via Dynamic Graph Score Matching

abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.
originalAbstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional object detection from point clouds often requires complex training and testing pipelines with substantial dataset-specific knowledge. Object DGCNN proposes an architecture that predicts a set of objects through message passing on a dynamic graph. It extends the DGCNN framework from its existing formulation to the task of object-set prediction.

The construction removes the need for post-processing through object-confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. These operations would otherwise be additional stages in producing the final detections. The paper therefore addresses the organization of the detection pipeline as well as the underlying prediction model, following the inspiration of suppression-free approaches to two-dimensional detection.

To help with sparse point clouds, the authors also introduce set-to-set knowledge distillation. Teacher and student outputs are aligned without depending on their ordering, matching the fact that detections form a set. The method achieves reported state-of-the-art performance on autonomous-driving benchmarks. Analyses of both detection and distillation accompany the results, supporting the proposed combination of direct object-set prediction and order-independent knowledge transfer.
summary.tldr: Object DGCNN predicts 3D object sets through dynamic graphs and uses order-independent distillation to support detection from sparse point clouds.

title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs

abstract: Model-based offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to find highly rewarding policy, by leveraging a previously collected static dataset and a dynamics model. While the dynamics model learned through reuse of the static dataset, its generalization ability hopefully promotes policy learning if properly utilized. To that end, several works propose to quantify the uncertainty of predicted dynamics, and explicitly apply it to penalize reward. However, as the dynamics and the reward are intrinsically different factors in context of MDP, characterizing the impact of dynamics uncertainty through reward penalty may incur unexpected tradeoff between model utilization and risk avoidance. In this work, we instead maintain a belief distribution over dynamics, and evaluate/optimize policy through biased sampling from the belief. The sampling procedure, biased towards pessimism, is derived based on an alternating Markov game formulation of offline RL. We formally show that the biased sampling naturally induces an updated dynamics belief with policy-dependent reweighting factor, termed Pessimism-Modulated Dynamics Belief. To improve policy, we devise an iterative regularized policy optimization algorithm for the game, with guarantee of monotonous improvement under certain condition. To make practical, we further devise an offline RL algorithm to approximately find the solution. Empirical results show that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Model-based offline reinforcement learning uses a fixed dataset to learn both environmental dynamics and a rewarding policy. Uncertainty in the learned dynamics creates a tension between exploiting the model and avoiding unreliable predictions. The paper argues that converting this uncertainty into reward penalties can produce unintended tradeoffs because rewards and dynamics play different roles.

The proposed approach maintains a distribution over possible dynamics and evaluates policies using samples biased toward pessimistic possibilities. The contribution places pessimism directly in how possible environmental dynamics are considered, with theory for the game and empirical support for the practical approximation.
summary.tldr: Pessimism-Modulated Dynamics Belief handles offline model uncertainty by biasing dynamics sampling, with conditional policy-improvement guarantees and strong benchmark results.

title: Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning with Pessimism-Modulated Dynamics Belief

abstract: Pre-training vision-language models with contrastive objectives has shown promising results that are both scalable to large uncurated datasets and transferable to many downstream applications. Some following works have targeted to improve data efficiency by adding self-supervision terms, but inter-domain (image-text) contrastive loss and intra-domain (image-image) contrastive loss are defined on individual spaces in those works, so many feasible combinations of supervision are overlooked. To overcome this issue, we propose UniCLIP, a Unified framework for Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training. UniCLIP integrates the contrastive loss of both inter-domain pairs and intra-domain pairs into a single universal space. The discrepancies that occur when integrating contrastive loss between different domains are resolved by the three key components of UniCLIP: (1) augmentation-aware feature embedding, (2) MP-NCE loss, and (3) domain dependent similarity measure. UniCLIP outperforms previous vision-language pre-training methods on various single- and multi-modality downstream tasks. In our experiments, we show that each component that comprises UniCLIP contributes well to the final performance.

paragraphs: Vision-language pretraining can learn from relationships between images and text, while additional self-supervision can exploit relationships among images. This paper argues that defining these contrastive objectives in separate spaces overlooks useful combinations of supervision. UniCLIP brings cross-domain and within-domain pairs into one universal contrastive space.

Combining these pair types creates discrepancies because their domains and relationships differ. UniCLIP addresses this with three components: augmentation-aware feature embeddings, an MP-NCE loss, and a domain-dependent similarity measure. Together, they support the shared training objective while accounting for distinctions among the kinds of pairs being compared.

The authors evaluate UniCLIP on downstream tasks involving a single modality as well as multiple modalities and report improvements over previous vision-language pretraining methods. Their experiments also show that each proposed component contributes to final performance. The findings support coordinating multiple sources of contrastive supervision within a common framework, with explicit mechanisms for their differences, as a useful way to improve the representations learned during pretraining.
summary.tldr: UniCLIP unifies image-text and within-domain contrastive supervision, improving performance on the evaluated downstream tasks.

title: UniCLIP: Unified Framework for Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training

abstract: We propose Okapi, a simple, efficient, and general method for robust semi-supervised learning based on online statistical matching. Our method uses a nearest-neighbours-based matching procedure to generate cross-domain views for a consistency loss, while eliminating statistical outliers. In order to perform the online matching in a runtime- and memory-efficient way, we draw upon the self-supervised literature and combine a memory bank with a slow-moving momentum encoder. The consistency loss is applied within the feature space, rather than on the predictive distribution, making the method agnostic to both the modality and the task in question. We experiment on the WILDS 2.0 datasets Sagawa et al., which significantly expands the range of modalities, applications, and shifts available for studying and benchmarking real-world unsupervised adaptation. Contrary to Sagawa et al., we show that it is in fact possible to leverage additional unlabelled data to improve upon empirical risk minimisation (ERM) results with the right method. Our method outperforms the baseline methods in terms of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalisation on the iWildCam (a multi-class classification task) and PovertyMap (a regression task) image datasets as well as the CivilComments (a binary classification task) text dataset. Furthermore, from a qualitative perspective, we show the matches obtained from the learned encoder are strongly semantically related. Code for our paper is publicly available at https://github.com/wearepal/okapi/.

paragraphs: Additional unlabeled data can help learning across domains only if the method uses it effectively. Okapi addresses this through online statistical matching. It finds neighboring examples across domains, removes statistical outliers, and uses the resulting pairs as different views whose learned features should agree.

The consistency objective operates on features rather than predicted outputs. This makes the method applicable across different input types and prediction tasks. A memory bank and a slowly updated momentum encoder support matching without excessive runtime or memory demands. Together, these components make cross-domain correspondence an ongoing part of training.

On WILDS 2.0 datasets, Okapi improves out-of-distribution generalization over the compared baselines for iWildCam image classification, PovertyMap image regression, and CivilComments text classification. The results also show that additional unlabeled data can improve on empirical risk minimization with this method. Qualitative inspection finds that learned matches are strongly related in meaning, supporting the idea that statistical matching can create useful consistency relationships across domains.
summary.tldr: Okapi matches examples across domains and aligns their features, improving out-of-distribution generalization using unlabeled data in the reported evaluations.

title: Okapi: Generalising Better by Making Statistical Matches Match

abstract: Variational Bayesian posterior inference often requires simplifying approximations such as mean-field parametrisation to ensure tractability. However, prior work has associated the variational mean-field approximation for Bayesian neural networks with underfitting in the case of small datasets or large model sizes. In this work, we show that invariances in the likelihood function of over-parametrised models contribute to this phenomenon because these invariances complicate the structure of the posterior by introducing discrete and/or continuous modes which cannot be well approximated by Gaussian mean-field distributions. In particular, we show that the mean-field approximation has an additional gap in the evidence lower bound compared to a purpose-built posterior that takes into account the known invariances. Importantly, this invariance gap is not constant; it vanishes as the approximation reverts to the prior. We proceed by first considering translation invariances in a linear model with a single data point in detail. We show that, while the true posterior can be constructed from a mean-field parametrisation, this is achieved only if the objective function takes into account the invariance gap. Then, we transfer our analysis of the linear model to neural networks. Our analysis provides a framework for future work to explore solutions to the invariance problem.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian inference often approximates a complicated posterior with a simpler distribution. Gaussian mean-field approximations make this tractable, but have been associated with underfitting in Bayesian neural networks with small datasets or large models. This paper identifies invariances in an overparameterized model's likelihood as one contributor to that behavior.

Likelihood invariances introduce discrete or continuous modes into the posterior that a Gaussian mean-field distribution cannot represent well. The authors show that this creates an additional gap in the evidence lower bound compared with a posterior designed to account for the invariances. Crucially, the gap changes with the approximation and disappears as it returns to the prior, connecting the objective's behavior to the underfitting phenomenon.

The analysis begins with translation invariance in a linear model containing one data point. There, the true posterior can be constructed from a mean-field parameterization, but only when the objective accounts for the invariance gap. The authors then extend their analysis to neural networks. The contribution is a framework for understanding this source of approximation error and investigating ways to address it.
summary.tldr: Likelihood invariances can worsen mean-field variational underfitting by creating a posterior approximation gap that vanishes as the approximation returns to the prior.

title: On the detrimental effect of invariances in the likelihood for variational inference

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection has recently gained substantial attention due to the importance of identifying out-of-domain samples in reliability and safety. Although OOD detection methods have advanced by a great deal, they are still susceptible to adversarial examples, which is a violation of their purpose. To mitigate this issue, several defenses have recently been proposed. Nevertheless, these efforts remained ineffective, as their evaluations are based on either small perturbation sizes, or weak attacks. In this work, we re-examine these defenses against an end-to-end PGD attack on in/out data with larger perturbation sizes, e.g. up to commonly used $\epsilon=8/255$ for the CIFAR-10 dataset. Surprisingly, almost all of these defenses perform worse than a random detection under the adversarial setting. Next, we aim to provide a robust OOD detection method. In an ideal defense, the training should expose the model to almost all possible adversarial perturbations, which can be achieved through adversarial training. That is, such training perturbations should based on both in- and out-of-distribution samples. Therefore, unlike OOD detection in the standard setting, access to OOD, as well as in-distribution, samples sounds necessary in the adversarial training setup. These tips lead us to adopt generative OOD detection methods, such as OpenGAN, as a baseline. We subsequently propose the Adversarially Trained Discriminator (ATD), which utilizes a pre-trained robust model to extract robust features, and a generator model to create OOD samples. We noted that, for the sake of training stability, in the adversarial training of the discriminator, one should attack real in-distribution as well as real outliers, but not generated outliers. Using ATD with CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as the in-distribution data, we could significantly outperform all previous methods in the robust AUROC while maintaining high standard AUROC and classification accuracy. The code repository is available at https://github.com/rohban-lab/ATD.

The findings show that ordinary detection performance can coexist with severe adversarial weakness, and support the proposed training choices in the evaluated settings. They do not establish that access to outliers is universally necessary.
summary.tldr: Stronger attacks expose weaknesses in evaluated OOD defenses, while ATD improves robust detection using robust features and adversarial discriminator training.

title: Your Out-of-Distribution Detection Method is Not Robust!

abstract: The logit outputs of a feedforward neural network at initialization are conditionally Gaussian, given a random covariance matrix defined by the penultimate layer. In this work, we study the distribution of this random matrix. Recent work has shown that shaping the activation function as network depth grows large is necessary for this covariance matrix to be non-degenerate. However, the current infinite-width-style understanding of this shaping method is unsatisfactory for large depth: infinite-width analyses ignore the microscopic fluctuations from layer to layer, but these fluctuations accumulate over many layers. To overcome this shortcoming, we study the random covariance matrix in the shaped infinite-depth-and-width limit. We identify the precise scaling of the activation function necessary to arrive at a non-trivial limit, and show that the random covariance matrix is governed by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) that we call the Neural Covariance SDE. Using simulations, we show that the SDE closely matches the distribution of the random covariance matrix of finite networks. Additionally, we recover an if-and-only-if condition for exploding and vanishing norms of large shaped networks based on the activation function.

This paper studies its distribution when both depth and width grow, focusing on activation shaping that prevents the covariance from becoming degenerate.

Analyses based on infinite width can overlook small random changes from one layer to the next. In very deep networks, those changes accumulate. The authors therefore study a joint infinite-depth-and-width limit and identify the precise activation scaling needed for a nontrivial limiting process. title: The Neural Covariance SDE: Shaped Infinite Depth-and-Width Networks at Initialization

abstract: Recently, Wong et al. (2020) showed that adversarial training with single-step FGSM leads to a characteristic failure mode named catastrophic overfitting (CO), in which a model becomes suddenly vulnerable to multi-step attacks. Experimentally they showed that simply adding a random perturbation prior to FGSM (RS-FGSM) could prevent CO. However, Andriushchenko & Flammarion (2020) observed that RS-FGSM still leads to CO for larger perturbations, and proposed a computationally expensive regularizer (GradAlign) to avoid it. In this work, we methodically revisit the role of noise and clipping in single-step adversarial training. Contrary to previous intuitions, we find that using a stronger noise around the clean sample combined with \textit{not clipping} is highly effective in avoiding CO for large perturbation radii. We then propose Noise-FGSM (N-FGSM) that, while providing the benefits of single-step adversarial training, does not suffer from CO. Empirical analyses on a large suite of experiments show that N-FGSM is able to match or surpass the performance of previous state of-the-art GradAlign while achieving 3$\times$ speed-up.

paragraphs: Single-step adversarial training is computationally attractive, but it can undergo catastrophic overfitting: a model suddenly becomes vulnerable to attacks that use multiple steps. Adding a random perturbation before the single-step attack can help, yet earlier work found that this approach still fails at larger perturbation sizes. A proposed regularizer addressed the failure at substantial computational cost.

This paper revisits two choices in the training procedure: how much noise to add around a clean sample and whether to clip it. The authors find that stronger noise combined with omitting clipping is highly effective at avoiding catastrophic overfitting for large perturbation radii. They build this finding into Noise-FGSM, or N-FGSM.

Across a broad experimental suite, N-FGSM avoids the reported failure while retaining the efficiency benefits of single-step training. It matches or exceeds the performance of GradAlign and runs three times faster in the reported comparisons. The findings show that the noise and clipping choices can materially change training stability, offering an empirically supported way to obtain robust training without the cost of that regularizer.
summary.tldr: Noise-FGSM combines stronger noise with no clipping to avoid catastrophic overfitting in experiments while accelerating adversarial training.

title: Make Some Noise: Reliable and Efficient Single-Step Adversarial Training

abstract: Continual learning on graph data, which aims to accommodate new tasks over newly emerged graph data while maintaining the model performance over existing tasks, is attracting increasing attention from the community. Unlike continual learning on Euclidean data ($\textit{e.g.}$, images, texts, etc.) that has established benchmarks and unified experimental settings, benchmark tasks are rare for Continual Graph Learning (CGL). Moreover, due to the variety of graph data and its complex topological structures, existing works adopt different protocols to configure datasets and experimental settings. This creates a great obstacle to compare different techniques and thus hinders the development of CGL. To this end, we systematically study the task configurations in different application scenarios and develop a comprehensive Continual Graph Learning Benchmark (CGLB) curated from different public datasets. Specifically, CGLB contains both node-level and graph-level continual graph learning tasks under task-incremental (currently widely adopted) and class-incremental (more practical, challenging, yet underexplored) settings, as well as a toolkit for training, evaluating, and visualizing different CGL methods. Within CGLB, we also systematically explain the difference among these task configurations by comparing them to classical continual learning settings. Finally, we comprehensively compare state-of-the-art baselines on CGLB to investigate their effectiveness. Given CGLB and the developed toolkit, the barrier to exploring CGL has been greatly lowered and researchers can focus more on the model development without worrying about tedious work on pre-processing of datasets or encountering unseen pitfalls. The benchmark and the toolkit are available through https://github.com/QueuQ/CGLB.

paragraphs: Continual graph learning asks models to learn new tasks from newly arriving graph data while retaining performance on earlier tasks. Comparing methods is difficult because graph datasets have varied structures, and existing studies configure tasks and evaluations differently. An apparent difference between methods can therefore be entangled with differences in experimental setup.

CGLB organizes this area into a common benchmark assembled from public datasets. It includes tasks that make predictions about individual nodes and tasks that make predictions about whole graphs. Both are considered under task-incremental and class-incremental settings. The authors describe class-incremental learning as more practical and challenging, while also being less explored in existing work.

The accompanying toolkit supports training, evaluation, and visualization, reducing the repeated work needed to prepare experiments. The paper also explains how its task configurations differ from one another and relate to classical continual learning settings, then compares leading baselines within this framework. Its central contribution is a shared experimental foundation that makes method comparisons easier to interpret and lets researchers spend more effort on models.
summary.tldr: CGLB standardizes continual graph learning tasks and provides tools for comparing methods across multiple experimental settings.

title: CGLB: Benchmark Tasks for Continual Graph Learning

abstract: We generalise the problem of reward modelling (RM) for reinforcement learning (RL) to handle non-Markovian rewards. Existing work assumes that human evaluators observe each step in a trajectory independently when providing feedback on agent behaviour. In this work, we remove this assumption, extending RM to capture temporal dependencies in human assessment of trajectories. We show how RM can be approached as a multiple instance learning (MIL) problem, where trajectories are treated as bags with return labels, and steps within the trajectories are instances with unseen reward labels. We go on to develop new MIL models that are able to capture the time dependencies in labelled trajectories. We demonstrate on a range of RL tasks that our novel MIL models can reconstruct reward functions to a high level of accuracy, and can be used to train high-performing agent policies.

We show how RM can be approached as a multiple instance learning (MIL) problem, where trajectories are treated as bags with return labels, and steps within the trajectories are instances with unseen reward labels. We go on to develop new MIL models that are able to capture the time dependencies in labelled trajectories. We demonstrate on a range of RL tasks that our novel MIL models can reconstruct reward functions to a high level of accuracy, and can be used to train high-performing agent policies.

paragraphs: Human judgments of an agent's behavior can depend on how events unfold over time. This paper extends reward modelling to account for such temporal dependencies. It removes an assumption attributed to existing work: that evaluators assess each step of a trajectory independently when providing feedback about the agent's behavior.

The authors formulate reward modelling as multiple instance learning. A complete trajectory is treated as a collection with an observed return label, while its individual steps have reward labels that are not observed. They develop models that capture time dependencies within these labeled trajectories. The approach connects an assessment of the whole sequence to the problem of learning rewards within it.

Across a range of reinforcement-learning tasks, the proposed models reconstruct reward functions with high reported accuracy and support training high-performing policies. These results indicate that trajectory-level labels can support learning temporally dependent rewards in the evaluated settings. The central contribution is broadening reward modelling to accommodate how earlier events can matter when interpreting later behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper learns temporally dependent rewards from whole-trajectory labels using multiple instance learning.

title: Non-Markovian Reward Modelling from Trajectory Labels via Interpretable Multiple Instance Learning

abstract: Learning representations of neural network weights given a model zoo is an emerg- ing and challenging area with many potential applications from model inspection, to neural architecture search or knowledge distillation. Recently, an autoencoder trained on a model zoo was able to learn a hyper-representation, which captures intrinsic and extrinsic properties of the models in the zoo. In this work, we ex- tend hyper-representations for generative use to sample new model weights. We propose layer-wise loss normalization which we demonstrate is key to generate high-performing models and several sampling methods based on the topology of hyper-representations. The models generated using our methods are diverse, per- formant and capable to outperform strong baselines as evaluated on several down- stream tasks: initialization, ensemble sampling and transfer learning. Our results indicate the potential of knowledge aggregation from model zoos to new models via hyper-representations thereby paving the avenue for novel research directions.

This paper extends that idea from representing existing models to generating new sets of weights.

The authors introduce layer-wise loss normalization, which they demonstrate is important for producing high-performing models. They also develop several sampling methods that use the topology of the learned hyper-representation. The aim is to draw useful new models from the structure learned across the collection, turning a representation of network weights into a generative resource.

The generated networks are evaluated for initialization, ensemble sampling, and transfer learning. Across these downstream tasks, the authors report diverse, capable models that can outperform strong baselines. The results suggest that information distributed across a model zoo can be aggregated into new networks through hyper-representations. This is evidence for the generative potential of learned weight spaces, rather than only their usefulness for inspecting existing models.
summary.tldr: Learned representations of model collections can generate diverse new network weights useful for initialization, ensembles, and transfer learning.

title: Hyper-Representations as Generative Models: Sampling Unseen Neural Network Weights

abstract: As language models grow ever larger, the need for large-scale high-quality text datasets has never been more pressing, especially in multilingual settings. The BigScience workshop, a 1-year international and multidisciplinary initiative, was formed with the goal of researching and training large language models as a values-driven undertaking, putting issues of ethics, harm, and governance in the foreground. This paper documents the data creation and curation efforts undertaken by BigScience to assemble the Responsible Open-science Open-collaboration Text Sources (ROOTS) corpus, a 1.6TB dataset spanning 59 languages that was used to train the 176-billion-parameter BigScience Large Open-science Open-access Multilingual (BLOOM) language model. We further release a large initial subset of the corpus and analyses thereof, and hope to empower large-scale monolingual and multilingual modeling projects with both the data and the processing tools, as well as stimulate research around this large multilingual corpus.

paragraphs: ROOTS is a large multilingual text corpus assembled through the BigScience collaboration. This paper documents the creation and curation work behind that resource, responding to the need for large, high-quality datasets as language models grow. The project frames data collection within a broader research effort that foregrounds ethics, potential harms, and governance.

The corpus contains 1.6 terabytes of text spanning 59 languages and was used to train BLOOM, a language model with 176 billion parameters. These figures establish both the scale of the data effort and its use in a concrete multilingual modeling project. The paper's focus is the dataset and the work required to assemble it.

The authors release a large initial subset of ROOTS together with analyses and provide processing tools intended to help other projects. They hope these resources support large-scale modeling in individual languages and across languages, as well as further study of the corpus itself. The contribution combines a substantial training-data resource with documentation and tools for subsequent research.
summary.tldr: ROOTS documents the curation of a 1.6-terabyte, 59-language corpus used to train BLOOM and releases an initial subset with supporting resources.

title: The BigScience ROOTS Corpus: A 1.6TB Composite Multilingual Dataset

abstract: Optimizing strategic decisions (a.k.a. computing equilibrium) is key to the success of many non-cooperative multi-agent applications. However, in many real-world situations, we may face the exact opposite of this game-theoretic problem --- instead of prescribing equilibrium of a given game, we may directly observe the agents' equilibrium behaviors but want to infer the underlying parameters of an unknown game. This research question, also known as inverse game theory, has been studied in multiple recent works in the context of Stackelberg games. Unfortunately, existing works exhibit quite negative results, showing statistical hardness and computational hardness, assuming follower's perfectly rational behaviors. Our work relaxes the perfect rationality agent assumption to the classic quantal response model, a more realistic behavior model of bounded rationality. Interestingly, we show that the smooth property brought by such bounded rationality model actually leads to provably more efficient learning of the follower utility parameters in general Stackelberg games. Systematic empirical experiments on synthesized games confirm our theoretical results and further suggest its robustness beyond the strict quantal response model.

paragraphs: Inverse game theory starts with observed strategic behavior and asks what underlying preferences could have produced it. This paper studies that question for Stackelberg games, which involve a leader and a follower. Earlier results found statistical and computational difficulties when the follower was assumed to behave with perfect rationality.

The authors replace perfect rationality with the classic quantal response model of bounded rationality. Under this model, the follower's behavior has a smooth dependence on utility. The paper shows that this smoothness makes the follower's utility parameters provably more efficient to learn in general Stackelberg games. A less idealized behavioral assumption therefore makes this inference problem more tractable.

Experiments on synthesized games confirm the theoretical results and suggest robustness even when behavior does not strictly follow the quantal response model. Those two conclusions have different strengths: efficient learning is proved under the modeled behavior, while performance beyond that model is supported empirically. The central finding is that bounded rationality can supply useful structure for recovering preferences from strategic observations.
summary.tldr: Modeling followers with quantal-response bounded rationality makes their utility parameters provably easier to learn in Stackelberg games.

title: Inverse Game Theory for Stackelberg Games: the Blessing of Bounded Rationality

abstract: Semantic segmentation is a practical and active task, but severely suffers from the expensive cost of pixel-level labels when extending to more classes in wider applications. To this end, we focus on the problem named weak-shot semantic segmentation, where the novel classes are learnt from cheaper image-level labels with the support of base classes having off-the-shelf pixel-level labels. To tackle this problem, we propose a dual similarity transfer framework, which is built upon MaskFormer to disentangle the semantic segmentation task into single-label classification and binary segmentation for each proposal. Specifically, the binary segmentation sub-task allows proposal-pixel similarity transfer from base classes to novel classes, which enables the mask learning of novel classes. We also learn pixel-pixel similarity from base classes and distill such class-agnostic semantic similarity to the semantic masks of novel classes, which regularizes the segmentation model with pixel-level semantic relationship across images. In addition, we propose a complementary loss to facilitate the learning of novel classes. Comprehensive experiments on the challenging COCO-Stuff-10K and ADE20K datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation needs labels for individual pixels, which makes adding new classes expensive. This paper studies a setting where existing classes have pixel-level annotations, while new classes have only image-level labels. Its goal is to transfer useful segmentation knowledge from the richly annotated classes so the new classes can be learned with cheaper supervision.

The framework builds on MaskFormer and separates each proposal into a single-label classification problem and a binary segmentation problem. It transfers two kinds of similarity. Proposal-to-pixel similarity supports learning masks for new classes, while pixel-to-pixel similarity learned from existing classes supplies class-independent semantic relationships across images.

Those pixel relationships are distilled into the new classes' masks to regularize segmentation learning. A complementary loss further supports learning the new classes. Experiments on COCO-Stuff-10K and ADE20K demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The approach matters because it transfers information about spatial and semantic relationships, allowing detailed annotations from existing categories to support mask learning for categories that have only image-level supervision.
summary.tldr: Transferring proposal-to-pixel and pixel-to-pixel similarities helps learn segmentation masks for new classes with only image-level labels.

title: Weak-shot Semantic Segmentation via Dual Similarity Transfer

abstract: Standard few-shot benchmarks are often built upon simplifying assumptions on the query sets, which may not always hold in practice. In particular, for each task at testing time, the classes effectively present in the unlabeled query set are known a priori, and correspond exactly to the set of classes represented in the labeled support set. We relax these assumptions and extend current benchmarks, so that the query-set classes of a given task are unknown, but just belong to a much larger set of possible classes. Our setting could be viewed as an instance of the challenging yet practical problem of extremely imbalanced $K$-way classification, $K$ being much larger than the values typically used in standard benchmarks, and with potentially irrelevant supervision from the support set. Expectedly, our setting incurs drops in the performances of state-of-the-art methods. Motivated by these observations, we introduce a \textbf{P}rim\textbf{A}l \textbf{D}ual Minimum \textbf{D}escription \textbf{LE}ngth (\textbf{PADDLE}) formulation, which balances data-fitting accuracy and model complexity for a given few-shot task, under supervision constraints from the support set. Our constrained MDL-like objective promotes competition among a large set of possible classes, preserving only effective classes that befit better the data of a few-shot task. It is hyper-parameter free, and could be applied on top of any base-class training. Furthermore, we derive a fast block coordinate descent algorithm for optimizing our objective, with convergence guarantee, and a linear computational complexity at each iteration. Comprehensive experiments over the standard few-shot datasets and the more realistic and challenging \textit{i-Nat} dataset show highly competitive performances of our method, more so when the numbers of possible classes in the tasks increase. Our code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/SegoleneMartin/PADDLE}.
