paragraphs: Few-shot benchmarks often assume that the classes in an unlabeled query set are known and exactly match those in the labeled support set. This paper relaxes that assumption: query examples come from an unknown subset of a much larger pool of possible classes. Some support-set supervision can therefore concern classes absent from the query set.

The authors show that this setting reduces the performance of existing methods and propose PADDLE to address it. Its minimum-description-length-style objective balances how well the model fits the data against model complexity, while respecting support-set supervision. Competition among candidate classes favors retaining those that best explain the current task's data.

The formulation is hyperparameter-free and can be placed on top of any base-class training. The authors provide a block coordinate descent optimizer with a convergence guarantee and linear complexity per iteration. Experiments on standard few-shot datasets and i-Nat show highly competitive performance, particularly as the number of possible classes grows. The contribution links a more demanding evaluation setting to an inference method that explicitly selects effective classes.
summary.tldr: PADDLE improves few-shot inference when query classes are an unknown subset of many candidates by balancing fit and model complexity.

title: Towards Practical Few-shot Query Sets: Transductive Minimum Description Length Inference

abstract: While numerous effective decentralized algorithms have been proposed with theoretical guarantees and empirical successes, the performance limits in decentralized optimization, especially the influence of network topology and its associated weight matrix on the optimal convergence rate, have not been fully understood. While Lu and Sa have recently provided an optimal rate for non-convex stochastic decentralized optimization using weight matrices associated with linear graphs, the optimal rate with general weight matrices remains unclear. This paper revisits non-convex stochastic decentralized optimization and establishes an optimal convergence rate with general weight matrices. In addition, we also establish the first optimal rate when non-convex loss functions further satisfy the Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition. Following existing lines of analysis in literature cannot achieve these results. Instead, we leverage the Ring-Lattice graph to admit general weight matrices while maintaining the optimal relation between the graph diameter and weight matrix connectivity. Lastly, we develop a new decentralized algorithm to attain the above two optimal rates up to logarithm factors.

paragraphs: In decentralized optimization, the communication network and its associated weight matrix influence how quickly distributed learning can converge. Existing results had established an optimal rate for certain linear-graph weight matrices, leaving the general case unclear. This paper establishes optimal convergence rates for smooth, nonconvex stochastic decentralized optimization with general weight matrices.

The authors also analyze losses satisfying the additional Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition and establish an optimal rate for that setting. The extra condition defines a distinct case within the analysis; its result should therefore be read separately from the broader nonconvex result. Both address the performance limits imposed by decentralized communication.

The proof approach uses a Ring-Lattice graph to accommodate general weight matrices while preserving the needed relationship between graph diameter and matrix connectivity. The authors explain that existing lines of analysis do not obtain these results. They then develop a decentralized algorithm attaining both optimal rates up to logarithmic factors, connecting the theoretical limits to an algorithm that nearly reaches them.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal decentralized nonconvex convergence rates for general weight matrices and an algorithm achieving them up to logarithmic factors.

title: Revisiting Optimal Convergence Rate for Smooth and Non-convex Stochastic Decentralized Optimization

abstract: There has been significant recent progress designing deep generative models that generate realistic sequence data such as text or music. Nevertheless, it remains difficult to incorporate high-level structure to guide the generative process, and many such models perform well on local coherence, but less so on global coherence. We propose a novel approach for incorporating global structure in the form of relational constraints between different subcomponents of an example (e.g., lines of a poem or measures of music). Our generative model has two parts: (i) one model to generate a realistic set of relational constraints, and (ii) a second model to generate realistic data satisfying these constraints. For model (i), we propose a constrained optimization algorithm that infers the relational constraints present in the training data, and then learn a generative model based on the resulting constraint data. In our experiments, we show that our approach significantly improves over state-of-the-art in terms of capturing high-level structure in the data, while performing comparably or better in terms of low-level structure. We also show that using constrained optimization for part (ii) as well leads to increased controllability with little decrease in quality compared to pure learning-based models.

paragraphs: A generated sequence can sound plausible locally while lacking a coherent overall structure. This paper addresses that problem by representing high-level organization through relationships between components, such as lines of a poem or measures of music. These relational constraints give the generation process an explicit description of how different parts should fit together.

The approach separates generation into two models. The first produces a realistic collection of relational constraints, and the second produces realistic sequence data that satisfies them. To train the first model, a constrained optimization procedure infers relationships present in training examples, creating constraint data from which the model can learn.

Experiments report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods in capturing high-level structure, while matching or improving low-level structure. The authors also explore using constrained optimization in the second stage. That version provides greater control over generation with only a small reduction in quality compared with purely learned models. The results show how explicitly modeling relationships between sequence components can improve global organization without sacrificing the local quality that generative models already handle well.
summary.tldr: Generating relational constraints before sequence content improves global structure and offers greater control over generated sequences.

title: Neurosymbolic Deep Generative Models for Sequence Data with Relational Constraints

abstract: Several existing works study either adversarial or natural distributional robustness of deep neural networks separately. In practice, however, models need to enjoy both types of robustness to ensure reliability. In this work, we bridge this gap and show that in fact, {\it explicit tradeoffs} exist between adversarial and natural distributional robustness. We first consider a simple linear regression setting on Gaussian data with disjoint sets of \emph{core} and \emph{spurious} features. In this setting, through theoretical and empirical analysis, we show that (i) adversarial training with $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ norms increases the model reliance on spurious features; (ii) For $\ell_\infty$ adversarial training, spurious reliance only occurs when the scale of the spurious features is larger than that of the core features; (iii) adversarial training can have {\it an unintended consequence} in reducing distributional robustness, specifically when spurious correlations are changed in the new test domain. Next, we present extensive empirical evidence, using a test suite of twenty adversarially trained models evaluated on five benchmark datasets (ObjectNet, RIVAL10, Salient ImageNet-1M, ImageNet-9, Waterbirds), that adversarially trained classifiers rely on backgrounds more than their standardly trained counterparts, validating our theoretical results. We also show that spurious correlations in training data (when preserved in the test domain) can {\it improve} adversarial robustness, revealing that previous claims that adversarial vulnerability is rooted in spurious correlations are incomplete.

It shows that these forms of robustness can conflict. The theoretical analysis starts with linear regression on Gaussian data, separating core features from spurious features whose training correlations may change in a new domain.

Within that setting, adversarial training using ℓ1 or ℓ2 norms increases reliance on spurious features. The authors also show that spurious correlations can improve adversarial robustness when those correlations persist at test time. The findings challenge a simple association between spurious features and adversarial vulnerability, showing why the type of robustness and the behavior of correlations both matter.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments show that adversarial training can increase spurious-feature reliance and weaken robustness when those correlations change.

title: Explicit Tradeoffs between Adversarial and Natural Distributional Robustness

abstract: Pre-training has achieved remarkable success when transferred to downstream tasks. In machine learning, we care about not only the good performance of a model but also its behavior under reasonable shifts of condition. The same philosophy holds when pre-training a foundation model. However, the foundation model may not uniformly behave well for a series of related downstream tasks. This happens, for example, when conducting mask recovery regression where the recovery ability or the training instances diverge like pattern features are extracted dominantly on pre-training, but semantic features are also required on a downstream task. This paper considers pre-training a model that guarantees a uniformly good performance over the downstream tasks. We call this goal as *downstream-task robustness*.Our method first separates the upstream task into several representative ones and applies a simple minimax loss for pre-training. We then design an efficient algorithm to solve the minimax lossand prove its convergence in the convex setting. In the experiments, we show both on large-scale natural language processing and computer vision datasets our method increases the metrics on worse-case downstream tasks. Additionally, some theoretical explanations for why our loss is beneficial are provided. Specifically, we show fewer samples are inherently required for the most challenging downstream task in some cases.

paragraphs: A pretrained model can transfer well overall while leaving some related downstream tasks poorly served. The paper studies downstream-task robustness: the goal of supporting consistently good adaptation across those tasks. Its motivating concern is that pretraining may emphasize one kind of feature even though another task requires different information.

The method divides the upstream task into several representative tasks and applies a minimax pretraining loss. This objective focuses on the most challenging represented task instead of relying only on aggregate performance. The authors develop an efficient optimization algorithm and prove convergence in the convex setting, giving a specific theoretical foundation for solving the proposed loss.

Experiments on large-scale language and vision datasets show improved metrics for worst-case downstream tasks. The theory also explains benefits of the objective, including cases where the most challenging downstream task inherently requires fewer samples. These findings support pretraining with difficult future adaptations in mind. The convergence guarantee is explicitly convex, and the sample-requirement improvement is established for some cases rather than all downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: Minimax pretraining over representative tasks improves worst-case downstream results, with convex convergence guarantees and sample-efficiency benefits in some cases.

title: Task-Robust Pre-Training for Worst-Case Downstream Adaptation

abstract: Formally verifying deep reinforcement learning (DRL) systems suffers from both inaccurate verification results and limited scalability. The major obstacle lies in the large overestimation introduced inherently during training and then transforming the inexplicable decision-making models, i.e., deep neural networks (DNNs), into easy-to-verify models. In this paper, we propose an inverse transform-then-train approach, which first encodes a DNN into an equivalent set of efficiently and tightly verifiable linear control policies and then optimizes them via reinforcement learning. We accompany our inverse approach with a novel neural network model called piece-wise linear decision neural networks (PLDNNs), which are compatible with most existing DRL training algorithms with comparable performance against conventional DNNs. Our extensive experiments show that, compared to DNN-based DRL systems, PLDNN-based systems can be more efficiently and tightly verified with up to $438$ times speedup and a significant reduction in overestimation. In particular, even a complex $12$-dimensional DRL system is efficiently verified with up to 7 times deeper computation steps.

paragraphs: Formal verification of deep reinforcement learning systems can become expensive and overly conservative. The paper attributes a major part of this difficulty to overestimation introduced during training and when converting a neural decision model into a form suitable for verification. Such overestimation makes the verification calculation less tightly reflect the system being analyzed.

The proposed approach reverses the usual order: it first encodes a neural network as an equivalent collection of linear control policies that can be verified efficiently and tightly, then optimizes them through reinforcement learning. Piece-wise linear decision neural networks, or PLDNNs, provide the model structure for this approach. They are compatible with most existing deep reinforcement learning training algorithms.

Experiments report task performance comparable to conventional neural networks, alongside verification speedups of up to 438 times and substantially reduced overestimation. The authors also verify a 12-dimensional system with up to seven times deeper computation steps. These results support designing verifiability into the policy representation before training, with the reported gains applying to the evaluated systems.
summary.tldr: PLDNNs structure reinforcement learning policies for verification before training, enabling tighter checks and reported speedups of up to 438 times.

title: Boosting Verification of Deep Reinforcement Learning via Piece-Wise Linear Decision Neural Networks

abstract: Expressing universal semantics common to all languages is helpful to understand the meanings of complex and culture-specific sentences. The research theme underlying this scenario focuses on learning universal representations across languages with the usage of massive parallel corpora. However, due to the sparsity and scarcity of parallel data, there is still a big challenge in learning authentic ``universals'' for any two languages. In this paper, we propose Emma-X: an EM-like Multilingual pre-training Algorithm, to learn Cross-lingual universals with the aid of excessive multilingual non-parallel data. Emma-X unifies the cross-lingual representation learning task and an extra semantic relation prediction task within an EM framework. Both the extra semantic classifier and the cross-lingual sentence encoder approximate the semantic relation of two sentences, and supervise each other until convergence. To evaluate Emma-X, we conduct experiments on xrete, a newly introduced benchmark containing 12 widely studied cross-lingual tasks that fully depend on sentence-level representations. Results reveal that Emma-X achieves state-of-the-art performance. Further geometric analysis of the built representation space with three requirements demonstrates the superiority of Emma-X over advanced models.

paragraphs: Learning sentence representations that express shared meaning across languages usually benefits from parallel corpora: collections of corresponding text in different languages. Such data can be scarce or unevenly available. EMMA-X aims to learn cross-lingual representations with the help of abundant multilingual text that does not come in parallel pairs.

The method combines sentence representation learning with an additional task that predicts semantic relationships between sentences. It places a sentence encoder and a semantic relation classifier within an expectation-maximization-like framework. Both components approximate the semantic relationship of a sentence pair, and their predictions provide supervision for each other until convergence. This makes the relation task part of the representation-learning process.

The authors evaluate EMMA-X on xrete, a newly introduced benchmark containing 12 cross-lingual tasks that depend on sentence-level representations, and report state-of-the-art performance. A geometric analysis using three requirements also favors its representation space over advanced comparison models. The evidence supports the usefulness of mutual supervision for learning shared meaning from multilingual nonparallel data.
summary.tldr: EMMA-X uses mutually supervising sentence and semantic-relation models to learn cross-lingual representations from multilingual nonparallel data.

title: EMMA-X: An EM-like Multilingual Pre-training Algorithm for Cross-lingual Representation Learning

abstract: In the task of semi-supervised video object segmentation, the input is the binary mask of an object in the first frame, and the desired output consists of the corresponding masks of that object in the subsequent frames. Existing leading solutions have two main drawbacks: 1) an expensive and typically-supervised training on videos; 2) a large memory footprint during inference. Here we present a training-free solution, with a low-memory footprint, that yields state-of-the-art results. The proposed method combines pre-trained deep learning-based features (trained on still images) with more classical methods for streaming-data clustering. Designed to adapt to temporal concept drifts and generalize to diverse video content without relying on annotated images or videos, the method eliminates the need for additional training or fine-tuning, ensuring fast inference and immediate applicability to new videos. Concretely, we represent an object via a dynamic ensemble of temporally- and spatially-coherent mixtures over a representation built from pre-trained ViT features and positional embeddings. A convolutional conditional random field further improves spatial coherence and helps reject outliers. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method on key benchmarks: the DAVIS-2017 and YouTube-VOS 2018 validation datasets. Moreover, by the virtue of the low-memory footprint of the compact cluster-based representation, the method scales gracefully to high-resolution ViT features. Our code is available at https://github.com/BGU-CS-VIL/Training-Free-VOS

paragraphs: The task begins with an object's binary mask in the first video frame and asks for its mask in later frames. Leading approaches typically require expensive video training and substantial memory during inference. This paper combines features from a vision transformer pretrained on still images with streaming-data clustering, avoiding additional training or fine-tuning for video segmentation.

The object is represented by a changing ensemble of mixture models over visual features and positional embeddings. These models maintain spatial and temporal coherence while adapting as video content changes. A convolutional conditional random field further encourages coherent regions and helps reject outliers, refining the masks produced from the representation.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on the DAVIS-2017 and YouTube-VOS 2018 validation datasets. Compact cluster representations keep memory use low and allow the method to scale to high-resolution transformer features. Here, training-free means using the pretrained features directly without further training; the method still receives the first-frame object mask specified by the task. Its contribution is efficient adaptation to a new video's evolving content.
summary.tldr: Pretrained image features and streaming mixture models enable low-memory video object segmentation without additional training or fine-tuning.

title: From ViT Features to Training-free Video Object Segmentation via Streaming-data Mixture Models

abstract: The Maximum Entropy (Max-Ent) framework has been effectively employed in a variety of Reinforcement Learning (RL) tasks. In this paper, we first propose a novel Max-Ent framework for policy evaluation in a distributional RL setting, named *Distributional Maximum Entropy Policy Evaluation* (D-Max-Ent PE). We derive a generalization-error bound that depends on the complexity of the representation employed, showing that this framework can explicitly take into account the features used to represent the state space while evaluating a policy. Then, we exploit these favorable properties to drive the representation learning of the state space in a Structural Risk Minimization fashion. We employ state-aggregation functions as feature functions and we specialize the D-Max-Ent approach into an algorithm, named *D-Max-Ent Progressive Factorization*, which constructs a progressively finer-grained representation of the state space by balancing the trade-off between preserving information (bias) and reducing the effective number of states, i.e., the complexity of the representation space (variance). Finally, we report the results of some illustrative numerical simulations, showing that the proposed algorithm matches the expected theoretical behavior and highlighting the relationship between aggregations and sample regimes.

paragraphs: Evaluating a reinforcement learning policy depends partly on how the environment’s states are represented. A detailed representation preserves distinctions, but its complexity can make estimation harder with limited data. This paper introduces Distributional Maximum Entropy Policy Evaluation, a framework that makes representation complexity an explicit part of policy evaluation.

The authors derive a generalization-error bound that depends on the complexity of the state representation. They then use this relationship to guide representation learning through structural risk minimization. Their concrete algorithm, D-Max-Ent Progressive Factorization, represents states through aggregation functions and gradually refines the resulting groups.

The refinement balances two competing effects. Keeping more distinctions preserves information and reduces bias, while combining states reduces the effective number of states and can reduce variance. This gives the algorithm a principled reason to choose a particular level of detail. Illustrative numerical simulations follow the expected theoretical behavior and show how useful aggregation depends on the available sample regime. The stated evidence supports this relationship between representation granularity and data availability.
summary.tldr: A maximum entropy framework guides policy evaluation toward state representations that balance information preservation and estimation complexity.

title: Distributional Policy Evaluation: a Maximum Entropy approach to Representation Learning

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become increasingly popular for classification tasks on graph-structured data. Yet, the interplay between graph topology and feature evolution in GNNs is not well understood. In this paper, we focus on node-wise classification, illustrated with community detection on stochastic block model graphs, and explore the feature evolution through the lens of the "Neural Collapse" (NC) phenomenon. When training instance-wise deep classifiers (e.g. for image classification) beyond the zero training error point, NC demonstrates a reduction in the deepest features' within-class variability and an increased alignment of their class means to certain symmetric structures. We start with an empirical study that shows that a decrease in within-class variability is also prevalent in the node-wise classification setting, however, not to the extent observed in the instance-wise case. Then, we theoretically study this distinction. Specifically, we show that even an "optimistic" mathematical model requires that the graphs obey a strict structural condition in order to possess a minimizer with exact collapse. Furthermore, by studying the gradient dynamics of this model, we provide reasoning for the partial collapse observed empirically. Finally, we present a study on the evolution of within- and between-class feature variability across layers of a well-trained GNN and contrast the behavior with spectral methods.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a graph neural network’s internal features change when it learns to classify nodes. Its starting point is neural collapse: in classifiers trained beyond zero training error, examples from the same class develop increasingly similar final features, while class averages approach symmetric arrangements. The authors ask how graph connections affect this behavior.

An empirical study, illustrated through community detection on stochastic block model graphs, finds that features within a class also become less variable in node classification. However, this contraction is weaker than in the instance classification setting. The theoretical analysis shows that even an optimistic mathematical model needs a strict condition on graph structure to admit a minimizing solution with exact collapse.

The authors also examine the model’s gradient dynamics to explain the partial collapse observed experimentally. A further study tracks variation within and between classes across a trained GNN’s layers and compares it with spectral methods. Together, these results connect feature geometry to graph topology and explain why collapse behavior from ordinary classifiers does not carry over unchanged.
summary.tldr: Graph structure constrains neural collapse in GNNs, helping explain why same-class node features become similar without necessarily collapsing completely.

title: A Neural Collapse Perspective on Feature Evolution in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Large scale field-phenotyping approaches have the potential to solve important questions about the relationship of plant genotype to plant phenotype. Computational approaches to measuring the phenotype (the observable plant features) are required to address the problem at a large scale, but machine learning approaches to extract phenotypes from sensor data have been hampered by limited access to (a) sufficiently large, organized multi-sensor datasets, (b) field trials that have a large scale and significant number of genotypes, (c) full genetic sequencing of those phenotypes, and (d) datasets sufficiently organized so that algorithm centered researchers can directly address the real biological problems. To address this, we present SGxP, a novel benchmark dataset from a large-scale field trial consisting of the complete genotype of over 300 sorghum varieties, and time sequences of imagery from several field plots growing each variety, taken with RGB and laser 3D scanner imaging. To lower the barrier to entry and facilitate further developments, we provide a set of well organized, multi-sensor imagery and corresponding genomic data. We implement baseline deep learning based phenotyping approaches to create baseline results for individual sensors and multi-sensor fusion for detecting genetic mutations with known impacts. We also provide and support an open-ended challenge by identifying thousands of genetic mutations whose phenotypic impacts are currently unknown. A web interface for machine learning researchers and practitioners to share approaches, visualizations and hypotheses supports engagement with plant biologists to further the understanding of the sorghum genotype x phenotype relationship. The full dataset, leaderboard (including baseline results) and discussion forums can be found at http://sorghumsnpbenchmark.com.

paragraphs: Studying how plant genetics relate to observable traits requires genetic information and measurements of plants growing in the field. Machine-learning work has been constrained by limited access to large, organized datasets combining those ingredients. SG×P addresses this with a sorghum benchmark linking complete genotypes for more than 300 varieties to repeated observations of field plots.

The observations include time sequences of RGB images and laser-based three-dimensional scans, with several plots growing each variety. The organized imagery and genomic data are intended to make biological questions more accessible to algorithm researchers. The authors establish deep-learning baselines using individual sensors and sensor fusion to detect mutations with known impacts.

The benchmark also identifies thousands of mutations whose effects on observable traits remain unknown, creating an open-ended research challenge. A web interface supports sharing approaches, visualizations, and hypotheses with plant biologists. The contribution combines structured evaluation on known mutation effects with a resource for investigating unresolved genotype–phenotype relationships, giving computational work a direct connection to biological questions.
summary.tldr: SG×P links sorghum genomes with repeated RGB and 3D field observations to benchmark prediction and investigate unknown mutation effects.

title: SG×P : A Sorghum Genotype × Phenotype Prediction Dataset and Benchmark

abstract: We consider the problem of interactive decision making, encompassing structured bandits and reinforcementlearning with general function approximation. Recently, Foster et al. (2021) introduced theDecision-Estimation Coefficient, a measure of statistical complexity that lower bounds the optimal regret for interactive decisionmaking, as well as a meta-algorithm, Estimation-to-Decisions, which achieves upperbounds in terms of the same quantity. Estimation-to-Decisions is a reduction, which liftsalgorithms for (supervised) online estimation into algorithms fordecision making. In this paper, we show that by combining Estimation-to-Decisions witha specialized form of "optimistic" estimation introduced byZhang (2022), it is possible to obtain guaranteesthat improve upon those of Foster et al. (2021) byaccommodating more lenient notions of estimation error. We use this approach to derive regret bounds formodel-free reinforcement learning with value function approximation, and give structural results showing when it can and cannot help more generally.

paragraphs: Interactive decision making includes problems in which an algorithm must learn while choosing actions, such as structured bandits and reinforcement learning. The Decision-Estimation Coefficient measures statistical difficulty in these settings. Earlier work used it both to lower-bound the best achievable regret and to express upper bounds for an approach called Estimation-to-Decisions.

Estimation-to-Decisions converts supervised online estimation algorithms into decision-making algorithms. This paper combines that reduction with a specialized optimistic form of estimation. The resulting analysis permits more lenient notions of estimation error, improving on the earlier guarantees. The key change is therefore in the estimation requirements that can support a rigorous decision-making guarantee.

The authors use this approach to derive regret bounds for model-free reinforcement learning with value-function approximation. They also establish structural results identifying when the optimistic approach can help and when it cannot. This makes the contribution more than a single bound: it clarifies the reach of a general reduction and shows how weaker estimation requirements can support learning good decisions in specified settings.
summary.tldr: Optimistic estimation strengthens Estimation-to-Decisions guarantees and yields regret bounds for model-free reinforcement learning with value-function approximation.

title: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning with the Decision-Estimation Coefficient

abstract: The rapid advancement and widespread use of large language models (LLMs) have raised significant concerns regarding the potential leakage of personally identifiable information (PII). These models are often trained on vast quantities of web-collected data, which may inadvertently include sensitive personal data. This paper presents ProPILE, a novel probing tool designed to empower data subjects, or the owners of the PII, with awareness of potential PII leakage in LLM-based services. ProPILE lets data subjects formulate prompts based on their own PII to evaluate the level of privacy intrusion in LLMs. We demonstrate its application on the OPT-1.3B model trained on the publicly available Pile dataset. We show how hypothetical data subjects may assess the likelihood of their PII being included in the Pile dataset being revealed. ProPILE can also be leveraged by LLM service providers to effectively evaluate their own levels of PII leakage with more powerful prompts specifically tuned for their in-house models. This tool represents a pioneering step towards empowering the data subjects for their awareness and control over their own data on the web.

paragraphs: Language models trained on large web collections may encounter personally identifiable information. ProPILE is a probing tool intended to help the people associated with that information assess potential exposure through model-based services. Its focus is giving data subjects a way to investigate privacy intrusion involving their own information.

Users formulate prompts based on their own personally identifiable information and examine the model’s behavior. The paper demonstrates this approach with OPT-1.3B, trained on the publicly available Pile dataset. The demonstration considers hypothetical data subjects assessing the likelihood that their information included in that dataset could be revealed.

The tool is also intended for service providers, who can use more powerful prompts tuned to their own models to evaluate leakage. These two uses connect individual awareness with internal model assessment. The paper presents ProPILE as an initial step toward greater awareness and control over personal data on the web, with probing providing evidence about potential disclosure rather than itself removing the information from a model.
summary.tldr: ProPILE helps people and model providers probe whether language models may reveal personally identifiable information.

title: ProPILE: Probing Privacy Leakage in Large Language Models

abstract: Federated bilevel optimization (FBO) has shown great potential recently in machine learning and edge computing due to the emerging nested optimization structure in meta-learning, fine-tuning, hyperparameter tuning, etc. However, existing FBO algorithms often involve complicated computations and require multiple sub-loops per iteration, each of which contains a number of communication rounds. In this paper, we propose a simple and flexible FBO framework named SimFBO, which is easy to implement without sub-loops, and includes a generalized server-side aggregation and update for improving communication efficiency. We further propose System-level heterogeneity robust FBO (ShroFBO) as a variant of SimFBO with stronger resilience to heterogeneous local computation. We show that SimFBO and ShroFBO provably achieve a linear convergence speedup with partial client participation and client sampling without replacement, as well as improved sample and communication complexities. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods over existing FBO algorithms.

paragraphs: Federated bilevel optimization addresses nested learning problems distributed across clients, with applications including meta-learning, fine-tuning, and hyperparameter selection. Existing methods can require several inner loops during each iteration, with repeated communication inside those loops. This makes the optimization procedure complicated and communication-intensive even before accounting for differences among participating clients.

SimFBO removes these sub-loops and introduces generalized server-side aggregation and updating to improve communication efficiency. The authors also propose ShroFBO, a variant designed to better tolerate heterogeneous local computation. The two methods therefore address related practical concerns: simplifying the coordination procedure and making it more resilient when clients perform different amounts of computation.

The analysis establishes linear convergence speedup with partial client participation and sampling without replacement, along with improved sample and communication complexities. Experiments show effectiveness relative to existing federated bilevel algorithms. Together, these results connect a simpler algorithmic structure with theoretical efficiency gains and empirical improvements in the distributed nested-optimization setting studied by the paper.
summary.tldr: SimFBO simplifies federated bilevel optimization by removing sub-loops, while ShroFBO adds resilience to heterogeneous client computation.

title: SimFBO: Towards Simple, Flexible and Communication-efficient Federated Bilevel Learning

abstract: Experimental design is a fundamental problem in many science and engineering fields. In this problem, sample efficiency is crucial due to the time, money, and safety costs of real-world design evaluations. Existing approaches either rely on active data collection or access to large, labeled datasets of past experiments, making them impractical in many real-world scenarios. In this work, we address the more challenging yet realistic setting of few-shot experimental design, where only a few labeled data points of input designs and their corresponding values are available. We approach this problem as a conditional generation task, where a model conditions on a few labeled examples and the desired output to generate an optimal input design. To this end, we introduce Experiment Pretrained Transformers (ExPT), a foundation model for few-shot experimental design that employs a novel combination of synthetic pretraining with in-context learning. In ExPT, we only assume knowledge of a finite collection of unlabelled data points from the input domain and pretrain a transformer neural network to optimize diverse synthetic functions defined over this domain. Unsupervised pretraining allows ExPT to adapt to any design task at test time in an in-context fashion by conditioning on a few labeled data points from the target task and generating the candidate optima. We evaluate ExPT on few-shot experimental design in challenging domains and demonstrate its superior generality and performance compared to existing methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/tung-nd/ExPT.git.

paragraphs: Choosing promising experimental designs is difficult when real evaluations consume substantial time, money, or safety resources. ExPT targets a setting with only a few measured examples of designs and their outcomes. It frames design selection as conditional generation: given those examples and a desired outcome, generate candidate inputs that could achieve it.

The pretraining assumption is access to a finite collection of unlabeled inputs from the design domain. The authors define diverse synthetic functions over those inputs and train a Transformer to optimize them. This supplies optimization experience without requiring a large collection of labeled results from previous real experiments.

At test time, ExPT adapts through in-context learning by conditioning on the few labeled examples available for the target task. It then generates candidate optima using the approach learned during synthetic pretraining. Evaluations in challenging design domains report better generality and performance than existing methods. These findings support synthetic optimization tasks as preparation for proposing designs when measured outcomes are scarce.
summary.tldr: ExPT learns from synthetic optimization tasks to propose experimental designs using only a few measured target-task examples.

title: ExPT: Synthetic Pretraining for Few-Shot Experimental Design

abstract: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) is a fundamental topic of geometric computer vision and a core technique for many downstream applications. Recently, several methods reframe the MDE as a classification-regression problem where a linear combination of probabilistic distribution and bin centers is used to predict depth. In this paper, we propose a novel concept of iterative elastic bins (IEBins) for the classification-regression-based MDE. The proposed IEBins aims to search for high-quality depth by progressively optimizing the search range, which involves multiple stages and each stage performs a finer-grained depth search in the target bin on top of its previous stage. To alleviate the possible error accumulation during the iterative process, we utilize a novel elastic target bin to replace the original target bin, the width of which is adjusted elastically based on the depth uncertainty. Furthermore, we develop a dedicated framework composed of a feature extractor and an iterative optimizer that has powerful temporal context modeling capabilities benefiting from the GRU-based architecture. Extensive experiments on the KITTI, NYU-Depth-v2 and SUN RGB-D datasets demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses prior state-of-the-art competitors. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ShuweiShao/IEBins.

To alleviate the possible error accumulation during the iterative process, we utilize a novel elastic target bin to replace the original target bin, the width of which is adjusted elastically based on the depth uncertainty. Furthermore, we develop a dedicated framework composed of a feature extractor and an iterative optimizer that has powerful temporal context modeling capabilities benefiting from the GRU-based architecture. Extensive experiments on the KITTI, NYU-Depth-v2 and SUN RGB-D datasets demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses prior state-of-the-art competitors. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ShuweiShao/IEBins.

paragraphs: Monocular depth estimation predicts distance from a single image. Some methods divide possible depths into bins and combine bin centers with predicted probabilities to obtain a depth estimate. IEBins develops this approach into a sequence of increasingly detailed searches, progressively refining the range in which a depth value is sought.

At each stage, the method searches more finely within a target bin selected from the preceding stage. An early mistake could otherwise constrain later searches to an unsuitable range. To alleviate that accumulation of error, IEBins makes the target bin elastic: its width changes according to depth uncertainty. This lets the refinement process account for uncertainty rather than treating every intermediate estimate as equally reliable.

The framework combines a feature extractor with a GRU-based iterative optimizer that models context across refinement stages. Experiments on KITTI, NYU-Depth-v2, and SUN RGB-D report performance beyond prior state-of-the-art competitors. These findings support uncertainty-adjusted search ranges as a useful way to refine depth predictions while addressing the errors that can accumulate during iterative estimation.
summary.tldr: IEBins refines depth estimates through progressively finer searches whose bin widths adapt to uncertainty, improving results on three depth-estimation datasets.

title: IEBins: Iterative Elastic Bins for Monocular Depth Estimation

abstract: It is a crucial challenge to reconstruct population dynamics using unlabeled samples from distributions at coarse time intervals. Recent approaches such as flow-based models or Schrödinger Bridge (SB) models have demonstrated appealing performance, yet the inferred sample trajectories either fail to account for the underlying stochasticity or are unnecessarily rigid. In this article, we extend SB into phase space and propose $\underline{D}$eep $\underline{M}$omentum Multi-Marginal $\underline{S}$chrödinger $\underline{B}$ridge (DMSB), a novel computational framework that learns the smooth measure-valued spline for stochastic systems that satisfy position marginal constraints across time. By tailoring the celebrated Bregman Iteration and extending the Iteration Proportional Fitting to phase space, we manage to handle high-dimensional multi-marginal trajectory inference tasks efficiently. Our algorithm outperforms baselines significantly, as evidenced by experiments for synthetic datasets and a real-world single-cell RNA sequence dataset. Additionally, the proposed approach can reasonably reconstruct the evolution of velocity distribution, from position snapshots only, when there is a ground truth velocity that is nevertheless inaccessible.

paragraphs: Population snapshots reveal how samples are distributed at particular times without identifying which earlier sample became which later one. Reconstructing the dynamics between widely separated snapshots is therefore difficult. The paper targets approaches whose inferred trajectories either omit stochastic behavior or constrain the possible motion too rigidly.

Deep Momentum Multi-Marginal Schrödinger Bridge, or DMSB, extends the Schrödinger Bridge framework into phase space, incorporating motion alongside position. It learns a smooth trajectory of distributions for a stochastic system while matching the observed position distributions at multiple times. This connects the snapshots through a distribution-level evolution that can account for randomness.

The computational method adapts Bregman iteration and extends iterative proportional fitting to phase space to handle high-dimensional trajectory inference efficiently. Experiments on synthetic data and a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset report substantial improvements over baselines. The method also reasonably reconstructs evolving velocity distributions from position snapshots when an underlying ground-truth velocity exists but is unavailable to the method. That result concerns the reported reconstruction setting, rather than universal recovery of hidden motion.
summary.tldr: DMSB reconstructs stochastic population dynamics across snapshots by learning smooth distribution trajectories in a space that includes position and motion.

title: Deep Momentum Multi-Marginal Schrödinger Bridge

abstract: Contextual batched bandit (CBB) is a setting where a batch of rewards is observed from the environment at the end of each episode, but the rewards of the non-executed actions are unobserved, resulting in partial-information feedback. Existing approaches for CBB often ignore the rewards of the non-executed actions, leading to underutilization of feedback information. In this paper, we propose an efficient approach called Sketched Policy Updating with Imputed Rewards (SPUIR) that completes the unobserved rewards using sketching, which approximates the full-information feedbacks. We formulate reward imputation as an imputation regularized ridge regression problem that captures the feedback mechanisms of both executed and non-executed actions. To reduce time complexity, we solve the regression problem using randomized sketching. We prove that our approach achieves an instantaneous regret with controllable bias and smaller variance than approaches without reward imputation. Furthermore, our approach enjoys a sublinear regret bound against the optimal policy. We also present two extensions, a rate-scheduled version and a version for nonlinear rewards, making our approach more practical. Experimental results show that SPUIR outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on synthetic, public benchmark, and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: In contextual batched bandits, rewards arrive together at the end of an episode, and only rewards for actions actually taken are observed. This leaves the learner with partial feedback. The paper proposes Sketched Policy Updating with Imputed Rewards, or SPUIR, to estimate missing rewards and approximate the information that fuller feedback would provide.

The method formulates reward completion as an imputation-regularized ridge regression problem that represents feedback from executed and non-executed actions. Randomized sketching reduces the cost of solving that regression. The missing rewards are therefore model-based estimates, incorporated into policy updating through a computationally efficient optimization procedure.

The authors add rate-scheduled and nonlinear-reward extensions. Experiments on synthetic, public benchmark, and real-world datasets report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the practical value of the proposed bias–variance trade-off and computational approach.
summary.tldr: SPUIR combines reward imputation with randomized sketching to improve batched-bandit learning with controllable bias, reduced variance, and sublinear regret.

title: Reward Imputation with Sketching for Contextual Batched Bandits

abstract: Several problems have been extensively studied in the learning-augmented setting, where the algorithm has access to some, possibly incorrect, predictions. However, it is assumed in most works that the predictions are provided to the algorithm as input, with no constraint on their size. In this paper, we consider algorithms with access to a limited number of predictions, that they can request at any time during their execution. We study three classical problems in competitive analysis, the ski rental problem, the secretary problem, and the non-clairvoyant job scheduling. We address the question of when to query predictions and how to use them.

paragraphs: Learning-augmented algorithms make decisions with help from predictions that may be wrong. Much of the existing work assumes these predictions arrive as part of the input, without restricting how much advice is available. This paper changes that setup by giving the algorithm a limited number of predictions that it can request during execution.

That restriction makes obtaining advice part of the decision problem itself. The algorithm must address both when a prediction is worth requesting and how to use the information it receives. Because requests can occur during execution, the framework explicitly brings the timing of advice into the study, alongside the possibility that advice is inaccurate.

The authors examine this setting through three classical problems: ski rental, the secretary problem, and non-clairvoyant job scheduling. These provide distinct contexts for studying decisions under limited advice. The contribution described in the abstract is the budget-constrained formulation and its investigation across these problems, centering attention on prediction access as a resource that algorithms must manage.
summary.tldr: The paper studies when online algorithms should request potentially incorrect predictions when only a limited number of requests is available.

title: Advice Querying under Budget Constraint for Online Algorithms

abstract: Decentralized learning has recently been attracting increasing attention for its applications in parallel computation and privacy preservation. Many recent studies stated that the underlying network topology with a faster consensus rate (a.k.a. spectral gap) leads to a better convergence rate and accuracy for decentralized learning. However, a topology with a fast consensus rate, e.g., the exponential graph, generally has a large maximum degree, which incurs significant communication costs. Thus, seeking topologies with both a fast consensus rate and small maximum degree is important. In this study, we propose a novel topology combining both a fast consensus rate and small maximum degree called the Base-$\left(k+1\right)$ Graph. Unlike the existing topologies, the Base-$\left(k+1\right)$ Graph enables all nodes to reach the exact consensus after a finite number of iterations for any number of nodes and maximum degree $k$. Thanks to this favorable property, the Base-$\left(k+1\right)$ Graph endows Decentralized SGD (DSGD) with both a faster convergence rate and more communication efficiency than the exponential graph. We conducted experiments with various topologies, demonstrating that the Base-$\left(k+1\right)$ Graph enables various decentralized learning methods to achieve higher accuracy with better communication efficiency than the existing topologies. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukiTakezawa/BaseGraph.

paragraphs: In decentralized learning, the communication network influences how quickly participating nodes reach agreement. A network with rapid consensus can help learning converge, but connecting each node to many others raises communication costs. The paper addresses this tension by designing a topology that combines fast agreement with a small maximum number of connections.

The proposed Base-(k+1) Graph supports exact consensus after finitely many iterations for any number of nodes and maximum degree k. The central feature is therefore stronger than simply approaching agreement progressively: the topology reaches agreement in a finite number of rounds while respecting the degree constraint.

The authors show that this property gives decentralized stochastic gradient descent faster convergence and greater communication efficiency than the exponential graph. Experiments with several topologies also find improved accuracy and communication efficiency across various decentralized learning methods. The contribution links a concrete network property to both theoretical learning behavior and measured outcomes, showing why topology design matters alongside the choice of optimization algorithm.
summary.tldr: The Base-(k+1) Graph combines finite-time exact consensus with limited connectivity to improve decentralized learning efficiency.

title: Beyond Exponential Graph: Communication-Efficient Topologies for Decentralized Learning via Finite-time Convergence

abstract: We demonstrate that numerous machine learning algorithms are specific instances of one single paradigm: reciprocal learning. These instances range from active learning over multi-armed bandits to self-training. We show that all these algorithms not only learn parameters from data but also vice versa: They iteratively alter training data in a way that depends on the current model fit. We introduce reciprocal learning as a generalization of these algorithms using the language of decision theory. This allows us to study under what conditions they converge. The key is to guarantee that reciprocal learning contracts such that the Banach fixed-point theorem applies. In this way, we find that reciprocal learning converges at linear rates to an approximately optimal model under some assumptions on the loss function, if their predictions are probabilistic and the sample adaption is both non-greedy and either randomized or regularized. We interpret these findings and provide corollaries that relate them to active learning, self-training, and bandits.

We introduce reciprocal learning as a generalization of these algorithms using the language of decision theory. This allows us to study under what conditions they converge. The key is to guarantee that reciprocal learning contracts such that the Banach fixed-point theorem applies. In this way, we find that reciprocal learning converges at linear rates to an approximately optimal model under some assumptions on the loss function, if their predictions are probabilistic and the sample adaption is both non-greedy and either randomized or regularized. paragraphs: Many learning algorithms change the data they learn from as training proceeds. Active learning, multi-armed bandits, and self-training all involve a feedback loop: data shape the current model, and the current model influences subsequent training data. This paper names that shared pattern reciprocal learning and formulates it using decision theory.

The common formulation makes it possible to study convergence across these otherwise distinct algorithms. The central mathematical condition is contraction: repeated updates must draw the learning process toward a stable point. When this holds, the Banach fixed-point theorem provides a route to proving convergence. The paper uses this perspective to identify sufficient conditions on both model predictions and data adaptation.

Under assumptions on the loss, probabilistic predictions, and sample adaptation that is non-greedy and either randomized or regularized, the authors establish linear-rate convergence to an approximately optimal model. These conditions are part of the result, not a claim that every reciprocal-learning algorithm converges. Corollaries connect the general theory back to active learning, self-training, and bandits, explaining how their update choices fit the shared framework.
summary.tldr: Reciprocal learning unifies algorithms that jointly update models and training data, establishing convergence under specified contraction-related conditions.

title: Reciprocal Learning

abstract: Nuanced expressiveness, especially through detailed hand and facial expressions, is pivotal for enhancing the realism and vitality of digital human representations.In this work, we aim to learn expressive human avatars from a monocular RGB video; a setting that introduces new challenges in capturing and animating fine-grained details.To this end, we introduce EVA, a drivable human model that can recover fine details based on 3D Gaussians and an expressive parametric human model, SMPL-X.Focused on enhancing expressiveness, our work makes three key contributions.First, we highlight the importance of aligning the SMPL-X model with the video frames for effective avatar learning.Recognizing the limitations of current methods for estimating SMPL-X parameters from in-the-wild videos, we introduce a reconstruction module that significantly improves the image-model alignment.Second, we propose a context-aware adaptive density control strategy, which is adaptively adjusting the gradient thresholds to accommodate the varied granularity across body parts.Third, we develop a feedback mechanism that predicts per-pixel confidence to better guide the optimization of 3D Gaussians.Extensive experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our approach both quantitatively and qualitatively, especially on the fine-grained hand and facial details. We make our code available at the project website: https://evahuman.github.io.

paragraphs: EVA learns an animatable human avatar from a single-camera RGB video, with particular attention to hands and facial expressions. These fine details are central to expressiveness but difficult to capture in this setting. The method combines 3D Gaussians with SMPL-X, an expressive parametric human model, to recover a detailed representation that can be driven.

The first contribution improves alignment between SMPL-X and the video frames. The authors introduce a reconstruction module to address weaknesses in estimating SMPL-X parameters from in-the-wild footage. Better alignment gives avatar learning a closer correspondence between the human model and the observed images, supporting the recovery of fine appearance details.

Two additional mechanisms guide Gaussian optimization. Context-aware density control adjusts gradient thresholds to account for different levels of detail across body parts, while a feedback mechanism predicts confidence for individual pixels. Experiments on two benchmarks report improvements in both quantitative measures and visual quality, especially for hands and faces. The results support combining better alignment with body-part-sensitive density control and pixel-level confidence when learning expressive avatars from monocular video.
summary.tldr: EVA improves human avatars learned from monocular video through better model alignment, adaptive Gaussian density control, and pixel-level confidence.

title: Expressive Gaussian Human Avatars from Monocular RGB Video

abstract: Enabling deep models to generalize in non-stationary environments is vital for real-world machine learning, as data distributions are often found to continually change. Recently, evolving domain generalization (EDG) has emerged to tackle the domain generalization in a time-varying system, where the domain gradually evolves over time in an underlying continuous structure. Nevertheless, it typically assumes multiple source domains simultaneously ready. It still remains an open problem to address EDG in the domain-incremental setting, where source domains are non-static and arrive sequentially to mimic the evolution of training domains. To this end, we propose Weight Diffusion (W-Diff), a novel framework that utilizes the conditional diffusion model in the parameter space to learn the evolving pattern of classifiers during the domain-incremental training process. Specifically, the diffusion model is conditioned on the classifier weights of different historical domain (regarded as a reference point) and the prototypes of current domain, to learn the evolution from the reference point to the classifier weights of current domain (regarded as the anchor point). In addition, a domain-shared feature encoder is learned by enforcing prediction consistency among multiple classifiers, so as to mitigate the overfitting problem and restrict the evolving pattern to be reflected in the classifier as much as possible. During inference, we adopt the ensemble manner based on a great number of target domain-customized classifiers, which are cheaply obtained via the conditional diffusion model, for robust prediction. Comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show the superior generalization performance of W-Diff on unseen domains in the future.

paragraphs: When data distributions evolve over time, a model must generalize to future conditions. W-Diff studies a setting where training domains arrive sequentially, rather than being available together. It learns how classifier weights change across domains, using a conditional diffusion model operating directly in the space of model parameters.

The diffusion model receives historical classifier weights as reference points and prototypes summarizing the current domain. It learns the transition from those references to the current classifier’s weights. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior generalization to unseen future domains. The method’s central idea is to learn a pattern of parameter evolution from sequential experience, then use generated classifier variation to support robust predictions as the data distribution continues to change.
summary.tldr: W-Diff learns how classifier weights evolve across sequential domains and generates ensembles that generalize to future distributions.

title: Weight Diffusion for Future: Learn to Generalize in Non-Stationary Environments

abstract: Laplace approximations are popular techniques for endowing deep networks with epistemic uncertainty estimates as they can be applied without altering the predictions of the trained network, and they scale to large models and datasets. While the choice of prior strongly affects the resulting posterior distribution, computational tractability and lack of interpretability of the weight space typically limit the Laplace approximation to isotropic Gaussian priors, which are known to cause pathological behavior as depth increases. As a remedy, we directly place a prior on function space. More precisely, since Lebesgue densities do not exist on infinite-dimensional function spaces, we recast training as finding the so-called weak mode of the posterior measure under a Gaussian process (GP) prior restricted to the space of functions representable by the neural network. Through the GP prior, one can express structured and interpretable inductive biases, such as regularity or periodicity, directly in function space, while still exploiting the implicit inductive biases that allow deep networks to generalize. After model linearization, the training objective induces a negative log-posterior density to which we apply a Laplace approximation, leveraging highly scalable methods from matrix-free linear algebra. Our method provides improved results where prior knowledge is abundant (as is the case in many scientific inference tasks). At the same time, it stays competitive for black-box supervised learning problems, where neural networks typically excel.

Those priors are difficult to interpret as beliefs about predictions and can behave pathologically as network depth increases.

FSP-Laplace instead places a Gaussian-process prior over functions the network can represent. Its stated advantage is therefore especially relevant when meaningful knowledge about the desired function is available.
summary.tldr: FSP-Laplace uses Gaussian-process priors over network functions to incorporate interpretable prior knowledge into scalable uncertainty estimation.

title: FSP-Laplace: Function-Space Priors for the Laplace Approximation in Bayesian Deep Learning

abstract: Multimodal interleaved datasets featuring free-form interleaved sequences of images and text are crucial for training frontier large multimodal models (LMMs). Despite the rapid progression of open-source LMMs, there remains a pronounced scarcity of large-scale, open-source multimodal interleaved datasets.In response, we introduce MINT-1T, the most extensive and diverse open-source Multimodal INTerleaved dataset to date. MINT-1T comprises of one trillion text tokens and 3.4 billion images, a 10x scale-up from existing open-source datasets. Additionally, we include previously untapped sources such as PDFs and ArXiv papers. As scaling multimodal interleaved datasets requires substantial engineering effort, sharing the data curation process and releasing the dataset greatly benefits the community. Our experiments show that LMMs trained on MINT-1T rival the performance of models trained on the previous leading dataset, OBELICS. We release our data at https://github.com/mlfoundations/MINT-1T.

These interleaved datasets preserve a form of mixed visual and written content that is important for training such models. The paper addresses the scarcity of large, openly available datasets with this structure.

This supports the dataset's usefulness for model training while distinguishing its large increase in available data from a claim of proportionally larger performance gains.
summary.tldr: MINT-1T releases a trillion-token interleaved multimodal dataset whose trained models rival those using the previous leading dataset.

title: MINT-1T: Scaling Open-Source Multimodal Data by 10x: A Multimodal Dataset with One Trillion Tokens

abstract: We address the problem of optimizing over functions defined on node subsets in a graph. The optimization of such functions is often a non-trivial task given their combinatorial, black-box and expensive-to-evaluate nature. Although various algorithms have been introduced in the literature, most are either task-specific or computationally inefficient and only utilize information about the graph structure without considering the characteristics of the function. To address these limitations, we utilize Bayesian Optimization (BO), a sample-efficient black-box solver, and propose a novel framework for combinatorial optimization on graphs. More specifically, we map each $k$-node subset in the original graph to a node in a new combinatorial graph and adopt a local modeling approach to efficiently traverse the latter graph by progressively sampling its subgraphs using a recursive algorithm. Extensive experiments under both synthetic and real-world setups demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed BO framework on various types of graphs and optimization tasks, where its behavior is analyzed in detail with ablation studies.

The number of possible groups creates a combinatorial search problem, and the objective may be available only as a black box. This paper develops a Bayesian optimization framework for learning which groups are worth evaluating.

The framework maps every subset containing k nodes to a node in a new combinatorial graph. Searching for a good subset then becomes a search over this transformed graph. To make traversal efficient, the method uses local models and a recursive algorithm that progressively samples subgraphs. This lets the search incorporate information about the objective function as well as the original graph's structure.

The authors evaluate the framework on synthetic and real-world problems spanning different graph types and optimization tasks. They report effective performance and use ablation studies to examine its behavior. The contribution is a general approach to expensive subset selection: it combines the sample efficiency of Bayesian optimization with a graph representation of the candidate combinations, while organizing the modeling locally to manage the search.
summary.tldr: The paper combines Bayesian optimization with local search on a graph of node subsets to tackle expensive combinatorial objectives.

title: Bayesian Optimization of Functions over Node Subsets in Graphs

abstract: Tabular data is prevalent in real-world machine learning applications, and new models for supervised learning of tabular data are frequently proposed. Comparative studies assessing performance differences typically have model-centered evaluation setups with overly standardized data preprocessing. This limits the external validity of these studies, as in real-world modeling pipelines, models are typically applied after dataset-specific preprocessing and feature engineering. We address this gap by proposing a data-centric evaluation framework. We select 10 relevant datasets from Kaggle competitions and implement expert-level preprocessing pipelines for each dataset. We conduct experiments with different preprocessing pipelines and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) regimes to quantify the impact of model selection, HPO, feature engineering, and test-time adaptation. Our main findings reveal: 1) After dataset-specific feature engineering, model rankings change considerably, performance differences decrease, and the importance of model selection reduces. 2) Recent models, despite their measurable progress, still significantly benefit from manual feature engineering. This holds true for both tree-based models and neural networks. 3) While tabular data is typically considered static, samples are often collected over time, and adapting to distribution shifts can be important even in supposedly static data. These insights suggest that research efforts should be directed toward a data-centric perspective, acknowledging that tabular data requires feature engineering and often exhibits temporal characteristics.

title: A Data-Centric Perspective on Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Tabular Data

abstract: Evaluating observational estimators of causal effects demands information that is rarely available: unconfounded interventions and outcomes from the population of interest, created either by randomization or adjustment. As a result, it is customary to fall back on simulators when creating benchmark tasks. Simulators offer great control but are often too simplistic to make challenging tasks, either because they are hand-designed and lack the nuances of real-world data, or because they are fit to observational data without structural constraints. In this work, we propose a general, repeatable strategy for turning observational data into sequential structural causal models and challenging estimation tasks by following two simple principles: 1) fitting real-world data where possible, and 2) creating complexity by composing simple, hand-designed mechanisms. We implement these ideas in a highly configurable software package and apply it to the well-known Adult income data set to construct the IncomeSCM simulator. From this, we devise multiple estimation tasks and sample data sets to compare established estimators of causal effects. The tasks present a suitable challenge, with effect estimates varying greatly in quality between methods, despite similar performance in the modeling of factual outcomes, highlighting the need for dedicated causal estimators and model selection criteria.

Simulators can provide that reference, but building challenging and realistic simulations is difficult. IncomeSCM addresses this by combining patterns fitted from real data with explicitly designed causal mechanisms.

The paper proposes a repeatable strategy for converting observational data into sequential structural causal models. Its two guiding principles are to fit real-world observations where possible and to create complexity by composing simple, hand-designed mechanisms. title: IncomeSCM: From tabular data set to time-series simulator and causal estimation benchmark

abstract: We introduce \textit{CoTextor}, a modular and training-free framework for multilingual text editing in images, designed to support human-AI co-creation through a user-controllable and reversible workflow. Unlike diffusion-based systems that operate as black boxes, \textit{CoTextor} separates the editing process into transparent layers—foreground extraction, background inpainting, semantic rewriting, and depth-aware reintegration—allowing precise user-guided operations such as rotation, translation, scaling, and warping. To ensure realism, we introduce a perceptually guided integration module that enhances photometric and geometric coherence during text reinsertion. Built entirely from publicly available pretrained components, \textit{CoTextor} is accessible to non-technical, multilingual users, requiring no retraining or annotation. Through real-world scenarios in poster localization, street art remixing, and educational content creation, we demonstrate how \textit{CoTextor} enables inclusive and expressive visual storytelling across cultural and linguistic contexts.

paragraphs: CoTextor is a framework for editing multilingual text inside images while giving users control over the process. The task involves more than changing words: the edited text must also fit the surrounding picture. The framework makes these parts of the workflow explicit and supports reversible edits, so users can guide and revisit individual operations.

The process separates foreground extraction, background repair, semantic rewriting, and depth-aware reintegration. Users can rotate, move, resize, and warp content. A perceptually guided integration module improves how reinserted text matches the image’s appearance and geometry. This layered structure connects control over the wording with control over the text’s visual placement.

The authors demonstrate it through poster localization, street art remixing, and educational content creation. These scenarios show how a modular editing workflow can support visual storytelling across languages and cultural settings. The emphasis is on accessible human-AI co-creation, with users able to direct both the meaning and presentation of edited text.
summary.tldr: CoTextor enables controllable multilingual text editing in images through reversible layers built from pretrained components.

title: CoTextor: Training-Free Modular Multilingual Text Editing via Layered Disentanglement and Depth-Aware Fusion

abstract: Sparse-reward reinforcement learning (RL) can model a wide range of highly complex tasks. Solving sparse-reward tasks is RL's core premise — requiring efficient exploration coupled with long-horizon credit assignment — and overcoming these challenges is key for building self-improving agents with superhuman ability. We argue that solving complex and high-dimensional tasks requires solving simpler tasks that are *relevant* to the target task. In contrast, most prior work designs strategies for selecting exploratory tasks with the objective of solving *any* task, making exploration of challenging high-dimensional, long-horizon tasks intractable. We find that the sense of direction, necessary for effective exploration, can be extracted from existing reinforcement learning algorithms, without needing any prior information. Based on this finding, we propose a method for _**di**rected **s**parse-reward goal-**co**nditioned **ve**ry long-horizon **R**L_ (DISCOVER), which selects exploratory goals in the direction of the target task. We connect DISCOVER to principled exploration in bandits, formally bounding the time until the target task becomes achievable in terms of the agent's initial distance to the target, but independent of the volume of the space of all tasks. Empirically, we perform a thorough evaluation in high-dimensional simulated environments. We find that the directed goal selection of DISCOVER solves exploration problems that are beyond the reach of prior state-of-the-art exploration methods in RL.
