paragraphs: Sparse rewards make learning difficult because agents receive little feedback while exploring and must connect eventual success to much earlier decisions. The authors argue that complex tasks call for simpler learning goals that are relevant to the target. Exploring tasks without that direction can become intractable in large spaces with long sequences of actions.

DISCOVER builds an automated curriculum by selecting exploratory goals that lead toward the target task. The paper finds that existing reinforcement learning algorithms already contain a useful directional signal, so this selection does not require prior information. The resulting approach aims to make intermediate practice contribute to a particular objective instead of merely expanding the collection of achievable tasks.

The authors connect the method to principled exploration in bandits and bound the time until the target becomes achievable. That bound depends on initial distance to the target but not the volume of the entire task space. In high-dimensional simulations, DISCOVER solves exploration problems that prior state-of-the-art methods could not solve in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: DISCOVER selects intermediate goals directed toward a target, enabling sparse-reward agents to solve difficult exploration problems in high-dimensional simulations.

title: DISCOVER: Automated Curricula for Sparse-Reward Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce MOSDT, the first algorithm designed for multi-agent offline safe reinforcement learning (MOSRL), alongside MOSDB, the first dataset and benchmark for this domain. Different from most existing knowledge distillation-based multi-agent RL methods, we propose policy self-distillation (PSD) with a new global information reconstruction scheme by fusing the observation features of all agents, streamlining training and improving parameter efficiency. We adopt full parameter sharing across agents, significantly slashing parameter count and boosting returns up to 38.4-fold by stabilizing training. We propose a new plug-and-play cost binary embedding (CBE) module, which binarizes cumulative costs as safety signals and embeds the signals into return features for efficient information aggregation. On the strong MOSDB benchmark, MOSDT achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) returns in 14 out of 18 tasks (across all base environments including MuJoCo, Safety Gym, and Isaac Gym) while ensuring complete safety, with only 65% of the execution parameter count of a SOTA single-agent offline safe RL method CDT. Code, dataset, and results are available at this website: https://github.com/Lucian1115/MOSDT.git

paragraphs: MOSDT addresses learning safe behavior for multiple agents from an existing dataset. The paper introduces both an algorithm for this setting and MOSDB, a dataset and benchmark intended to make the problem systematically testable. Its design combines policy self-distillation, shared parameters, and an explicit representation of safety-related costs.

The self-distillation method reconstructs global information by fusing observation features from all agents. Full parameter sharing reduces the model's parameter count and stabilizes training; the authors report return improvements of up to 38.4 times from this design. A cost binary embedding module converts cumulative costs into binary safety signals and incorporates those signals into return features, bringing reward and safety information together efficiently.

It uses 65% of the execution parameters of CDT, a state-of-the-art single-agent offline safe RL method. The results connect multi-agent information sharing with stronger returns and efficient execution.
summary.tldr: MOSDT combines shared policies, self-distillation, and cost embeddings to achieve strong multi-agent offline returns with complete safety in its reported benchmark evaluation.

title: MOSDT: Self-Distillation-Based Decision Transformer for Multi-Agent Offline Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce Modular Region-Based Implicit Codec (MoRIC), a novel image compression algorithm that relies on implicit neural representations (INRs). Unlike previous INR-based codecs that model the entire image with a single neural network, MoRIC assigns dedicated models to distinct regions in the image, each tailored to its local distribution. This region-wise design enhances adaptation to local statistics and enables flexible, single-object compression with fine-grained rate-distortion (RD) control. MoRIC allows regions of arbitrary shapes, and provides the contour information for each region as separate information. In particular, it incorporates adaptive chain coding for lossy and lossless contour compression, and a shared global modulator that injects multi-scale global context into local overfitting processes in a coarse-to-fine manner. MoRIC achieves state-of-the-art performance in single-object compression with significantly lower decoding complexity than existing learned neural codecs, which results in a highly efficient compression approach for fixed-background scenarios, e.g., for surveillance cameras. It also sets a new benchmark among overfitted codecs for standard image compression. Additionally, MoRIC naturally supports semantically meaningful layered compression through selective region refinement, paving the way for scalable and flexible INR-based codecs.

Giving each region its own model allows compression to adapt to local image statistics and offers finer control over the tradeoff between storage size and reconstruction quality. The same design supports compressing an individual object within an image.

Regions can have arbitrary shapes, with their boundaries transmitted as separate contour information. Adaptive chain coding supports both lossy and lossless contour compression. A shared global modulator supplies multiscale context while local models are fitted, progressing from coarse information toward finer detail. This connects region-specific modeling with information about the image as a whole.

They also report a new performance benchmark among overfitted codecs for standard image compression. Selectively refining regions enables semantically meaningful compression layers, allowing the representation to allocate additional detail to particular parts of an image.
summary.tldr: MoRIC uses region-specific neural representations and shared global context for flexible image compression with efficient single-object decoding.

title: MoRIC: A Modular Region-based Implicit Codec for Image Compression

abstract: A fundamental challenge in probabilistic modeling is to balance expressivity and inference efficiency. Tractable probabilistic models (TPMs) aim to directly address this tradeoff by imposing constraints that guarantee efficient inference of certain queries while maintaining expressivity. In particular, probabilistic circuits (PCs) provide a unifying framework for many TPMs, by characterizing families of models as circuits satisfying different structural properties. Because the complexity of inference on PCs is a function of the circuit size, understanding the size requirements of different families of PCs is fundamental in mapping the trade-off between tractability and expressive efficiency. However, the study of expressive efficiency of circuits are often concerned with exact representations, which may not align with model learning, where we look to approximate the underlying data distribution closely by some distance measure. Moreover, due to hardness of inference tasks, exactly representing distributions while supporting tractable inference often incurs exponential size blow-ups. In this paper, we consider a natural, yet so far underexplored, question: can we avoid such size blow-up by allowing for some small approximation error? We study approximating distributions with probabilistic circuits with guarantees based on $f$-divergences, and analyze which inference queries remain well-approximated under this framework. We show that approximating an arbitrary distribution with bounded $f$-divergence is NP-hard for any model that can tractably compute marginals. In addition, we prove an exponential size gap for approximation between the class of decomposable PCs and that of decomposable and deterministic PCs.

paragraphs: Tractable probabilistic models impose structure so that particular inference queries can be answered efficiently. Probabilistic circuits provide a framework for studying these structures, but efficient inference also depends on circuit size. This paper asks whether allowing a small approximation error can avoid the large representations sometimes required to represent a distribution exactly.

The authors study approximation guarantees expressed through f-divergences and analyze which inference queries remain well approximated under those guarantees. This connects closeness between distributions with the usefulness of the answers a model produces. It also shifts the expressivity question toward approximate representation, which better reflects the goal of learning a distribution from data.

Two hardness results show that approximation does not generally remove the difficulty. Approximating an arbitrary distribution with bounded f-divergence is NP-hard for any model that supports tractable marginal computation. The authors also prove an exponential approximation-size gap between decomposable circuits and circuits that are both decomposable and deterministic. These results identify persistent computational and representational barriers even when exact equality is relaxed.
summary.tldr: Allowing distributional approximation does not generally eliminate computational hardness or exponential representation-size gaps in tractable probabilistic models.

title: On the Hardness of Approximating Distributions with Tractable Probabilistic Models

abstract: We develop optimization methods which offer new trade-offs between the number of gradient and Hessian computations needed to compute the critical point of a non-convex function. We provide a method that for a twice-differentiable $f\colon \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with $L_2$-Lipschitz Hessian, and input initial point with $\Delta$-bounded sub-optimality and sufficiently small $\epsilon > 0$ outputs an $\epsilon$-critical point, i.e., a point $x$ such that $\|\nabla f(x)\| \leq \epsilon$, using $\tilde{O}(\Delta L_2^{1/4} n_H^{-1/2}\epsilon^{-9/4})$ queries to a gradient oracle and $n_H$ queries to a Hessian oracle. As a consequence, we obtain an improved gradient query complexity of $\tilde{O}(d^{1/3}L_2^{1/2}\Delta\epsilon^{-3/2})$ in the case of bounded dimension and of $\tilde{O}(\Delta^{3/2} L_2^{3/4}\epsilon^{-9/4})$ in the case where we are allowed only a single Hessian query. We obtain these results through a more general algorithm which can handle approximate Hessian computations and recovers known prior state-of-the-art bounds of computing an $\epsilon$-critical point, under the additional assumption that $f$ has an $L_1$-Lipschitz gradient, with $O(\Delta L_2^{1/4}\epsilon^{-7/4})$-gradient queries.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to divide optimization work between gradient computations, which describe local slope, and Hessian computations, which describe curvature. Its target is an approximate critical point of a nonconvex function: a point where the gradient's magnitude falls below a chosen tolerance. That target concerns a small gradient and does not itself establish that the point is a minimum.

The main method assumes a twice-differentiable objective whose Hessian changes at a controlled rate, an initial point with bounded suboptimality, and a sufficiently small tolerance. Its theoretical bound explicitly connects the number of gradient queries to the allocated Hessian queries. Within the stated result, increasing the Hessian budget reduces the gradient requirement through an inverse-square-root dependence.

The analysis yields improved gradient-query bounds for bounded dimension and for the restrictive case of just one Hessian query. A broader algorithm also accommodates approximate Hessians. With an additional Lipschitz-gradient assumption, it recovers established state-of-the-art bounds. The contribution is a set of provable computation trade-offs under specified smoothness conditions.
summary.tldr: New nonconvex optimization methods provide provable trade-offs between gradient and Hessian queries for finding points with small gradients.

title: Balancing Gradient and Hessian Queries in Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: Spatial transcriptomics technologies can be used to align transcriptomes with histopathological morphology, presenting exciting new opportunities for biomolecular discovery. Using spatial transcriptomic gene expression and corresponding histology data, we construct a novel framework, GeneFlow, to map single- and multi-cell gene expression onto paired cellular images. By combining an attention-based RNA encoder with a conditional UNet guided by rectified flow, we generate high-resolution images with different staining methods (e.g., H\&E, DAPI) to highlight various cellular/ tissue structures. Rectified flow with high-order ODE solvers creates a continuous, bijective mapping between expression and image manifolds, addressing the many-to-one relationship inherent in this problem. Our method enables the generation of realistic cellular morphology features and spatially resolved intercellular interactions under genetic or chemical perturbations. This enables minimally invasive disease diagnosis by revealing dysregulated patterns in imaging phenotypes. Our rectified flow based method outperforms diffusion methods and baselines in all experiments. Code is available at https://github.com/wangmengbo/GeneFlow.

Using paired spatial transcriptomics and histology data, it learns to map expression from single cells or multiple cells to corresponding cellular images. The goal is to connect molecular activity with observable morphology, including images produced with different staining methods.

The framework combines an attention-based RNA encoder with a conditional UNet guided by rectified flow. It generates high-resolution images for stains such as H&E and DAPI, which emphasize different structures. The authors describe a continuous, bijective mapping between expression and image manifolds, computed using high-order differential-equation solvers, as their way of addressing the underlying many-to-one relationship.

The paper reports realistic cellular features and spatially resolved interactions under genetic or chemical perturbations, with performance exceeding diffusion methods and other baselines in all reported experiments. It also presents revealing abnormal imaging patterns as a route toward minimally invasive disease diagnosis. The central contribution is the learned connection between molecular measurements and morphology; the diagnostic claim is an application of that connection.
summary.tldr: GeneFlow uses rectified flow to generate cellular histology images from gene expression, linking molecular activity with tissue appearance.

title: GeneFlow: Translation of Single-cell Gene Expression to Histopathological Images via Rectified Flow

abstract: Generative modeling of discrete variables is challenging yet crucial for applications in natural language processing and biological sequence design. We introduce the Shortlisting Model (SLM), a novel simplex-based diffusion model inspired by progressive candidate pruning. SLM operates on simplex centroids, reducing generation complexity and enhancing scalability. Additionally, SLM incorporates a flexible implementation of classifier-free guidance, enhancing unconditional generation performance. Extensive experiments on DNA promoter and enhancer design, protein design, character-level and large-vocabulary language modeling demonstrate the competitive performance and strong potential of SLM. Our code can be found at https://github.com/GenSI-THUAIR/SLM.

We introduce the Shortlisting Model (SLM), a novel simplex-based diffusion model inspired by progressive candidate pruning. SLM operates on simplex centroids, reducing generation complexity and enhancing scalability. Additionally, SLM incorporates a flexible implementation of classifier-free guidance, enhancing unconditional generation performance. Extensive experiments on DNA promoter and enhancer design, protein design, character-level and large-vocabulary language modeling demonstrate the competitive performance and strong potential of SLM. Our code can be found at https://github.com/GenSI-THUAIR/SLM.

paragraphs: The Shortlisting Model addresses generation of discrete variables, a problem shared by language modeling and biological sequence design. Its organizing idea is progressive candidate pruning: generation is framed around narrowing a set of possible choices. This motivates a diffusion model designed specifically for discrete outcomes.

SLM operates on simplex centroids, using that representation to reduce generation complexity and improve scalability. The shortlisted-candidate perspective gives the approach a common structure across tasks with different discrete vocabularies. The model also includes a flexible implementation of classifier-free guidance, which the authors report improves unconditional generation performance.

Experiments cover DNA promoter and enhancer design, protein design, character-level language modeling, and language modeling with large vocabularies. The authors report competitive performance across these settings, supporting the potential of the same modeling approach in both biological and textual applications. The contribution centers on simplifying discrete diffusion through its representation and generation process, with empirical evidence of usefulness across several kinds of sequence generation.
summary.tldr: The Shortlisting Model uses simplex-centroid diffusion inspired by candidate pruning for scalable discrete generation across language and biological sequences.

title: ShortListing Model: A Streamlined Simplex Diffusion for Discrete Variable Generation

abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) learn probability distributions over natural protein sequences. By learning from hundreds of millions of natural protein sequences, protein understanding and design capabilities emerge. Recent works have shown that scaling these models improves structure prediction, but does not seem to improve mutation understanding and representation quality for protein function prediction. We introduce PoET-2, a multimodal, retrieval-augmented protein foundation model that incorporates in-context learning of family-specific evolutionary constraints with optional structure conditioning to learn generative distributions over protein sequences. PoET-2 uses a hierarchical transformer encoder that is equivariant to sequence context ordering and a dual decoder architecture with both causal and masked language modeling objectives, allowing PoET-2 to operate in both fully generative and bidirectional representation learning modes. PoET-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot variant effect prediction, excelling at scoring variants with multiple mutations and challenging indel mutations. In supervised settings, PoET-2 embeddings outperform previous methods for learning sequence-function relationships, especially with small datasets. This work highlights the benefits of combining retrieval augmentation with multimodal, family-centric modeling for advancing protein foundation models.

title: Understanding protein function with a multimodal retrieval-augmented foundation model

abstract: Large language model (LLM) routers improve the efficiency of multi-model systems by directing each query to the most appropriate model while leveraging the diverse strengths of heterogeneous LLMs. Most existing approaches frame routing as a classification problem based solely on the input query. While this reduces overhead by avoiding inference across all models, it overlooks valuable information that could be gleaned from potential outputs and fails to capture implicit intent or contextual nuances that often emerge only during response generation. These limitations can result in suboptimal routing decisions, particularly for complex or ambiguous queries that require deeper semantic understanding. To address this challenge, we propose Lookahead, a routing framework that "foresees" potential model outputs by predicting their latent representations and uses these predictions to guide model selection, thus enabling more informed routing without full inference. Within this framework, we implement two approaches based on causal and masked language models. Empirical evaluations across seven public benchmarks—spanning instruction following, mathematical reasoning, and code generation—show that Lookahead consistently outperforms existing routing baselines, achieving an average performance gain of 7.7\% over the state-of-the-art. Our code is available at https://github.com/huangcb01/lookahead-routing.

paragraphs: A language-model router chooses which model should answer a query. Many routers make that choice using only the input, avoiding the expense of asking every candidate model to generate an answer. The paper identifies a weakness in this approach: important intent or context may become clearer only when considering what a response would look like.

Lookahead addresses this by predicting latent representations of potential outputs. These internal representations supply information about possible responses without requiring full generation from every candidate. The router then uses those predictions to select a model. The authors implement this idea in two forms, based on causal language models and masked language models.

Across seven public benchmarks covering instruction following, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, Lookahead consistently exceeds the tested routing baselines. The reported average gain over the state of the art is 7.7%. These results support using anticipated response information to improve routing, particularly for the complex or ambiguous queries that motivate the framework.
summary.tldr: Lookahead improves model routing by predicting representations of possible responses without fully generating them.

title: Lookahead Routing for Large Language Models

abstract: We introduce Perception Encoder (PE), a family of state-of-the-art vision encoders for image and video understanding. Traditionally, vision encoders have relied on a variety of pretraining objectives, each excelling at different downstream tasks. Surprisingly, after scaling a carefully tuned image pretraining recipe and refining with a robust video data engine, we find that contrastive vision-language training alone can produce strong, general embeddings for all of these downstream tasks. There is only one caveat: these embeddings are hidden within the intermediate layers of the network. To draw them out, we introduce two alignment methods: language alignment for multimodal language modeling, and spatial alignment for dense prediction. Together, our PE family of models achieves state-of-the-art results on a wide variety of tasks, including zero-shot image and video classification and retrieval; document, image, and video Q&A; and spatial tasks such as detection, tracking, and depth estimation. We release our models, code, and novel dataset of synthetically and human-annotated videos: https://github.com/facebookresearch/perception_models

paragraphs: Perception Encoder is a family of vision encoders for image and video understanding. The paper investigates whether contrastive vision-language training can produce representations useful across tasks that traditionally favor different pretraining objectives. After scaling a carefully tuned image-training recipe and refining it with a video data engine, the authors find broad capabilities within the resulting network.

The key qualification is where those capabilities appear: the useful general representations reside in intermediate layers. To make them available for downstream use, the authors introduce language alignment for multimodal language modeling and spatial alignment for dense prediction. These two methods adapt the internal visual information to the requirements of different task families.

The resulting models achieve reported state-of-the-art performance across classification, retrieval, question answering, detection, tracking, and depth estimation. This range includes both images and videos. The findings suggest that assessing a vision encoder only through its final output can overlook valuable internal representations. The release includes models, code, and a video dataset with synthetic and human annotations.
summary.tldr: Perception Encoder extracts broadly useful intermediate visual representations through language and spatial alignment.

title: Perception Encoder: The best visual embeddings are not at the output of the network

abstract: In-the-wild photo collections often contain limited volumes of imagery and exhibit multiple appearances, e.g., taken at different times of day or seasons, posing significant challenges to scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. Although recent adaptations of Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have improved in these areas, they tend to oversmooth and are prone to overfitting. In this paper, we present MS-GS, a novel framework designed with \textbf{M}ulti-appearance capabilities in \textbf{S}parse-view scenarios using 3D\textbf{GS}. To address the lack of support due to sparse initializations, our approach is built on the geometric priors elicited from monocular depth estimations. The key lies in extracting and utilizing local semantic regions with a Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points anchored algorithm for reliable alignment and geometry cues. Then, to introduce multi-view constraints, we propose a series of geometry-guided supervision steps at virtual views in pixel and feature levels to encourage 3D consistency and reduce overfitting. We also introduce a dataset and an in-the-wild experiment setting to set up more realistic benchmarks. We demonstrate that MS-GS achieves photorealistic renderings under various challenging sparse-view and multi-appearance conditions, and outperforms existing approaches significantly across different datasets.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a scene from a small photo collection is difficult when the images also differ in lighting, season, or time of day. Existing reconstruction methods can oversmooth details or fit the available views too closely. MS-GS adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting to this combination of sparse viewpoints and changing appearances.

The method draws geometric guidance from depth estimated from individual images. To align that guidance reliably, it extracts local semantic regions and anchors them using Structure-from-Motion points. This supplies useful geometry where sparse initialization offers insufficient support. The framework also supervises virtual viewpoints at both pixel and feature levels, using geometry to encourage consistency between views.

These additional constraints are intended to reduce overfitting and strengthen the reconstructed three-dimensional structure. The authors introduce a dataset and an experimental setting aimed at more realistic photo collections. Across different datasets, they report photorealistic renderings under challenging sparse-view and multi-appearance conditions, with substantial improvements over existing approaches. The results support combining depth priors, local alignment, and virtual-view supervision.
summary.tldr: MS-GS uses depth guidance and virtual-view supervision to reconstruct scenes from sparse photographs with varying appearances.

title: MS-GS: Multi-Appearance Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting in the Wild

abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is a widely used method for optimizing expensive black-box functions, relying on probabilistic surrogate models such as Gaussian Processes (GPs). The quality of the surrogate model is crucial for good optimization performance, especially in the few-shot setting where only a small number of batches of points can be evaluated. In this setting, the initialization plays a critical role in shaping the surrogate's predictive quality and guiding subsequent optimization. Despite this, practitioners typically rely on (quasi-)random designs to cover the input space. However, such approaches neglect two key factors: (a) random designs may not be space-filling, and (b) efficient hyperparameter learning during initialization is essential for high-quality prediction, which may conflict with space-filling designs. To address these limitations, we propose Hyperparameter-Informed Predictive Exploration (HIPE), a novel acquisition strategy that balances space-filling exploration with hyperparameter learning using information-theoretic principles. We derive a closed-form expression for HIPE in the GP setting and demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive experiments in active learning and few-shot BO. Our results show that HIPE outperforms standard initialization strategies in terms of predictive accuracy, hyperparameter identification, and optimization performance, particularly in large-batch, few-shot settings relevant to many real-world BO applications.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization relies on a probabilistic surrogate to guide evaluations of an expensive function. When only a few batches can be evaluated, the initial observations strongly influence both predictive quality and later choices. This paper argues that selecting initial points solely to cover the input space overlooks the need to learn the surrogate's hyperparameters.

The proposed Hyperparameter-Informed Predictive Exploration strategy balances these goals using information-theoretic principles. Broad coverage and informative hyperparameter estimation can favor different points, so the acquisition strategy considers both. The authors derive a closed-form expression for the method when the surrogate is a Gaussian process.

Experiments in active learning and few-shot Bayesian optimization report improvements over standard initialization strategies in prediction, hyperparameter identification, and optimization performance. The gains are particularly evident when batches are large and only a few rounds are available. These findings highlight initialization as a learning problem in its own right: early evaluations should help establish a useful model of the function as well as explore its domain.
summary.tldr: HIPE improves Bayesian optimization initialization by balancing input-space coverage with learning the surrogate model's hyperparameters.

title: Informed Initialization for Bayesian Optimization and Active Learning

abstract: Offline meta-RL usually tackles generalization by inferring task beliefs from high-quality samples or warmup explorations. The restricted form limits their generality and usability since these supervision signals are expensive and even infeasible to acquire in advance for unseen tasks. Learning directly from the raw text about decision tasks is a promising alternative to leverage a much broader source of supervision. In the paper, we propose **T**ext-to-**D**ecision **A**gent (**T2DA**), a simple and scalable framework that supervises offline meta-RL with natural language. We first introduce a generalized world model to encode multi-task decision data into a dynamics-aware embedding space. Then, inspired by CLIP, we predict which textual description goes with which decision embedding, effectively bridging their semantic gap via contrastive language-decision pre-training and aligning the text embeddings to comprehend the environment dynamics. After training the text-conditioned generalist policy, the agent can directly realize zero-shot text-to-decision generation in response to language instructions. Comprehensive experiments on MuJoCo and Meta-World benchmarks show that T2DA facilitates high-capacity zero-shot generalization and outperforms various types of baselines. Our code is available at [https://github.com/NJU-RL/T2DA](https://github.com/NJU-RL/T2DA).

paragraphs: An offline meta-reinforcement learning agent needs a way to understand which task it should perform. Common approaches infer this from high-quality examples or exploratory interaction, which may be expensive or unavailable for a new task. Text-to-Decision Agent investigates natural-language descriptions as a broader source of task supervision.

T2DA first uses a generalized world model to map decision data from multiple tasks into representations that capture environment dynamics. Contrastive language-decision pre-training then learns which textual descriptions correspond to which decision representations. This alignment gives text representations a connection to how the environment behaves. A generalist policy is subsequently trained to condition its decisions on text.

After training, the agent can respond to language instructions with zero-shot decisions. Experiments on MuJoCo and Meta-World report strong zero-shot generalization and improvements over several types of baselines. The key contribution is the bridge between language and dynamics-aware decision data. It makes task descriptions useful to a policy by connecting their meaning to the behavior of the environments represented during training.
summary.tldr: T2DA aligns natural-language descriptions with dynamics-aware decision representations to support zero-shot, text-conditioned reinforcement learning.

title: Text-to-Decision Agent: Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning from Natural Language Supervision

abstract: Test-time compute has empowered multimodal large language models to generate extended reasoning chains, yielding strong performance on tasks such as multimodal math reasoning. However, we observe that this improved reasoning ability often comes with increased hallucination: as generations become longer, models tend to drift away from image-grounded content and rely more on language priors. Attention analysis reveals that longer reasoning chains reduce focus on visual inputs, contributing to hallucination. To systematically study this phenomenon, we introduce RH-AUC, a metric that quantifies how a model's perception accuracy changes with reasoning length, enabling evaluation of whether the model preserves visual grounding while reasoning. We also release RH-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark covering diverse multimodal tasks, designed to jointly assess the balance of reasoning ability and hallucination. We find that (i) larger models generally exhibit a better balance between reasoning and perception; (ii) reasoning and perception balance depends more on the types and domains of the training data than its volume. Our findings highlight the need for evaluation frameworks that account for both reasoning quality and perceptual reliability.

paragraphs: Longer reasoning can improve a multimodal model's problem solving, but this paper finds that it often accompanies increased hallucination. As responses grow, models tend to move away from image-supported content and rely more heavily on language-based expectations. Attention analysis associates longer reasoning chains with reduced focus on visual inputs.

The authors introduce RH-AUC to measure how perception accuracy changes with reasoning length. This allows evaluation of whether a model remains visually grounded as it reasons. They also release RH-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark covering multiple multimodal tasks and assessing reasoning ability alongside hallucination, so that stronger reasoning scores can be considered together with perceptual reliability.

The study finds that larger models generally achieve a better balance between reasoning and perception. It also reports that training-data types and domains matter more to this balance than data volume. These are qualified empirical findings, rather than a claim that extra reasoning always harms perception. The work motivates evaluating the connection between reasoning length and visual evidence whenever extended reasoning is used to improve multimodal performance.
summary.tldr: Longer multimodal reasoning often weakens visual grounding, motivating a metric and benchmark that assess reasoning alongside hallucination.

title: More Thinking, Less Seeing? Assessing Amplified Hallucination in Multimodal Reasoning Models

abstract: Graph Prompt Learning (GPL) has emerged as a promising paradigm that bridges graph pretraining models and downstream scenarios, mitigating label dependency and the misalignment between upstream pretraining and downstream tasks. Although existing GPL studies explore various prompt strategies, their effectiveness and underlying principles remain unclear. We identify two critical limitations: (1) Lack of consensus on underlying mechanisms: Despite current GPLs have advanced the field, there is no consensus on how prompts interact with pretrained models, as different strategies intervene at varying spaces within the model, i.e., input-level, layer-wise, and representation-level prompts. (2) Limited scenario adaptability: Most methods fail to generalize across diverse downstream scenarios, especially under data distribution shifts (e.g., homophilic-to-heterophilic graphs). To address these issues, we theoretically analyze existing GPL approaches and reveal that representation-level prompts essentially function as fine-tuning a simple downstream classifier, proposing that graph prompt learning should focus on unleashing the capability of pretrained models, and the classifier should adapt to downstream scenarios. Based on our findings, we propose UniPrompt, a novel GPL method that adapts any pretrained models, unleashing the capability of pretrained models while preserving the input graph. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can effectively integrate with various pretrained models and achieve strong performance across in-domain and cross-domain scenarios.

paragraphs: Graph prompt learning adapts pretrained graph models to downstream tasks, but prompts can intervene at very different places: inputs, internal layers, or final representations. This makes their underlying role difficult to compare. Existing approaches also struggle to adapt across different graph distributions, including shifts in whether connected nodes tend to be similar.

The authors theoretically analyze these approaches and find that representation-level prompts essentially act like fine-tuning a simple downstream classifier. They use this result to motivate a division of responsibilities: prompting should draw out the pretrained model’s capabilities, while the classifier should adapt to the downstream scenario. This analysis gives the proposed method a specific rationale beyond choosing another prompt placement.

UniPrompt follows that principle while preserving the input graph. It is proposed as an adaptation method for arbitrary pretrained models, and experiments demonstrate integration with various pretrained models. The reported results show strong performance both within a domain and across domains. The empirical evidence supports broad compatibility across the models and scenarios evaluated, alongside the paper’s more general design aim.
summary.tldr: UniPrompt uses a theoretical analysis of graph prompts to guide adaptation across pretrained models and downstream domains while preserving the input graph.

title: One Prompt Fits All: Universal Graph Adaptation for Pretrained Models

abstract: Stream networks, a unique class of spatiotemporal graphs, exhibit complex directional flow constraints and evolving dependencies, making uncertainty quantification a critical yet challenging task. Traditional conformal prediction methods struggle in this setting due to the need for joint predictions across multiple interdependent locations and the intricate spatio-temporal dependencies inherent in stream networks. Existing approaches either neglect dependencies, leading to overly conservative predictions, or rely solely on data-driven estimations, failing to capture the rich topological structure of the network. To address these challenges, we propose Spatio-Temporal Adaptive Conformal Inference (STACI), a novel framework that integrates network topology and temporal dynamics into the conformal prediction framework. STACI introduces a topology-aware nonconformity score that respects directional flow constraints and dynamically adjusts prediction sets to account for temporal distributional shifts. We provide theoretical guarantees on the validity of our approach and demonstrate its superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results show that STACI effectively balances prediction efficiency and coverage, outperforming existing conformal prediction methods for stream networks.

paragraphs: Uncertainty estimation in stream networks must account for locations connected by directional flow and dependencies that change over time. Predictions at these locations are interrelated, making joint uncertainty difficult to represent. The paper argues that existing conformal methods either overlook these dependencies and become overly conservative or fail to use the network's topological structure.

Spatio-Temporal Adaptive Conformal Inference, or STACI, incorporates both network structure and temporal dynamics. Its topology-aware nonconformity score measures prediction mismatch while respecting directional flow constraints. The framework also adjusts prediction sets dynamically as the data distribution shifts over time, connecting spatial structure with adaptation to changing conditions.

The authors provide theoretical validity guarantees and evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world datasets. STACI achieves a better balance between coverage and prediction efficiency than existing conformal approaches for stream networks. This balance matters because uncertainty sets should include the outcomes they are intended to cover without becoming unnecessarily broad. The reported results support using known network structure to make those sets more informative.
summary.tldr: STACI incorporates directional network structure and temporal adaptation into conformal prediction to improve uncertainty sets for stream networks.

title: Topology-Aware Conformal Prediction for Stream Networks

abstract: Recent advancements in 3D object detection and novel category detection have made significant progress, yet research on learning generalized 3D objectness remains insufficient. In this paper, we delve into learning open-world 3D objectness, which focuses on detecting all objects in a 3D scene, including novel objects unseen during training. Traditional closed-set 3D detectors struggle to generalize to open-world scenarios, while directly incorporating 3D open-vocabulary models for open-world ability struggles with vocabulary expansion and semantic overlap. To achieve generalized 3D object discovery, We propose OP3Det, a class-agnostic Open-World Prompt-free 3D Detector to detect any objects within 3D scenes without relying on hand-crafted text prompts. We introduce the strong generalization and zero-shot capabilities of 2D foundation models, utilizing both 2D semantic priors and 3D geometric priors for class-agnostic proposals to broaden 3D object discovery. Then, by integrating complementary information from point cloud and RGB image in the cross-modal mixture of experts, OP3Det dynamically routes uni-modal and multi-modal features to learn generalized 3D objectness. Extensive experiments demonstrate the extraordinary performance of OP3Det, which significantly surpasses existing open-world 3D detectors by up to 16.0% in AR and achieves a 13.5% improvement compared to closed-world 3D detectors.

In this paper, we delve into learning open-world 3D objectness, which focuses on detecting all objects in a 3D scene, including novel objects unseen during training. Traditional closed-set 3D detectors struggle to generalize to open-world scenarios, while directly incorporating 3D open-vocabulary models for open-world ability struggles with vocabulary expansion and semantic overlap. To achieve generalized 3D object discovery, We propose OP3Det, a class-agnostic Open-World Prompt-free 3D Detector to detect any objects within 3D scenes without relying on hand-crafted text prompts. We introduce the strong generalization and zero-shot capabilities of 2D foundation models, utilizing both 2D semantic priors and 3D geometric priors for class-agnostic proposals to broaden 3D object discovery. Then, by integrating complementary information from point cloud and RGB image in the cross-modal mixture of experts, OP3Det dynamically routes uni-modal and multi-modal features to learn generalized 3D objectness. Extensive experiments demonstrate the extraordinary performance of OP3Det, which significantly surpasses existing open-world 3D detectors by up to 16.0% in AR and achieves a 13.5% improvement compared to closed-world 3D detectors.

paragraphs: Open-world 3D object detection aims to find objects even when their categories were absent from training. This paper focuses on generalized objectness: recognizing that something is an object without first requiring a known category name. Its proposed detector, OP3Det, is class-agnostic and does not depend on handcrafted text prompts.

OP3Det combines semantic information from 2D foundation models with geometric information from 3D data to produce class-agnostic object proposals. It then brings together point-cloud and RGB-image information through a cross-modal mixture of experts. Dynamic routing uses both single-modality and combined features to learn objectness from complementary sources. This addresses difficulties that arise when open-world detection depends on an expanding vocabulary with overlapping meanings.

The reported experiments show gains of up to 16.0% in average recall over existing open-world 3D detectors and a 13.5% improvement compared with closed-world detectors. These results support using semantic and geometric evidence together to broaden object discovery. The method’s goal is to find objects beyond the training categories, with the reported improvements reflecting the evaluated detection settings.
summary.tldr: OP3Det combines 2D semantics, 3D geometry, and cross-modal experts to improve prompt-free detection of objects beyond known training categories.

title: Towards 3D Objectness Learning in an Open World

abstract: Deep learning-based computational methods have achieved promising results in predicting protein-protein interactions (PPIs). However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on isolated pairwise evaluations, overlooking a model's capability to reconstruct biologically meaningful PPI networks, which is crucial for biology research. To address this gap, we introduce PRING, the first comprehensive benchmark that evaluates PRotein-protein INteraction prediction from a Graph-level perspective. PRING curates a high-quality, multi-species PPI network dataset comprising 21,484 proteins and 186,818 interactions, with well-designed strategies to address both data redundancy and leakage. Building on this golden-standard dataset, we establish two complementary evaluation paradigms: (1) topology-oriented tasks, which assess intra and cross-species PPI network construction, and (2) function-oriented tasks, including protein complex pathway prediction, GO module analysis, and essential protein justification. These evaluations not only reflect the model's capability to understand the network topology but also facilitate protein function annotation, biological module detection, and even disease mechanism analysis. Extensive experiments on four representative model categories, consisting of sequence similarity-based, naive sequence-based, protein language model-based, and structure-based approaches, demonstrate that current PPI models have potential limitations in recovering both structural and functional properties of PPI networks, highlighting the gap in supporting real-world biological applications. We believe PRING provides a reliable platform to guide the development of more effective PPI prediction models for the community. The dataset and source code of PRING are available at https://github.com/SophieSarceau/PRING.

title: PRING: Rethinking Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction from Pairs to Graphs

abstract: High dynamic range (HDR) images, with their rich tone and detail reproduction, hold significant potential to enhance computer vision systems, particularly in autonomous driving. However, most neural networks for embedded vision are trained on low dynamic range (LDR) inputs and suffer substantial performance degradation when handling high-bit-depth HDR images due to the challenges posed by extreme dynamic ranges. In this paper, we propose a novel tone mapping method that not only bridges the gap between HDR RAW inputs and the LDR sRGB requirements of detection networks but also achieves end-to-end optimization with the downstream tasks. Instead of relying on traditional image signal processing (ISP) pipeline, we introduce neural photometric calibration to regularize dynamic ranges and a scaling-invariant local tone mapping module to preserve image details. In addition, our architecture also supports performance transfer finetuning, enabling efficient adaptation from the LDR model to the HDR RAW model with minimal cost. The proposed method outperforms traditional tone mapping algorithms and advanced AI-ISP methods in challenging automotive HDR scenes. Moreover, our pipeline achieves real-time processing of 4K high-bit-depth HDR inputs on the Nvidia Jetson platform.

paragraphs: High-dynamic-range cameras capture brightness differences and details that conventional image inputs cannot represent as easily. Yet embedded object detectors are usually trained on low-dynamic-range images, creating a mismatch when they receive high-bit-depth HDR data. This paper proposes a tone-mapping pipeline that converts HDR RAW inputs into the LDR sRGB representation expected by detection networks.

The conversion is optimized end to end with the downstream task. Neural photometric calibration regularizes the dynamic range, while a scaling-invariant local tone-mapping module preserves image details. They also demonstrate real-time processing of 4K high-bit-depth HDR inputs on Nvidia Jetson. The findings combine detection effectiveness with an embedded deployment result, showing that task-optimized HDR conversion can operate at the reported resolution in real time.
summary.tldr: Task-optimized neural tone mapping improves automotive HDR object detection and processes 4K high-bit-depth inputs in real time on Jetson.

title: Real-Time Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping for High-Dynamic Range Object Detection

abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) assumes the agents make decisions based on Markov decision processes (MDPs) with one-step transition models. In many real-world applications, such as energy management and stock investment, agents can access multi-step predictions of future states, which provide additional advantages for decision making. However, multi-step predictions are inherently high-dimensional: naively embedding these predictions into an MDP leads to an exponential blow-up in state space and the curse of dimensionality. Moreover, existing RL theory provides few tools to analyze prediction-augmented MDPs, as it typically works on one-step transition kernels and cannot accommodate multi-step predictions with errors or partial action-coverage. We address these challenges with three key innovations: First, we propose the \emph{Bayesian value function} to characterize the optimal prediction-aware policy tractably. Second, we develop a novel \emph{Bellman–Jensen Gap} analysis on the Bayesian value function, which enables characterizing the value of imperfect predictions. Third, we introduce BOLA (Bayesian Offline Learning with Online Adaptation), a two-stage model-based RL algorithm that separates offline Bayesian value learning from lightweight online adaptation to real-time predictions. We prove that BOLA remains sample-efficient even under imperfect predictions. We validate our theory and algorithm on synthetic MDPs and a real-world wind energy storage control problem.

paragraphs: Decision-making agents may have forecasts covering several future steps, rather than only a one-step transition model. Such forecasts can improve decisions, but incorporating them directly into the state can cause an exponential increase in the state space. Forecasts can also be inaccurate or cover only some actions, creating difficulties for standard reinforcement learning analysis.

The paper introduces a Bayesian value function to characterize an optimal policy that uses predictions in a tractable way. A Bellman–Jensen Gap analysis then characterizes the value of imperfect predictions. This supplies a theoretical framework for reasoning about forecast usefulness even when predictions are incomplete or contain errors.

The proposed algorithm, BOLA, separates learning into two stages. It learns Bayesian values offline, then performs lightweight online adaptation to current predictions. The authors prove sample efficiency under imperfect predictions and validate the approach on synthetic decision processes and a wind-energy storage control problem. The contribution is both analytical and algorithmic: it provides a way to assess forecast value and a learning procedure that uses forecasts without naively expanding the state representation.
summary.tldr: BOLA combines offline Bayesian value learning with lightweight online adaptation to use imperfect multi-step forecasts efficiently.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Imperfect Transition Predictions: A Bellman-Jensen Approach

abstract: Training deep neural networks (DNNs) is a structured optimization problem, because the parameters are naturally represented by matrices and tensors rather than simple vectors. Under this structural representation, it has been widely observed that gradients are low-rank and Hessians are approximately block-wise diagonal. These structured properties are crucial for designing efficient optimization algorithms but may not be utilized by current popular optimizers like Adam. In this paper, we present a novel optimization algorithm ASGO that capitalizes on these properties by employing a preconditioner that is adaptively updated using structured gradients. By fine-grained theoretical analysis, ASGO is proven to achieve superior convergence rates compared to existing structured gradient methods. Based on the convergence theory, we further demonstrate that ASGO can benefit from the low-rank and block-wise diagonal properties. We also discuss practical modifications of ASGO and empirically verify the effectiveness of the algorithm on language model tasks.

paragraphs: ASGO starts from the observation that neural-network parameters have meaningful matrix and tensor structure. Treating them simply as a collection of individual numbers can miss useful patterns. The paper focuses on two commonly observed patterns: gradients often have low rank, and the Hessian, which describes local curvature, is approximately block diagonal.

The proposed optimizer uses these structures through an adaptive preconditioner. A preconditioner changes how a gradient translates into a parameter update; here, its updates depend on structured gradients. The purpose is to make optimization respond to relationships within the parameters, rather than leaving those relationships unused.

The authors prove improved convergence rates relative to existing structured-gradient methods in their theoretical analysis. They also use that theory to show how low-rank gradients and block-diagonal curvature can benefit ASGO. Practical modifications are evaluated on language-model tasks, providing empirical support for the algorithm. The contribution therefore connects an optimization design to both mathematical convergence results and observed training effectiveness.
summary.tldr: ASGO adapts gradient updates to neural-network structure, with improved theoretical convergence rates and empirical support on language-model tasks.

title: ASGO: Adaptive Structured Gradient Optimization

abstract: Palpation, the use of touch in medical examination, is almost exclusively performed by humans. We investigate a proof of concept for an artificial palpation method based on self-supervised learning. Our key idea is that an encoder-decoder framework can learn a **representation** from a sequence of tactile measurements that contains all the relevant information about the palpated object. We conjecture that such a representation can be used for downstream tasks such as tactile imaging and change detection. With enough training data, it should capture intricate patterns in the tactile measurements that go beyond a simple map of forces -- the current state of the art. To validate our approach, we both develop a simulation environment and collect a real-world dataset of soft objects and corresponding ground truth images obtained by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We collect palpation sequences using a robot equipped with a tactile sensor, and train a model that predicts sensory readings at different positions on the object. We investigate the representation learned in this process, and demonstrate its use in imaging and change detection.

paragraphs: Palpation uses touch to examine an object or body, and medical palpation is performed almost entirely by humans. This paper explores a proof of concept for artificial palpation through self-supervised learning. Its central idea is to learn a representation of a soft object from a sequence of tactile measurements.

The authors develop a simulation environment and collect real-world soft-object data with corresponding MRI ground-truth images. A robot equipped with a tactile sensor gathers palpation sequences. An encoder-decoder model is trained to predict sensory readings at different positions, creating a learning task grounded in the relationships among touches across the object.

The researchers then examine the learned representation and demonstrate its use for imaging and change detection. They conjecture that, given enough training data, such representations could capture intricate tactile patterns beyond simple force maps. The demonstrated downstream uses support the proof of concept, while the broader idea of capturing all relevant object information remains a proposed capability.
summary.tldr: A robotic palpation proof of concept learns tactile representations and demonstrates their use in imaging soft objects and detecting changes.

title: Toward Artificial Palpation: Representation Learning of Touch on Soft Bodies

abstract: Machine unlearning updates machine learning models to remove information from specific training data samples, complying with data protection regulations that allow individuals to request the removal of their personal data. Despite the recent development of numerous unlearning algorithms, reliable evaluation of these algorithms remains an open research question. In this work, we focus on membership inference attack (MIA) based evaluation, one of the most common approaches for evaluating unlearning algorithms, and address various pitfalls of existing evaluation metrics that lack theoretical understanding and reliability. Specifically, by modeling the proposed evaluation process as a cryptographic game between unlearning algorithms and MIA adversaries, the naturally-induced evaluation metric measures the data removal efficacy of unlearning algorithms and enjoys provable guarantees that existing evaluation metrics fail to satisfy. Furthermore, we propose a practical and efficient approximation of the induced evaluation metric and demonstrate its effectiveness through both theoretical analysis and empirical experiments. Overall, this work presents a novel and reliable approach to empirically evaluating unlearning algorithms, paving the way for the development of more effective unlearning techniques.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove information associated with particular training samples from an already trained model. Evaluating whether removal worked is difficult. A common approach uses membership inference attacks, which try to determine whether a sample belonged to the training data. This paper examines reliability problems in the metrics used for that evaluation.

The authors formulate evaluation as a cryptographic game between an unlearning algorithm and an adversary performing membership inference. The rules of this game induce a metric for measuring removal efficacy. This connects the evaluation score to a formal adversarial setting and gives it provable guarantees that existing metrics do not satisfy.

The paper also develops an efficient practical approximation to the induced metric, supported by theoretical analysis and empirical experiments. Its contribution concerns how to assess unlearning algorithms: it provides a more principled connection between an attack-based test and the removal behavior that test is intended to measure. That connection can support more reliable comparisons when developing unlearning methods.
summary.tldr: A cryptographic game provides a principled metric and practical approximation for evaluating machine unlearning through membership inference attacks.

title: A Reliable Cryptographic Framework for Empirical Machine Unlearning Evaluation

abstract: World Models have vastly permeated the field of Reinforcement Learning. Their ability to model the transition dynamics of an environment have led to tremendous improvements in sample efficiency for online RL. Among them, the most notorious example is Dreamer, a model that learns to act in a diverse set of image-based environments. In this paper, we leverage similarity search and stochastic representations to approximate a world model without a training procedure. We establish a comparison with PlaNet, a well-established world model of the Dreamer family. We evaluate the models on the quality of latent reconstruction and on the perceived similarity of the reconstructed image, on both next-step and long horizon dynamics prediction. The results of our study demonstrate that a search-based world model is comparable to a training based one in both cases. Notably, our model shows stronger performance in long-horizon prediction with respect to the baseline on a range of visually different environments.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a world model can approximate an environment's dynamics through memory search without a training procedure. World models predict how environments change, supporting more sample-efficient reinforcement learning. The proposed approach combines similarity search with stochastic representations to construct a search-based approximation of that predictive capability.

The authors compare the method with PlaNet, a trained world model from the Dreamer family. Evaluation considers both the quality of reconstructed latent representations and the perceived similarity of reconstructed images. It covers predictions of the next step as well as longer future sequences, testing whether the approach remains useful beyond an immediate transition.

The search-based model is reported to be comparable to the trained model across these evaluation settings. It performs more strongly than the baseline on long-horizon predictions in a range of visually different environments. These results support memory search as an alternative mechanism for the dynamics-prediction tasks studied. The evidence centers on reconstruction and prediction quality, which are the capabilities directly examined in the comparison.
summary.tldr: A world model built from similarity search and stochastic representations matches a trained baseline in reported prediction tests and improves long-horizon results.

title: Zero-shot World Models via Search in Memory

abstract: Although applications involving long-context inputs are crucial for the effective utilization of large language models (LLMs), they also result in increased computational costs and reduced performance. To address this challenge, we propose an efficient, training-free prompt compression method that retains key information within compressed prompts. We identify specific attention heads in transformer-based LLMs, which we designate as evaluator heads, that are capable of selecting tokens in long inputs that are most significant for inference. Building on this discovery, we develop EHPC, an Evaluator Head-based Prompt Compression method, which enables LLMs to rapidly "skim through'' input prompts by leveraging only the first few layers with evaluator heads during the pre-filling stage, subsequently passing only the important tokens to the model for inference. EHPC achieves state-of-the-art results across two mainstream benchmarks: prompt compression and long-context inference acceleration. Consequently, it effectively improves performance with the reduced costs associated with commercial API calls compared to prompt compressing methods. We further demonstrate that EHPC attains competitive results compared to key-value cache-based acceleration methods, thereby highlighting its potential to enhance the efficiency of LLMs for long-context tasks.

paragraphs: Long prompts increase language-model computation and can also reduce performance. This paper studies whether parts of the model itself can identify which input tokens are most useful before full inference. The authors find particular attention heads, called evaluator heads, that can select important information from long inputs.

Their method, EHPC, uses these heads in the first few Transformer layers during prompt processing. The model effectively skims the input, selects significant tokens, and passes the resulting shorter prompt onward for inference. This compression procedure requires no training, and its efficiency comes from using a limited initial computation to reduce the amount of text processed afterward.

EHPC achieves reported state-of-the-art results on benchmarks for prompt compression and long-context acceleration. It also improves performance while reducing commercial API costs compared with other prompt compression methods. Comparisons with key-value cache acceleration show competitive results. Together, the findings suggest that early attention heads can provide useful token selection signals for reducing the cost of long-context tasks.
summary.tldr: EHPC uses selected attention heads in early Transformer layers to compress long prompts without training and improve inference efficiency.

title: Efficient Prompt Compression with Evaluator Heads for Long-Context Transformer Inference

abstract: Recent advances in LVLMs have improved vision-language understanding, but they still struggle with spatial perception, limiting their ability to reason about complex 3D scenes. Unlike previous approaches that incorporate 3D representations into models to improve spatial understanding, we aim to unlock the potential of VLMs by leveraging spatially relevant image data. To this end, we introduce a novel 2D spatial data generation and annotation pipeline built upon scene data with 3D ground-truth. This pipeline enables the creation of a diverse set of spatial tasks, ranging from basic perception tasks to more complex reasoning tasks. Leveraging this pipeline, we construct SPAR-7M, a large-scale dataset generated from thousands of scenes across multiple public datasets. In addition, we introduce SPAR-Bench, a benchmark designed to offer a more comprehensive evaluation of spatial capabilities compared to existing spatial benchmarks, supporting both single-view and multi-view inputs. Training on both SPAR-7M and large-scale 2D datasets enables our models to achieve state-of-the-art performance on 2D spatial benchmarks. Further fine-tuning on 3D task-specific datasets yields competitive results, underscoring the effectiveness of our dataset in enhancing spatial reasoning.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can understand many aspects of images yet still struggle with spatial relationships in complex three-dimensional scenes. This paper investigates improving those abilities through spatially informative image data. Its approach uses scenes with known three-dimensional structure to generate and annotate two-dimensional training examples.

The resulting pipeline creates tasks ranging from basic spatial perception to more involved reasoning. The authors use it to build SPAR-7M from thousands of scenes across multiple public datasets. They also introduce SPAR-Bench, which evaluates spatial capabilities with both single-view and multi-view inputs. This pairs a training resource with an evaluation setup designed to cover spatial understanding more comprehensively.

Models trained on SPAR-7M together with large-scale two-dimensional datasets achieve state-of-the-art results on two-dimensional spatial benchmarks. Additional fine-tuning on datasets for specific three-dimensional tasks yields competitive results. These findings support the value of supervision derived from three-dimensional ground truth for teaching spatial reasoning through image inputs, with the reported three-dimensional task results involving further task-specific training.
summary.tldr: SPAR-7M uses image tasks grounded in known 3D scenes to improve vision-language models’ spatial perception and reasoning.

title: From Flatland to Space: Teaching Vision-Language Models to Perceive and Reason in 3D

abstract: Weak-to-strong generalization refers to the phenomenon where a stronger model trained under supervision from a weaker one can outperform its teacher. While prior studies aim to explain this effect, most theoretical insights are limited to abstract frameworks or linear/random feature models. In this paper, we provide a formal analysis of weak-to-strong generalization from a linear CNN (weak) to a two-layer ReLU CNN (strong). We consider structured data composed of label-dependent signals of varying difficulty and label-independent noise, and analyze gradient descent dynamics when the strong model is trained on data labeled by the pretrained weak model. Our analysis identifies two regimes—data-scarce and data-abundant—based on the signal-to-noise characteristics of the dataset, and reveals distinct mechanisms of weak-to-strong generalization. In the data-scarce regime, generalization occurs via benign overfitting or fails via harmful overfitting, depending on the amount of data, and we characterize the transition boundary. In the data-abundant regime, generalization emerges in the early phase through label correction, but we observe that overtraining can subsequently degrade performance.

In the data-abundant regime, generalization emerges in the early phase through label correction, but we observe that overtraining can subsequently degrade performance.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization occurs when a more capable model learns from a weaker model’s labels and nevertheless performs better than its teacher. This paper analyzes that phenomenon in a concrete nonlinear setting: a linear convolutional network provides supervision for a two-layer convolutional network with ReLU activations. The analysis follows the stronger model’s gradient descent training.

The data model contains label-related signals of different difficulty alongside noise unrelated to the labels. Within this structured setting, the authors identify data-scarce and data-abundant regimes based on signal and noise characteristics. When data are scarce, fitting the training examples can either support generalization through benign overfitting or undermine it through harmful overfitting. The analysis characterizes the boundary between those outcomes.

With abundant data, a different mechanism appears: the stronger model initially corrects errors in its teacher’s labels. Continuing training too long can then reduce performance. These results explain why surpassing a weak teacher depends on both the available data and training dynamics. They establish distinct mechanisms within the analyzed model and data assumptions, rather than a universal promise that stronger students will outperform their supervisors.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows how data availability and training duration determine whether a nonlinear student can outperform a linear teacher.

title: From Linear to Nonlinear: Provable Weak-to-Strong Generalization through Feature Learning

abstract: We study the problem of global maximization of a function f given a finite number of evaluations perturbed by noise. We consider a very weak assumption on the function, namely that it is locally smooth (in some precise sense) with respect to some semi-metric, around one of its global maxima. Compared to previous works on bandits in general spaces (Kleinberg et al., 2008; Bubeck et al., 2011a) our algorithm does not require the knowledge of this semi-metric. Our algorithm, StoSOO, follows an optimistic strategy to iteratively construct upper confidence bounds over the hierarchical partitions of the function domain to decide which point to sample next. A finite-time analysis of StoSOO shows that it performs almost as well as the best specifically-tuned algorithms even though the local smoothness of the function is not known.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to maximize a function globally when only a finite number of noisy evaluations are available. Its assumption is local: near at least one global maximum, the function must be smooth in a specified sense relative to some semi-metric. The algorithm does not need to know that semi-metric.

Stochastic Simultaneous Optimistic Optimization, or StoSOO, organizes the search through hierarchical partitions of the domain. It repeatedly constructs upper confidence bounds and uses them to decide which point to evaluate next. The optimistic strategy directs evaluations using what regions could plausibly offer, while accounting for uncertainty introduced by noisy observations.

The guarantee remains conditional on the stated local regularity around a global maximum.
summary.tldr: StoSOO uses optimistic hierarchical search to approach tuned algorithms' performance under noisy evaluations without knowing the function's local smoothness.

title: Stochastic Simultaneous Optimistic Optimization

abstract: In this paper we develop new dependence and conditional dependence measures and provide their estimators. An attractive property of these measures and estimators is that they are invariant to any monotone increasing transformations of the random variables, which is important in many applications including feature selection. Under certain conditions we show the consistency of these estimators, derive upper bounds on their convergence rates, and show that the estimators do not suffer from the curse of dimensionality. However, when the conditions are less restrictive, we derive a lower bound which proves that in the worst case the convergence can be arbitrarily slow similarly to some other estimators. Numerical illustrations demonstrate the applicability of our method.

Numerical illustrations demonstrate the applicability of our method.

paragraphs: The paper develops measures of dependence and conditional dependence, together with procedures for estimating them from data. A central property is invariance to monotone increasing transformations of the variables. Consequently, changing a variable's scale in a way that preserves its ordering does not change these measures or their estimators.

This property is useful in applications such as feature selection, where dependence assessments should not hinge on an arbitrary choice of scale. Under specified conditions, the authors establish consistency, bound convergence rates from above, and show that the estimators avoid the curse of dimensionality. These favorable conclusions are explicitly conditional on the setting covered by the analysis.

The paper also examines what happens under less restrictive conditions. A lower bound shows that worst-case convergence can then be arbitrarily slow, as with some other estimators. Numerical illustrations demonstrate applicability. Together, the results establish both the attraction of scale-invariant dependence estimation and the importance of the conditions supporting its statistical guarantees.
summary.tldr: Scale-invariant dependence estimators have favorable guarantees under certain conditions, but weaker conditions permit arbitrarily slow worst-case convergence.

title: Scale Invariant Conditional Dependence Measures

abstract: Online Passive-Aggressive (PA) learning is an effective framework for performing max-margin online learning. But the deterministic formulation and estimated single large-margin model could limit its capability in discovering descriptive structures underlying complex data. This paper presents online Bayesian Passive-Aggressive (BayesPA) learning, which subsumes the online PA and extends naturally to incorporate latent variables and perform nonparametric Bayesian inference, thus providing great flexibility for explorative analysis. We apply BayesPA to topic modeling and derive efficient online learning algorithms for max-margin topic models. We further develop nonparametric methods to resolve the number of topics. Experimental results on real datasets show that our approaches significantly improve time efficiency while maintaining comparable results with the batch counterparts.
