This paper develops a Bayesian version that includes ordinary Passive-Aggressive learning while extending it to richer probabilistic models.

BayesPA naturally accommodates latent variables and nonparametric Bayesian inference. These extensions allow the framework to represent hidden structure and address model complexity within the learning process. The authors apply it to topic modeling, deriving efficient online algorithms for max-margin topic models. They also develop nonparametric methods to determine the number of topics.

Experiments on real datasets show substantial gains in time efficiency while maintaining results comparable to batch counterparts. The findings support online learning as a practical way to fit these structured Bayesian predictors. The main contribution is a unified framework that combines large-margin online updates with latent representations, illustrated by topic models that can also resolve how many topics to use.
summary.tldr: Bayesian Passive-Aggressive learning extends online large-margin methods to latent and nonparametric models, improving training efficiency for topic modeling.

title: Online Bayesian Passive-Aggressive Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose several improvements on the block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe (BCFW) algorithm from Lacoste-Julien et al. (2013) recently used to optimize the structured support vector machine (SSVM) objective in the context of structured prediction, though it has wider applications. The key intuition behind our improvements is that the estimates of block gaps maintained by BCFW reveal the block suboptimality that can be used as an *adaptive* criterion. First, we sample objects at each iteration of BCFW in an adaptive non-uniform way via gap-based sampling. Second, we incorporate pairwise and away-step variants of Frank-Wolfe into the block-coordinate setting. Third, we cache oracle calls with a cache-hit criterion based on the block gaps. Fourth, we provide the first method to compute an approximate regularization path for SSVM. Finally, we provide an exhaustive empirical evaluation of all our methods on four structured prediction datasets.

paragraphs: This paper improves block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe optimization, focusing on structured support vector machines. Its central observation is that estimated gaps for individual blocks reveal how suboptimal those blocks remain. These estimates can therefore guide adaptive decisions throughout optimization, giving the algorithm information about where work is most useful.

The authors use block gaps to sample training objects nonuniformly at each iteration. They also incorporate pairwise and away-step Frank-Wolfe variants into the block-coordinate framework. A further improvement caches oracle calls and uses a gap-based criterion to decide when a cached result is acceptable. Together, these changes apply the same suboptimality information to sampling, updates, and reuse of computation.

The paper additionally introduces what it identifies as the first method for computing an approximate regularization path for structured support vector machines. An extensive empirical evaluation covers all proposed methods on four structured-prediction datasets. The contribution is a coordinated set of optimization tools built around block-gap estimates, with applications extending beyond the principal structured-SVM setting.
summary.tldr: Block-gap estimates guide adaptive sampling, update variants, caching, and regularization-path computation for structured-SVM optimization.

title: Minding the Gaps for Block Frank-Wolfe Optimization of Structured SVMs

abstract: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) is a classical representation learning technique for finding correlated variables in multi-view data. Several nonlinear extensions of the original linear CCA have been proposed, including kernel and deep neural network methods. These approaches seek maximally correlated projections among families of functions, which the user specifies (by choosing a kernel or neural network structure), and are computationally demanding. Interestingly, the theory of nonlinear CCA, without functional restrictions, had been studied in the population setting by Lancaster already in the 1950s, but these results have not inspired practical algorithms. We revisit Lancaster’s theory to devise a practical algorithm for nonparametric CCA (NCCA). Specifically, we show that the solution can be expressed in terms of the singular value decomposition of a certain operator associated with the joint density of the views. Thus, by estimating the population density from data, NCCA reduces to solving an eigenvalue system, superficially like kernel CCA but, importantly, without requiring the inversion of any kernel matrix. We also derive a partially linear CCA (PLCCA) variant in which one of the views undergoes a linear projection while the other is nonparametric. Using a kernel density estimate based on a small number of nearest neighbors, our NCCA and PLCCA algorithms are memory-efficient, often run much faster, and perform better than kernel CCA and comparable to deep CCA.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis learns representations that reveal correlations between different views of the same data. Nonlinear versions often restrict the transformations through a chosen kernel or neural architecture and can be computationally demanding. This paper revisits population-level theory for unrestricted nonlinear CCA and turns it into a practical nonparametric algorithm.

The authors express the solution through a singular value decomposition of an operator associated with the views’ joint density. Estimating that density from data reduces the practical task to an eigenvalue problem without requiring inversion of a kernel matrix. They also introduce partially linear CCA, which applies a linear projection to one view and a nonparametric transformation to the other.

They perform better than kernel CCA and comparably to deep CCA. These results show how the theoretical formulation can lead to useful representations with a favorable computational profile.
summary.tldr: Nonparametric CCA uses density estimation and an eigenvalue problem to learn correlated views without kernel-matrix inversion.

title: Nonparametric Canonical Correlation Analysis

abstract: The classic algorithm of Viterbi computes the most likely path in a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) that results in a given sequence of observations. It runs in time $O(Tn^2)$ given a sequence of T observations from a HMM with n states. Despite significant interest in the problem and prolonged effort by different communities, no known algorithm achieves more than a polylogarithmic speedup. In this paper, we explain this difficulty by providing matching conditional lower bounds. Our lower bounds are based on assumptions that the best known algorithms for the All-Pairs Shortest Paths problem (APSP) and for the Max-Weight k-Clique problem in edge-weighted graphs are essentially tight. Finally, using a recent algorithm by Green Larsen and Williams for online Boolean matrix-vector multiplication, we get a $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ speedup for the Viterbi algorithm when there are few distinct transition probabilities in the HMM.
originalAbstract: The classic algorithm of Viterbi computes the most likely path in a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) that results in a given sequence of observations. It runs in time $O(Tn^2)$ given a sequence of T observations from a HMM with n states. Despite significant interest in the problem and prolonged effort by different communities, no known algorithm achieves more than a polylogarithmic speedup. In this paper, we explain this difficulty by providing matching conditional lower bounds. Our lower bounds are based on assumptions that the best known algorithms for the All-Pairs Shortest Paths problem (APSP) and for the Max-Weight k-Clique problem in edge-weighted graphs are essentially tight. paragraphs: The Viterbi algorithm finds the most likely hidden-state path explaining a sequence of observations in a Hidden Markov Model. With T observations and n states, its standard running time is O(Tn²). This paper investigates why obtaining substantially faster general algorithms has remained difficult despite sustained interest.

The authors establish matching conditional lower bounds. These rely on assumptions that the best known algorithms for All-Pairs Shortest Paths and maximum-weight k-clique are essentially optimal. The implication is conditional: major Viterbi improvements would also imply faster algorithms for those underlying problems. The results explain the obstacle through connections to other computational tasks without claiming an unconditional impossibility theorem.

The paper also identifies an opportunity when a model has few distinct transition probabilities. Using an online Boolean matrix-vector multiplication algorithm, the authors obtain a speedup factor of 2 raised to an order of square root log n. This special-case improvement shows how structure in transition probabilities can permit acceleration even while the general problem faces the stated conditional barriers.
summary.tldr: Conditional lower bounds explain Viterbi’s resistance to speedups, while few distinct transition probabilities enable a faster special case.

title: Improving Viterbi is Hard: Better Runtimes Imply Faster Clique Algorithms

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning methods attain super-human performance in a wide range of environments. Such methods are grossly inefficient, often taking orders of magnitudes more data than humans to achieve reasonable performance. We propose Neural Episodic Control: a deep reinforcement learning agent that is able to rapidly assimilate new experiences and act upon them. Our agent uses a semi-tabular representation of the value function: a buffer of past experience containing slowly changing state representations and rapidly updated estimates of the value function. We show across a wide range of environments that our agent learns significantly faster than other state-of-the-art, general purpose deep reinforcement learning agents.

Such methods are grossly inefficient, often taking orders of magnitudes more data than humans to achieve reasonable performance. We propose Neural Episodic Control: a deep reinforcement learning agent that is able to rapidly assimilate new experiences and act upon them. Our agent uses a semi-tabular representation of the value function: a buffer of past experience containing slowly changing state representations and rapidly updated estimates of the value function. paragraphs: Neural Episodic Control addresses the amount of experience required by deep reinforcement learning. Strong eventual performance can come with a large data cost, delaying the point at which an agent behaves usefully. The paper proposes an agent designed to incorporate new experiences quickly and use them promptly when choosing how to act.

Its central component is a semi-tabular value-function representation stored in a buffer of past experience. The buffer combines state representations that change slowly with value estimates that update rapidly. This separates two rates of adaptation: how the agent represents a situation and how quickly it revises the value associated with experience of that situation.

Across a wide range of environments, the authors report significantly faster learning than other leading general-purpose deep reinforcement learning agents. The stated finding concerns learning speed, directly matching the motivation of making experience useful sooner. The contribution is therefore a concrete memory-based representation that couples relatively stable state descriptions with rapidly adjustable value information, supported by comparative learning results.
summary.tldr: Neural Episodic Control combines slowly changing state representations with rapidly updated stored values to learn faster from experience.

title: Neural Episodic Control

abstract: We introduce a scalable method for training robust neural networks based on abstract interpretation. We present several abstract transformers which balance efficiency with precision and show these can be used to train large neural networks that are certifiably robust to adversarial perturbations.
originalAbstract: We introduce a scalable method for training robust neural networks based on abstract interpretation. We present several abstract transformers which balance efficiency with precision and show these can be used to train large neural networks that are certifiably robust to adversarial perturbations.

paragraphs: This paper develops a method for training neural networks with certifiable robustness to adversarial perturbations. The central aim is to make robustness something supported by a guarantee within the method’s scope. Training is based on abstract interpretation, which supplies the framework for reasoning about the network’s behavior under perturbation.

The authors present several abstract transformers that trade off computational efficiency and precision. These alternatives matter because a robustness analysis must be informative enough to support certification while remaining practical to use during training. The contribution therefore includes choices about how that analysis is carried out, alongside the overall training method.

The stated result is that these transformers can train large neural networks that are certifiably robust to adversarial perturbations. This links the precision of the underlying analysis with the scale of the learning procedure. The paper’s contribution is a scalable way to bring certification into network training, with multiple transformer designs for balancing the computational cost and precision of the robustness reasoning.
summary.tldr: The paper uses abstract interpretation to train large neural networks with certified robustness while balancing computational efficiency and analysis precision.

title: Differentiable Abstract Interpretation for Provably Robust Neural Networks

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have been shown to produce realistic samples from high-dimensional distributions, but training them is considered hard. A possible explanation for training instabilities is the inherent imbalance between the networks: While the discriminator is trained directly on both real and fake samples, the generator only has control over the fake samples it produces since the real data distribution is fixed by the choice of a given dataset. We propose a simple modification that gives the generator control over the real samples which leads to a tempered learning process for both generator and discriminator. The real data distribution passes through a lens before being revealed to the discriminator, balancing the generator and discriminator by gradually revealing more detailed features necessary to produce high-quality results. The proposed module automatically adjusts the learning process to the current strength of the networks, yet is generic and easy to add to any GAN variant. In a number of experiments, we show that this can improve quality, stability and/or convergence speed across a range of different GAN architectures (DCGAN, LSGAN, WGAN-GP).

paragraphs: GAN training places the discriminator and generator in an uneven position: the discriminator learns from real and generated examples, while the generator controls only generated examples. This paper proposes that imbalance as a possible explanation for instability. It changes the interaction by giving the generator influence over how real samples are presented.

Real data pass through a learned lens before reaching the discriminator. The lens gradually reveals more detailed features, tempering the learning process for both networks. The proposed module adjusts automatically to their current strength, making the difficulty of the interaction responsive to how learning is progressing rather than exposing the same real-data representation throughout.

The authors describe the module as generic and easy to incorporate into GAN variants. Experiments across DCGAN, LSGAN, and WGAN-GP show that it can improve sample quality, stability, or convergence speed. The results support benefits across multiple architectures, with the qualification that the improvements need not cover every one of those outcomes in every experiment.
summary.tldr: An adaptive lens on real data tempers GAN training and can improve quality, stability, or convergence speed across several architectures.

title: Tempered Adversarial Networks

abstract: To cope with changing environments, recent developments in online learning have introduced the concepts of adaptive regret and dynamic regret independently. In this paper, we illustrate an intrinsic connection between these two concepts by showing that the dynamic regret can be expressed in terms of the adaptive regret and the functional variation. This observation implies that strongly adaptive algorithms can be directly leveraged to minimize the dynamic regret. As a result, we present a series of strongly adaptive algorithms that have small dynamic regrets for convex functions, exponentially concave functions, and strongly convex functions, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that exponential concavity is utilized to upper bound the dynamic regret. Moreover, all of those adaptive algorithms do not need any prior knowledge of the functional variation, which is a significant advantage over previous specialized methods for minimizing dynamic regret.

As a result, we present a series of strongly adaptive algorithms that have small dynamic regrets for convex functions, exponentially concave functions, and strongly convex functions, respectively. paragraphs: Online learning in a changing environment needs ways to measure whether a learner keeps adapting. Adaptive regret and dynamic regret approach this concern from different directions. This paper connects them by showing how dynamic regret can be expressed using adaptive regret together with functional variation, a measure of how the learning problem changes.

That connection makes strongly adaptive algorithms useful for controlling dynamic regret directly. The authors develop a series of such algorithms for convex, exponentially concave, and strongly convex functions. The result gives a common route to dynamic regret guarantees across these different classes, rather than treating adaptation and changing objectives as separate topics.

A practical feature is that the algorithms do not require advance knowledge of functional variation. They therefore avoid needing the amount of environmental change as an input. The authors also identify their use of exponential concavity to bound dynamic regret as a first, to their knowledge. Overall, the contribution is a theoretical bridge that yields algorithms with small dynamic regret.
summary.tldr: A connection between adaptive and dynamic regret yields algorithms that handle changing objectives without knowing their variation in advance.

title: Dynamic Regret of Strongly Adaptive Methods

abstract: We consider the problem of the optimization of bidding strategies in prior-dependent revenue-maximizing auctions, when the seller fixes the reserve prices based on the bid distributions. Our study is done in the setting where one bidder is strategic. Using a variational approach, we study the complexity of the original objective and we introduce a relaxation of the objective functional in order to use gradient descent methods. Our approach is simple, general and can be applied to various value distributions and revenue-maximizing mechanisms. The new strategies we derive yield massive uplifts compared to the traditional truthfully bidding strategy.

Our approach is simple, general and can be applied to various value distributions and revenue-maximizing mechanisms. The new strategies we derive yield massive uplifts compared to the traditional truthfully bidding strategy.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a bidder should act when an auction seller sets reserve prices using bid distributions. In these prior-dependent, revenue-maximizing auctions, the distribution of submitted bids is part of the seller’s pricing procedure. The study considers a setting with one strategic bidder and asks how that bidder can optimize a bidding strategy.

The authors use a variational approach to analyze the original objective, treating the bidding strategy as the object being optimized. They then introduce a relaxed objective that can be handled with gradient descent. The relaxation supplies a practical route for searching over strategies when directly working with the original objective is difficult.

The approach is presented as general enough to accommodate various value distributions and revenue-maximizing mechanisms. The derived strategies deliver very large gains compared with truthful bidding in the study. This finding concerns the specified setting in which reserve prices depend on bid distributions and one bidder behaves strategically. It highlights the value of optimizing behavior with the seller’s pricing rule explicitly in view.
summary.tldr: A relaxed optimization objective enables bidding strategies that substantially outperform truthful bidding in the studied reserve-price setting.

title: Learning to bid in revenue-maximizing auctions

abstract: Optimal transport is a foundational problem in optimization, that allows to compare probability distributions while taking into account geometric aspects. Its optimal objective value, the Wasserstein distance, provides an important loss between distributions that has been used in many applications throughout machine learning and statistics. Recent algorithmic progress on this problem and its regularized versions have made these tools increasingly popular. However, existing techniques require solving an optimization problem to obtain a single gradient of the loss, thus slowing down first-order methods to minimize the sum of losses, that require many such gradient computations. In this work, we introduce an algorithm to solve a regularized version of this problem of Wasserstein estimators, with a time per step which is sublinear in the natural dimensions of the problem. We introduce a dual formulation, and optimize it with stochastic gradient steps that can be computed directly from samples, without solving additional optimization problems at each step. Doing so, the estimation and computation tasks are performed jointly. We show that this algorithm can be extended to other tasks, including estimation of Wasserstein barycenters. We provide theoretical guarantees and illustrate the performance of our algorithm with experiments on synthetic data.

paragraphs: Wasserstein losses compare probability distributions while accounting for geometry. Optimizing a sum of these losses can be expensive because existing techniques solve an optimization problem merely to obtain each gradient. Repeating that inner computation throughout a first-order method creates a substantial bottleneck. This paper develops an algorithm for a regularized version of the Wasserstein estimation problem.

The authors introduce a dual formulation that can be optimized with stochastic gradient steps computed directly from samples. Each step avoids an additional optimization problem, so estimation and computation proceed jointly. The time per step is sublinear in the problem's natural dimensions, addressing the cost of individual updates as well as the nested structure of the earlier computation.

Its contribution is a way to reorganize regularized Wasserstein estimation around directly sampled updates, making repeated inner solves unnecessary for the proposed algorithm while retaining a theoretical account of its behavior.
summary.tldr: A stochastic dual method computes sample-based updates for regularized Wasserstein estimation without solving an extra optimization problem at each step.

title: Stochastic Optimization for Regularized Wasserstein Estimators

abstract: This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50. When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100X fewer labels.

We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50. When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100X fewer labels.

paragraphs: SimCLR studies how to learn useful image representations without labels through contrastive learning. Its framework avoids specialized network architectures and a memory bank, making the learning setup simpler. The paper’s central contribution is a systematic examination of which components make the contrastive prediction task produce representations that work well for subsequent classification.

Three findings guide the design. Combining data augmentations appropriately is critical because these transformations define the prediction task. A learned nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves representation quality. The experiments also find that contrastive learning benefits from larger batches and more training steps compared with supervised learning.

Together, these choices produce strong ImageNet results. A linear classifier on the learned representations reaches 76.5% top-1 accuracy, matching a supervised ResNet-50 and improving relatively by 7% over the previous state of the art. Fine-tuning with only 1% of labels reaches 85.8% top-5 accuracy. These evaluations show that the learned features support both direct classification and adaptation with limited labels.
summary.tldr: SimCLR shows how augmentation, a nonlinear transformation, and training scale combine to produce strong image representations without labels.

title: A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations

abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) in reinforcement learning allows one to evaluate novel decision policies without needing to conduct exploration, which is often costly or otherwise infeasible. We consider for the first time the semiparametric efficiency limits of OPE in Markov decision processes (MDPs), where actions, rewards, and states are memoryless. We show existing OPE estimators may fail to be efficient in this setting. We develop a new estimator based on cross-fold estimation of $q$-functions and marginalized density ratios, which we term double reinforcement learning (DRL). We show that DRL is efficient when both components are estimated at fourth-root rates and is also doubly robust when only one component is consistent. We investigate these properties empirically and demonstrate the performance benefits due to harnessing memorylessness.

This paper studies the statistical efficiency limits of that task in Markov decision processes. They propose double reinforcement learning, which combines cross-fold estimates of q-functions with marginalized density ratios. Efficiency and robustness thus offer separate advantages, with different requirements on the component estimates.
summary.tldr: Double reinforcement learning exploits Markov structure to provide efficient off-policy evaluation with a doubly robust estimator.

title: Double Reinforcement Learning for Efficient and Robust Off-Policy Evaluation

abstract: In recent years, a variety of gradient-based bi-level optimization methods have been developed for learning tasks. However, theoretical guarantees of these existing approaches often heavily rely on the simplification that for each fixed upper-level variable, the lower-level solution must be a singleton (a.k.a., Lower-Level Singleton, LLS). In this work, by formulating bi-level models from the optimistic viewpoint and aggregating hierarchical objective information, we establish Bi-level Descent Aggregation (BDA), a flexible and modularized algorithmic framework for bi-level programming. Theoretically, we derive a new methodology to prove the convergence of BDA without the LLS condition. Furthermore, we improve the convergence properties of conventional first-order bi-level schemes (under the LLS simplification) based on our proof recipe. Extensive experiments justify our theoretical results and demonstrate the superiority of the proposed BDA for different tasks, including hyper-parameter optimization and meta learning.

Many gradient-based approaches assume that each upper-level choice gives exactly one lower-level solution. The paper introduces Bi-level Descent Aggregation, or BDA, to work beyond that restriction. It uses an optimistic formulation, meaning that lower-level solutions are considered with the upper-level objective in mind. The framework combines objective information from both levels and organizes the algorithm into flexible, modular components. The authors develop a convergence proof that does not require the lower-level solution to be unique.

Their proof approach also improves convergence properties for conventional first-order schemes that retain the singleton assumption. Experiments on tasks including hyperparameter optimization and meta learning support the theoretical results and report advantages for BDA. The key advance is extending convergence analysis to a broader bi-level setting, rather than treating uniqueness as indispensable.
summary.tldr: BDA combines information from both optimization levels and provides convergence guarantees without requiring a unique lower-level solution.

title: A Generic First-Order Algorithmic Framework for Bi-Level Programming Beyond Lower-Level Singleton

abstract: Despite the remarkable performance of deep neural networks on various computer vision tasks, they are known to be susceptible to adversarial perturbations, which makes it challenging to deploy them in real-world safety-critical applications. In this paper, we conjecture that the leading cause of adversarial vulnerability is the distortion in the latent feature space, and provide methods to suppress them effectively. Explicitly, we define \emph{vulnerability} for each latent feature and then propose a new loss for adversarial learning, \emph{Vulnerability Suppression (VS)} loss, that aims to minimize the feature-level vulnerability during training. We further propose a Bayesian framework to prune features with high vulnerability to reduce both vulnerability and loss on adversarial samples. We validate our \emph{Adversarial Neural Pruning with Vulnerability Suppression (ANP-VS)} method on multiple benchmark datasets, on which it not only obtains state-of-the-art adversarial robustness but also improves the performance on clean examples, using only a fraction of the parameters used by the full network. Further qualitative analysis suggests that the improvements come from the suppression of feature-level vulnerability.

summary.tldr: Training to suppress vulnerable internal features and pruning them improves reported adversarial robustness while reducing network size.

title: Adversarial Neural Pruning with Latent Vulnerability Suppression

abstract: Generative models in molecular design tend to be richly parameterized, data-hungry neural models, as they must create complex structured objects as outputs. Estimating such models from data may be challenging due to the lack of sufficient training data. In this paper, we propose a surprisingly effective self-training approach for iteratively creating additional molecular targets. We first pre-train the generative model together with a simple property predictor. The property predictor is then used as a likelihood model for filtering candidate structures from the generative model. Additional targets are iteratively produced and used in the course of stochastic EM iterations to maximize the log-likelihood that the candidate structures are accepted. A simple rejection (re-weighting) sampler suffices to draw posterior samples since the generative model is already reasonable after pre-training. We demonstrate significant gains over strong baselines for both unconditional and conditional molecular design. In particular, our approach outperforms the previous state-of-the-art in conditional molecular design by over 10% in absolute gain. Finally, we show that our approach is useful in other domains as well, such as program synthesis.

summary.tldr: Iteratively filtering generated structures with a property predictor creates additional training targets and improves reported molecular-design performance.

title: Improving Molecular Design by Stochastic Iterative Target Augmentation

abstract: We consider the problem of learning to repair programs from diagnostic feedback (e.g., compiler error messages). Program repair is challenging for two reasons: First, it requires reasoning and tracking symbols across source code and diagnostic feedback. Second, labeled datasets available for program repair are relatively small. In this work, we propose novel solutions to these two challenges. First, we introduce a program-feedback graph, which connects symbols relevant to program repair in source code and diagnostic feedback, and then apply a graph neural network on top to model the reasoning process. Second, we present a self-supervised learning paradigm for program repair that leverages unlabeled programs available online to create a large amount of extra program repair examples, which we use to pre-train our models. We evaluate our proposed approach on two applications: correcting introductory programming assignments (DeepFix dataset) and correcting the outputs of program synthesis (SPoC dataset). Our final system, DrRepair, significantly outperforms prior work, achieving 68.2% full repair rate on DeepFix (+22.9% over the prior best), and 48.4% synthesis success rate on SPoC (+3.7% over the prior best).

Training such systems is also difficult because labeled repair examples are relatively scarce. This paper tackles both issues in DrRepair, a system that combines graph-based reasoning with self-supervised pretraining.

Its program-feedback graph links symbols in the source code with symbols in diagnostic feedback. A graph neural network then models the reasoning needed for repair through these connections. To expand training data, the authors use unlabeled programs available online to create additional repair examples. Those examples support pretraining before evaluation on the target repair applications.

The system is tested on introductory programming assignments in DeepFix and on program-synthesis outputs in SPoC. It achieves a 68.2% full repair rate on DeepFix and a 48.4% synthesis success rate on SPoC, substantially exceeding prior work as reported in the abstract. These results support addressing both the representation of diagnostic relationships and the shortage of repair training data.
summary.tldr: DrRepair combines graphs linking code to diagnostic feedback with self-supervised pretraining to improve program repair and synthesis success.

title: Graph-based, Self-Supervised Program Repair from Diagnostic Feedback

abstract: We consider learning a multi-class classification model in the federated setting, where each user has access to the positive data associated with only a single class. As a result, during each federated learning round, the users need to locally update the classifier without having access to the features and the model parameters for the negative classes. Thus, naively employing conventional decentralized learning such as distributed SGD or Federated Averaging may lead to trivial or extremely poor classifiers. In particular, for embedding based classifiers, all the class embeddings might collapse to a single point. To address this problem, we propose a generic framework for training with only positive labels, namely Federated Averaging with Spreadout (FedAwS), where the server imposes a geometric regularizer after each round to encourage classes to be spreadout in the embedding space. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that FedAwS can almost match the performance of conventional learning where users have access to negative labels. We further extend the proposed method to settings with large output spaces.

paragraphs: This paper considers federated classification in an unusually restricted setting: each user holds positive examples from only one class. During local updates, that user cannot access the features or model parameters for negative classes. Conventional distributed training can consequently produce poor or trivial classifiers because local learning lacks information that distinguishes one class from the others.

For classifiers based on embeddings, a particular failure is that all class representations may collapse to the same point. The proposed framework, Federated Averaging with Spreadout, or FedAwS, addresses this through a server-side geometric regularizer. After each federated round, the server encourages class embeddings to remain spread apart, adding separation that positive-only local updates do not provide.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that FedAwS can nearly match conventional learning in which users have negative labels available. They also extend the method to large output spaces. The result suggests that coordinating the geometry of class representations can compensate substantially for this restricted form of local supervision.
summary.tldr: FedAwS separates class embeddings at the server so federated learning with only positive local labels can nearly match conventional training.

title: Federated Learning with Only Positive Labels

abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is one of the most successful sampling methods in machine learning. However, its performance is significantly affected by the choice of hyperparameter values. Existing approaches for optimizing the HMC hyperparameters either optimize a proxy for mixing speed or consider the HMC chain as an implicit variational distribution and optimize a tractable lower bound that can be very loose in practice. Instead, we propose to optimize an objective that quantifies directly the speed of convergence to the target distribution. Our objective can be easily optimized using stochastic gradient descent. We evaluate our proposed method and compare to baselines on a variety of problems including sampling from synthetic 2D distributions, reconstructing sparse signals, learning deep latent variable models and sampling molecular configurations from the Boltzmann distribution of a 22 atom molecule. We find that our method is competitive with or improves upon alternative baselines in all these experiments.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is a sampling method whose effectiveness depends strongly on its hyperparameters. Choosing these settings well matters because the sampler must move toward the distribution of interest efficiently. The paper addresses this tuning problem by changing what the optimization procedure tries to improve.

Existing approaches either optimize a substitute measure for mixing speed or treat the sampling chain as a variational distribution and optimize a tractable lower bound. That bound can be loose in practice. The authors instead propose an objective that directly quantifies convergence speed toward the target distribution and can be optimized using stochastic gradient descent.

Across these experiments, the method matches or improves on alternative baselines. These findings support the practical value of tuning against a more direct convergence objective across several different sampling tasks, without establishing superiority for every possible target distribution.
summary.tldr: The paper tunes Hamiltonian Monte Carlo using a directly optimized convergence-speed objective, matching or improving on baselines in its experiments.

title: A Gradient Based Strategy for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo Hyperparameter Optimization

abstract: Submodular optimization has numerous applications such as crowdsourcing and viral marketing. In this paper, we study the problem of non-negative submodular function maximization subject to a $k$-system constraint, which generalizes many other important constraints in submodular optimization such as cardinality constraint, matroid constraint, and $k$-extendible system constraint. The existing approaches for this problem are all based on deterministic algorithmic frameworks, and the best approximation ratio achieved by these algorithms (for a general submodular function) is $k+2\sqrt{k+2}+3$. We propose a randomized algorithm with an improved approximation ratio of $(1+\sqrt{k})^2$, while achieving nearly-linear time complexity significantly lower than that of the state-of-the-art algorithm. We also show that our algorithm can be further generalized to address a stochastic case where the elements can be adaptively selected, and propose an approximation ratio of $(1+\sqrt{k+1})^2$ for the adaptive optimization case. The empirical performance of our algorithms is extensively evaluated in several applications related to data mining and social computing, and the experimental results demonstrate the superiorities of our algorithms in terms of both utility and efficiency.

This paper studies non-negative objectives under a k-system constraint, a broad family that includes cardinality, matroid, and k-extendible constraints. The challenge is to obtain a high-value feasible selection while keeping the computation manageable.

Its approximation factor is (1+sqrt(k))², improving on the previous factor k+2sqrt(k+2)+3 for general submodular functions. In this convention, a smaller factor gives a stronger approximation guarantee. The algorithm also runs in nearly linear time, which the authors describe as substantially faster than the state-of-the-art alternative.

Experiments in data mining and social computing demonstrate advantages in both utility and efficiency. The paper therefore combines a stronger theoretical quality guarantee with a computational improvement, while carrying the randomized framework into a setting where choices can respond to observed information.
summary.tldr: A nearly linear randomized algorithm improves approximation guarantees for submodular maximization under k-system constraints and extends to adaptive selection.

title: Randomized Algorithms for Submodular Function Maximization with a $k$-System Constraint

abstract: We study neural-linear bandits for solving problems where {\em both} exploration and representation learning play an important role. Neural-linear bandits harnesses the representation power of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) and combines it with efficient exploration mechanisms by leveraging uncertainty estimation of the model, designed for linear contextual bandits on top of the last hidden layer. In order to mitigate the problem of representation change during the process, new uncertainty estimations are computed using stored data from an unlimited buffer. Nevertheless, when the amount of stored data is limited, a phenomenon called catastrophic forgetting emerges. To alleviate this, we propose a likelihood matching algorithm that is resilient to catastrophic forgetting and is completely online. We applied our algorithm, Limited Memory Neural-Linear with Likelihood Matching (NeuralLinear-LiM2) on a variety of datasets and observed that our algorithm achieves comparable performance to the unlimited memory approach while exhibits resilience to catastrophic forgetting.

paragraphs: Neural-linear bandits combine a neural network's learned features with uncertainty-based exploration from a linear contextual bandit. This is useful when a decision-making system needs both a good representation and a way to explore uncertain choices. A difficulty arises as the neural representation changes: uncertainty estimates must remain meaningful under the updated features.

An existing approach recomputes those estimates from an unlimited buffer of stored observations. When storage is restricted, that strategy can suffer catastrophic forgetting. This paper introduces a likelihood-matching algorithm designed to alleviate forgetting while operating completely online. The resulting method is called Limited Memory Neural-Linear with Likelihood Matching, or NeuralLinear-LiM2.

Across a variety of datasets, the authors observe performance comparable to an approach with unlimited memory, together with resilience to catastrophic forgetting. The finding matters because representation learning and exploration depend on each other through the uncertainty model. The proposed method offers an empirically supported way to sustain that combination when retaining all historical observations is not an option.
summary.tldr: NeuralLinear-LiM2 uses online likelihood matching to reduce forgetting in limited-memory neural-linear bandits, with performance comparable to unlimited-memory training in experiments.

title: Online Limited Memory Neural-Linear Bandits with Likelihood Matching

abstract: Model-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a popular learning paradigm due to its potential sample efficiency compared to model-free RL. However, existing empirical model-based RL approaches lack the ability to explore. This work studies a computationally and statistically efficient model-based algorithm for both Kernelized Nonlinear Regulators (KNR) and linear Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). For both models, our algorithm guarantees polynomial sample complexity and only uses access to a planning oracle. Experimentally, we first demonstrate the flexibility and the efficacy of our algorithm on a set of exploration challenging control tasks where existing empirical model-based RL approaches completely fail. We then show that our approach retains excellent performance even in common dense reward control benchmarks that do not require heavy exploration.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning has the potential to learn efficiently from limited interactions, but successful exploration remains a difficulty for existing empirical methods. PC-MLP addresses that gap with policy-cover-guided exploration. The paper studies an algorithm intended to be efficient both in computation and in the number of samples needed for learning.

The theoretical results cover two model classes: Kernelized Nonlinear Regulators and linear Markov decision processes. For each, the algorithm guarantees polynomial sample complexity and requires access only to a planning oracle. This makes the planning-oracle interface an explicit part of the result, while the sample-efficiency guarantee applies to the specified model classes.

Experiments first test control tasks where exploration is challenging and existing empirical model-based approaches fail completely. The proposed method succeeds in demonstrating flexibility and effectiveness there. It also retains excellent performance on common dense-reward control benchmarks that require less exploration. Together, these findings show that addressing exploration can improve difficult tasks while preserving strong results in the more routinely rewarded settings examined.
summary.tldr: PC-MLP improves model-based exploration and provides polynomial sample-complexity guarantees for two model classes using a planning oracle.

title: PC-MLP: Model-based Reinforcement Learning with Policy Cover Guided Exploration

abstract: The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a crucial metric for machine learning, which evaluates the average performance over all possible True Positive Rates (TPRs) and False Positive Rates (FPRs). Based on the knowledge that a skillful classifier should simultaneously embrace a high TPR and a low FPR, we turn to study a more general variant called Two-way Partial AUC (TPAUC), where only the region with $\mathsf{TPR} \ge \alpha, \mathsf{FPR} \le \beta$ is included in the area. Moreover, a recent work shows that the TPAUC is essentially inconsistent with the existing Partial AUC metrics where only the FPR range is restricted, opening a new problem to seek solutions to leverage high TPAUC. Motivated by this, we present the first trial in this paper to optimize this new metric. The critical challenge along this course lies in the difficulty of performing gradient-based optimization with end-to-end stochastic training, even with a proper choice of surrogate loss. To address this issue, we propose a generic framework to construct surrogate optimization problems, which supports efficient end-to-end training with deep-learning. Moreover, our theoretical analyses show that: 1) the objective function of the surrogate problems will achieve an upper bound of the original problem under mild conditions, and 2) optimizing the surrogate problems leads to good generalization performance in terms of TPAUC with a high probability. Finally, empirical studies over several benchmark datasets speak to the efficacy of our framework.

Motivated by this, we present the first trial in this paper to optimize this new metric. The critical challenge along this course lies in the difficulty of performing gradient-based optimization with end-to-end stochastic training, even with a proper choice of surrogate loss. To address this issue, we propose a generic framework to construct surrogate optimization problems, which supports efficient end-to-end training with deep-learning. Moreover, our theoretical analyses show that: 1) the objective function of the surrogate problems will achieve an upper bound of the original problem under mild conditions, and 2) optimizing the surrogate problems leads to good generalization performance in terms of TPAUC with a high probability. Finally, empirical studies over several benchmark datasets speak to the efficacy of our framework.

paragraphs: Overall ROC area averages classifier performance across operating points, including regions that may not meet an application’s requirements. This paper focuses on two-way partial AUC, which counts only the region where the true-positive rate exceeds a chosen threshold and the false-positive rate stays below another. It therefore targets both requirements simultaneously.

Optimizing this metric is challenging for end-to-end stochastic training, even when a surrogate loss is available. The authors propose a general framework for constructing surrogate optimization problems that support efficient deep-learning training. The focus is on making the desired restricted region of classifier performance accessible to gradient-based optimization.

The theoretical analysis shows that, under mild conditions, the surrogate objectives upper-bound the original optimization objective. It also gives a high-probability guarantee of good generalization in terms of two-way partial AUC. Benchmark experiments support the framework’s effectiveness. These findings provide conditional theoretical support and empirical evidence for training toward the specific combination of high detection and low false-positive rates.
summary.tldr: A surrogate optimization framework enables deep models to target ROC regions with both high true-positive and low false-positive rates.

title: When All We Need is a Piece of the Pie: A Generic Framework for Optimizing Two-way Partial AUC

abstract: In this paper, we propose a robust imitation learning (IL) framework that improves the robustness of IL when environment dynamics are perturbed. The existing IL framework trained in a single environment can catastrophically fail with perturbations in environment dynamics because it does not capture the situation that underlying environment dynamics can be changed. Our framework effectively deals with environments with varying dynamics by imitating multiple experts in sampled environment dynamics to enhance the robustness in general variations in environment dynamics. In order to robustly imitate the multiple sample experts, we minimize the risk with respect to the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the agent’s policy and each of the sample experts. Numerical results show that our algorithm significantly improves robustness against dynamics perturbations compared to conventional IL baselines.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can produce a policy that works in its training environment but fails badly when the environment’s dynamics change. Dynamics determine how actions affect what happens next. A learner trained in a single setting may therefore reproduce behavior that depends too heavily on that particular setting.

The paper proposes learning from multiple experts associated with sampled versions of the environment dynamics. This exposes the learner to expert behavior across different conditions. To combine those sources of guidance robustly, the method minimizes a risk expressed through the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the agent’s policy and each sampled expert’s policy.

Numerical results show significantly improved robustness to dynamics perturbations compared with conventional imitation-learning baselines. The approach makes variation part of the imitation problem itself, rather than relying on demonstrations from only one environment. The stated findings support its effectiveness across the evaluated perturbations, with multiple sampled experts providing the basis for learning behavior that is less tied to a single set of dynamics.
summary.tldr: Imitating multiple experts across sampled environment dynamics improves robustness to dynamics changes in numerical evaluations.

title: Robust Imitation Learning against Variations in Environment Dynamics

abstract: We propose State Matching Offline DIstribution Correction Estimation (SMODICE), a novel and versatile regression-based offline imitation learning algorithm derived via state-occupancy matching. We show that the SMODICE objective admits a simple optimization procedure through an application of Fenchel duality and an analytic solution in tabular MDPs. Without requiring access to expert actions, SMODICE can be effectively applied to three offline IL settings: (i) imitation from observations (IfO), (ii) IfO with dynamics or morphologically mismatched expert, and (iii) example-based reinforcement learning, which we show can be formulated as a state-occupancy matching problem. We extensively evaluate SMODICE on both gridworld environments as well as on high-dimensional offline benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that SMODICE is effective for all three problem settings and significantly outperforms prior state-of-art.

It is derived by matching state occupancy, meaning the pattern of states associated with the behavior or examples being imitated. This focus allows the method to use information about desirable states even when the expert’s action choices are unavailable.

The authors derive a regression-based objective and use Fenchel duality to obtain a simple optimization procedure. For tabular Markov decision processes, they also provide an analytic solution. The same framework covers imitation from observations, imitation when the expert has different dynamics or morphology, and example-based reinforcement learning. The paper shows that the last of these can also be expressed as state-occupancy matching.

Evaluations span gridworlds and high-dimensional offline benchmarks. The reported results show effectiveness across all three settings and significant improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods. The main value is the unification: one state-based learning formulation handles several forms of supervision that do not supply matching expert actions. The empirical evidence supports that versatility across the environments and problem settings evaluated.
summary.tldr: SMODICE uses state-occupancy matching to learn offline from observations or examples without expert actions, including settings with mismatched expert dynamics or morphology.

title: Versatile Offline Imitation from Observations and Examples via Regularized State-Occupancy Matching

abstract: The trade-off between robustness and accuracy has been widely studied in the adversarial literature. Although still controversial, the prevailing view is that this trade-off is inherent, either empirically or theoretically. Thus, we dig for the origin of this trade-off in adversarial training and find that it may stem from the improperly defined robust error, which imposes an inductive bias of local invariance — an overcorrection towards smoothness. Given this, we advocate employing local equivariance to describe the ideal behavior of a robust model, leading to a self-consistent robust error named SCORE. By definition, SCORE facilitates the reconciliation between robustness and accuracy, while still handling the worst-case uncertainty via robust optimization. By simply substituting KL divergence with variants of distance metrics, SCORE can be efficiently minimized. Empirically, our models achieve top-rank performance on RobustBench under AutoAttack. Besides, SCORE provides instructive insights for explaining the overfitting phenomenon and semantic input gradients observed on robust models.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness is often presented as requiring a sacrifice in ordinary predictive accuracy. This paper examines whether part of that tension may originate in how robust error is defined. The authors argue that a conventional definition can encourage excessive local invariance, pushing a model toward too much smoothness.

They propose local equivariance as a better description of desired behavior: responses should change appropriately with nearby input changes. This leads to SCORE, a revised robust-error definition designed to make robustness and accuracy compatible while retaining worst-case optimization. The authors describe efficient minimization by replacing KL divergence with variants of distance metrics.

Their models achieve top-ranked performance on RobustBench under AutoAttack in the reported evaluation. SCORE also provides insights into overfitting and semantic input gradients in robust models. The paper’s claim is that the objective’s definition can help reconcile robustness and accuracy; its account of the origin of the tradeoff is explicitly a possible explanation, supported by the proposed formulation and experiments.
summary.tldr: SCORE revises robust error around local equivariance, offering a way to reconcile accuracy with worst-case robustness.

title: Robustness and Accuracy Could Be Reconcilable by (Proper) Definition

abstract: Inverting an image onto the latent space of pre-trained generators, e.g., StyleGAN-v2, has emerged as a popular strategy to leverage strong image priors for ill-posed restoration. Several studies have showed that this approach is effective at inverting images similar to the data used for training. However, with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that the generator has not been exposed to, existing inversion techniques produce sub-optimal results. In this paper, we propose SPHInX (StyleGAN with Projection Heads for Inverting X), an approach for accurately embedding OOD images onto the StyleGAN latent space. SPHInX optimizes a style projection head using a novel training strategy that imposes a vicinal regularization in the StyleGAN latent space. To further enhance OOD inversion, SPHInX can additionally optimize a content projection head and noise variables in every layer. Our empirical studies on a suite of OOD data show that, in addition to producing higher quality reconstructions over the state-of-the-art inversion techniques, SPHInX is effective for ill-posed restoration tasks while offering semantic editing capabilities.

paragraphs: Image inversion seeks a representation in a pretrained generator’s latent space that reconstructs a given image. This can make the generator’s learned image structure useful for restoration tasks. However, existing inversion methods produce suboptimal results when the input differs from the data on which the generator was trained.

SPHInX addresses this problem for StyleGAN-v2 by optimizing a style projection head with a training strategy that imposes vicinal regularization in latent space. This is the central mechanism for embedding out-of-distribution images more accurately. The approach can additionally optimize a content projection head and the noise variables in every layer to further enhance inversion.

On a suite of out-of-distribution data, the authors report higher-quality reconstructions than leading inversion techniques. They also find that SPHInX is effective for ill-posed restoration tasks and retains semantic editing capabilities. Together, these findings support adapting the inversion process so that a pretrained generator can serve a broader set of images while remaining useful for restoration and editing.
summary.tldr: SPHInX improves StyleGAN-v2 inversion of out-of-distribution images through projection heads and latent-space regularization.

title: Improved StyleGAN-v2 based Inversion for Out-of-Distribution Images

abstract: Scene graphs are powerful abstractions that capture relationships between objects in images by modeling objects as nodes and relationships as edges. Generation of realistic synthetic scene graphs has applications like scene synthesis and data augmentation for supervised learning. Existing graph generative models are predominantly targeted toward molecular graphs, leveraging the limited vocabulary of atoms and bonds and also the well-defined semantics of chemical compounds. In contrast, scene graphs have much larger object and relation vocabularies, and their semantics are latent. To address this challenge, we propose a variational autoencoder for scene graphs, which is optimized for the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the ground truth scene graph distribution and distribution of the generated scene graphs. Our method views a scene graph as a collection of star graphs and encodes it into a latent representation of the underlying stars. The decoder generates scene graphs by learning to sample the component stars and edges between them. Our experiments show that our method is able to mimic the underlying scene graph generative process more accurately than several state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Scene graphs represent objects as nodes and their relationships as edges. Generating realistic examples can support scene synthesis and training-data augmentation. The challenge differs from molecular graph generation: scene graphs contain much larger vocabularies of objects and relationships, and their semantic rules are implicit rather than defined by chemical structure.

VarScene addresses this with a variational autoencoder that treats a scene graph as a collection of star-shaped subgraphs. The encoder represents those component stars in a latent space. The decoder learns to sample stars and the edges connecting them, building a complete graph from these local components and their connections.

Training uses maximum mean discrepancy to compare the distribution of generated scene graphs with the ground-truth distribution. Experiments show that VarScene reproduces the underlying scene-graph generation process more accurately than several leading baselines. The stated result supports decomposing complex scene graphs into structured local pieces while learning how those pieces combine into realistic whole-graph configurations.
summary.tldr: VarScene generates scene graphs by learning latent representations of star-shaped components and how to connect them.

title: VarScene: A Deep Generative Model for Realistic Scene Graph Synthesis

abstract: We address the problem of learning the dynamics of an unknown non-parametric system linking a target and a feature time series. The feature time series is measured on a sparse and irregular grid, while we have access to only a few points of the target time series. Once learned, we can use these dynamics to predict values of the target from the previous values of the feature time series. We frame this task as learning the solution map of a controlled differential equation (CDE). By leveraging the rich theory of signatures, we are able to cast this non-linear problem as a high-dimensional linear regression. We provide an oracle bound on the prediction error which exhibits explicit dependencies on the individual-specific sampling schemes. Our theoretical results are illustrated by simulations which show that our method outperforms existing algorithms for recovering the full time series while being computationally cheap. We conclude by demonstrating its potential on real-world epidemiological data.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to predict a target time series when both its observations and those of a related feature series are scarce. The feature measurements arrive at irregular times, and only a few target values are available. The goal is to learn their unknown dynamical relationship and predict target values from earlier feature observations.

The authors formulate this relationship through the solution map of a controlled differential equation. They then use signature theory to transform the nonlinear learning problem into high-dimensional linear regression. This creates a way to model complex temporal dependence while retaining the computational convenience of a linear estimation problem.

The theoretical contribution is an oracle bound on prediction error that explicitly reflects each individual's sampling scheme. Thus, the analysis accounts for how observation timing differs across series. Simulations show better recovery of complete time series than existing algorithms at low computational cost, and an epidemiological application demonstrates real-world potential. Together, the results connect an approach to irregularly sampled dynamics with both prediction-error analysis and empirical reconstruction performance.
summary.tldr: A signature-based formulation turns learning nonlinear dynamics from sparse, irregular observations into efficient high-dimensional linear regression.

title: Learning the Dynamics of Sparsely Observed Interacting Systems

abstract: Noisy-OR Bayesian Networks (BNs) are a family of probabilistic graphical models which express rich statistical dependencies in binary data. Variational inference (VI) has been the main method proposed to learn noisy-OR BNs with complex latent structures (Jaakkola & Jordan, 1999; Ji et al., 2020; Buhai et al., 2020). However, the proposed VI approaches either (a) use a recognition network with standard amortized inference that cannot induce "explaining-away"; or (b) assume a simple mean-field (MF) posterior which is vulnerable to bad local optima. Existing MF VI methods also update the MF parameters sequentially which makes them inherently slow. In this paper, we propose parallel max-product as an alternative algorithm for learning noisy-OR BNs with complex latent structures and we derive a fast stochastic training scheme that scales to large datasets. We evaluate both approaches on several benchmarks where VI is the state-of-the-art and show that our method (a) achieves better test performance than Ji et al. (2020) for learning noisy-OR BNs with hierarchical latent structures on large sparse real datasets; (b) recovers a higher number of ground truth parameters than Buhai et al. (2020) from cluttered synthetic scenes; and (c) solves the 2D blind deconvolution problem from Lazaro-Gredilla et al. (2021) and variants - including binary matrix factorization - while VI catastrophically fails and is up to two orders of magnitude slower.

paragraphs: Noisy-OR Bayesian networks model dependencies in binary data, including relationships involving hidden variables. Learning complex hidden structures has largely relied on variational inference. This paper identifies problems with existing approaches: some cannot represent explaining-away, while mean-field approaches can become trapped in poor local optima and require slow sequential parameter updates.

The authors propose parallel max-product inference as an alternative and derive a fast stochastic training procedure that scales to large datasets. The approach directly addresses the computational bottleneck of sequential updates while providing a different way to learn networks with complex latent structure.

On large, sparse real datasets, the method improves test performance over a prior approach for hierarchical noisy-OR networks. It also recovers more ground-truth parameters from cluttered synthetic scenes. For a two-dimensional blind deconvolution problem and related variants, including binary matrix factorization, it succeeds where the evaluated variational approach fails severely and is up to two orders of magnitude slower. These findings support the alternative across several distinct learning and reconstruction settings.
summary.tldr: Parallel max-product learning improves noisy-OR network results and speed over evaluated variational approaches on several benchmarks.

title: Learning Noisy OR Bayesian Networks with Max-Product Belief Propagation

abstract: Although data diffusion embeddings are ubiquitous in unsupervised learning and have proven to be a viable technique for uncovering the underlying intrinsic geometry of data, diffusion embeddings are inherently limited due to their discrete nature. To this end, we propose neural FIM, a method for computing the Fisher information metric (FIM) from point cloud data - allowing for a continuous manifold model for the data. Neural FIM creates an extensible metric space from discrete point cloud data such that information from the metric can inform us of manifold characteristics such as volume and geodesics. We demonstrate Neural FIM’s utility in selecting parameters for the PHATE visualization method as well as its ability to obtain information pertaining to local volume illuminating branching points and cluster centers embeddings of a toy dataset and two single-cell datasets of IPSC reprogramming and PBMCs (immune cells).

paragraphs: Diffusion embeddings help reveal the intrinsic geometry of data represented by a collection of points. Their discrete nature, however, limits the geometric description they provide. Neural FIM addresses this by learning a Fisher information metric from point-cloud data, creating a continuous manifold model from the discrete observations.

The learned metric defines an extensible space in which geometric properties can be studied. In particular, it can inform calculations concerning volume and geodesics, the paths associated with the manifold's geometry. This shifts the focus from placing observed points in an embedding to learning a continuous geometric description that supports additional questions about the data's structure.

The authors demonstrate the method for choosing parameters of the PHATE visualization technique. They also use local-volume information to illuminate branching points and cluster centers in a toy dataset and two single-cell datasets: induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. These examples show how a learned metric can support visualization choices and interpretation of local structure in the evaluated data.
summary.tldr: Neural FIM learns a continuous geometric metric from point clouds to study manifold structure and support data visualization.

title: Neural FIM for learning Fisher information metrics from point cloud data

abstract: The main aim of this paper is to conduct the convergence analysis of the gradient descent for two-layer physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). Here, the loss function involves derivatives of neural network outputs with respect to its inputs, so the interaction between the trainable parameters is more complicated compared with simple regression and classification tasks. We first develop the positive definiteness of Gram matrices and prove that the gradient flow finds the global optima of the empirical loss under over-parameterization. Then, we demonstrate that the standard gradient descent converges to the global optima of the loss with proper choices of learning rates. The framework of our analysis works for various categories of PDEs (e.g., linear second-order PDEs) and common types of network initialization (LecunUniform etc.). Our theoretical results do not need a very strict hypothesis for training samples and have a looser requirement on the network width compared with some previous works.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks use losses that include derivatives of network outputs with respect to their inputs. Those derivative terms make interactions among trainable parameters more complicated than in ordinary regression or classification. This paper analyzes whether gradient-based training can nevertheless reach global optima for two-layer networks of this kind.

The analysis first establishes positive definiteness of relevant Gram matrices. Under overparameterization, the authors then prove that gradient flow, the continuous-time version of gradient descent, reaches a global optimum of the empirical loss. They extend the result to standard gradient descent when the learning rate is chosen appropriately.

The framework covers several categories of partial differential equations, including linear second-order equations, and common initialization schemes such as LecunUniform. The authors also report less restrictive network-width requirements than some earlier work and avoid very strict assumptions on training samples. These are conditional optimization guarantees for the empirical training objective: their significance is showing that the additional derivative structure of PINN losses can still permit provable global convergence under the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper proves global empirical-loss convergence for overparameterized two-layer PINNs, with suitable learning rates for gradient descent.

title: Gradient Descent Finds the Global Optima of Two-Layer Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: We study reinforcement learning (RL) with linear function approximation. For episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes (linear MDPs) whose transition probability can be parameterized as a linear function of a given feature mapping, we propose the first computationally efficient algorithm that achieves the nearly minimax optimal regret $\tilde O(d\sqrt{H^3K})$, where $d$ is the dimension of the feature mapping, $H$ is the planning horizon, and $K$ is the number of episodes. Our algorithm is based on a weighted linear regression scheme with a carefully designed weight, which depends on a new variance estimator that (1) directly estimates the variance of the optimal value function, (2) monotonically decreases with respect to the number of episodes to ensure a better estimation accuracy, and (3) uses a rare-switching policy to update the value function estimator to control the complexity of the estimated value function class. Our work provides a complete answer to optimal RL with linear MDPs, and the developed algorithm and theoretical tools may be of independent interest.
