paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in episodic linear Markov decision processes. The key structural assumption is that transition probabilities are linear functions of a given feature mapping, while the dynamics may vary across steps within an episode. The objective is to learn efficiently while controlling regret, the accumulated cost of acting below optimal performance.

The proposed computationally efficient algorithm uses weighted linear regression with weights determined by a new variance estimator. That estimator directly targets the variance of the optimal value function and decreases monotonically as episodes accumulate. A rare-switching policy limits updates to the value-function estimator, helping control the complexity of the class of estimates involved in learning.

The resulting regret bound is nearly minimax optimal: up to logarithmic factors, it scales as d times the square root of H cubed times K, where d is feature dimension, H is horizon, and K is episode count. The contribution combines near-optimal statistical performance with computational efficiency for this specified model class, rather than asserting an optimal solution for unrestricted reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: A computationally efficient weighted-regression algorithm achieves nearly minimax-optimal regret for episodic linear Markov decision processes.

title: Nearly Minimax Optimal Reinforcement Learning for Linear Markov Decision Processes

abstract: We describe PromptBoosting, a query-efficient procedure for building a text classifier from a neural language model (LM) without access to the LM’s parameters, gradients, or hidden representations. This form of "black-box" classifier training has become increasingly important as the cost of training and inference in large-scale LMs has grown. But existing black-box LM classifier learning approaches are themselves computationally inefficient, typically specializing LMs to the target task by searching in a large space of (discrete or continuous) prompts using zeroth-order optimization methods. Instead of directly optimizing in prompt space, PromptBoosting obtains a small pool of prompts via a gradient-free approach and then constructs a large pool of weak learners by pairing these prompts with different elements of the LM’s output distribution. These weak learners are then ensembled using the AdaBoost algorithm. The entire learning process requires only a small number of forward passes and no backward pass. Experiments show that PromptBoosting achieves state-of-the-art performance in multiple black-box few-shot classification tasks, and matches or outperforms full fine-tuning in both few-shot and standard learning paradigms, while training 10x faster than existing black-box methods.

In this black-box setting, adapting a model can become expensive when learning repeatedly searches a large prompt space. The paper seeks to obtain strong classifiers with relatively few model queries.

The method first obtains a small collection of prompts through a gradient-free procedure. It then pairs those prompts with different components of the model's output distribution to create many weak learners. AdaBoost combines these learners into an ensemble. This design extracts multiple candidate classification rules from a limited prompt pool, and the learning process uses few forward passes with no backward pass.

The experiments report state-of-the-art results on multiple black-box few-shot classification tasks. They also show performance matching or exceeding full fine-tuning in the tested few-shot and standard learning settings, alongside training ten times faster than existing black-box methods. These are empirical findings for the evaluated tasks. They support the usefulness of ensembling information already available in model outputs for query-efficient adaptation.
summary.tldr: PromptBoosting combines prompt-based weak learners with AdaBoost to train competitive black-box text classifiers using few language-model forward passes.

title: PromptBoosting: Black-Box Text Classification with Ten Forward Passes

abstract: Despite the widespread application of latent factor analysis, existing methods suffer from the following weaknesses: requiring the number of factors to be known, lack of theoretical guarantees for learning the model structure, and nonidentifiability of the parameters due to rotation invariance properties of the likelihood. We address these concerns by proposing a fast correlation thresholding (CT) algorithm that simultaneously learns the number of latent factors and a rotationally identifiable model structure. Our novel approach translates this structure learning problem into the search for so-called independent maximal cliques in a thresholded correlation graph that can be easily constructed from the observed data. Our clique analysis technique scales well up to thousands of variables, while competing methods are not applicable in a reasonable amount of running time. We establish a finite-sample error bound and high-dimensional consistency for the structure learning of our method. Through a series of simulation studies and a real data example, we show that the CT algorithm is an accurate method for learning the structure of factor analysis models and is robust to violations of its assumptions.

Existing approaches may require the factor count in advance, lack structural guarantees, or leave parameters ambiguous because rotating the latent representation preserves the likelihood. This paper proposes correlation thresholding to learn both the number of factors and a rotationally identifiable structure.

The algorithm builds a graph by thresholding correlations between observed variables. It then translates structure learning into a search for particular groups called independent maximal cliques. This reformulation makes the observed correlation graph the main object of analysis. The authors report that their clique-search technique handles thousands of variables, at scales where competing approaches take impractical amounts of time.

The paper establishes a finite-sample error bound and high-dimensional consistency for structure recovery. Simulations and a real-data example show accurate recovery and empirical robustness when assumptions are violated. The theoretical guarantees and robustness experiments provide different kinds of support: the former characterize recovery formally, while the latter examine behavior beyond the assumptions in tested cases.
summary.tldr: Searching cliques in a thresholded correlation graph learns latent-factor counts and identifiable structures with theoretical guarantees and favorable scaling.

title: Structure Learning of Latent Factors via Clique Search on Correlation Thresholded Graphs

abstract: An emerging line of work has shown that machine-learned predictions are useful to warm-start algorithms for discrete optimization problems, such as bipartite matching. Previous studies have shown time complexity bounds proportional to some distance between a prediction and an optimal solution, which we can approximately minimize by learning predictions from past optimal solutions. However, such guarantees may not be meaningful when multiple optimal solutions exist. Indeed, the dual problem of bipartite matching and, more generally, $\text{L}$-/$\text{L}^\\natural$-convex function minimization have arbitrarily many optimal solutions, making such prediction-dependent bounds arbitrarily large. To resolve this theoretically critical issue, we present a new warm-start-with-prediction framework for $\text{L}$-/$\text{L}^\\natural$-convex function minimization. Our framework offers time complexity bounds proportional to the distance between a prediction and the set of all optimal solutions . The main technical difficulty lies in learning predictions that are provably close to sets of all optimal solutions, for which we present an online-gradient-descent-based method. We thus give the first polynomial-time learnability of predictions that can provably warm-start algorithms regardless of multiple optimal solutions.

paragraphs: Machine-learned predictions can speed up discrete optimization by supplying useful starting points. Existing runtime guarantees often measure the distance from a prediction to an optimal solution. When a problem has many optima, however, distance to one selected optimum can be misleading: a prediction may be near another equally valid solution.

The paper addresses this issue for L-convex and L-natural-convex function minimization, a setting that includes the dual of bipartite matching. Its framework bounds runtime using distance to the entire set of optimal solutions. This makes the guarantee reflect proximity to any optimum, avoiding arbitrarily large distances caused by choosing an unrepresentative optimal target.

Learning such predictions is the main technical challenge because the desired target is a solution set. The authors provide a method based on online gradient descent and establish polynomial-time learnability of predictions that provably help warm-start optimization despite multiple optima. The contribution aligns the learning goal with what the downstream solver actually needs: a starting point close to some optimal solution.
summary.tldr: Learning predictions close to optimal-solution sets yields meaningful warm-start guarantees even when discrete optimization problems have many optima.

title: Rethinking Warm-Starts with Predictions: Learning Predictions Close to Sets of Optimal Solutions for Faster $\text{L}$-/$\text{L}^\natural$-Convex Function Minimization

abstract: Segmentation models predominantly optimize pixel-overlap-based loss, an objective that is actually inadequate for many segmentation tasks. In recent years, their limitations fueled a growing interest in topology-aware methods, which aim to recover the topology of the segmented structures. However, so far, existing methods only consider global topological properties, ignoring the need to preserve topological features spatially, which is crucial for accurate segmentation. We introduce the concept of induced matchings from persistent homology to achieve a spatially correct matching between persistence barcodes in a segmentation setting. Based on this concept, we define the Betti matching error as an interpretable, topologically and feature-wise accurate metric for image segmentations, which resolves the limitations of the Betti number error. Our Betti matching error is differentiable and efficient to use as a loss function. We demonstrate that it improves the topological performance of segmentation networks significantly across six diverse datasets while preserving the performance with respect to traditional scores. Our code is publicly available (https://github.com/nstucki/Betti-matching/).

paragraphs: A segmentation can overlap the target image well while still getting its structural organization wrong. Topology-aware objectives address that problem, but global topological summaries can overlook where individual features occur. This paper focuses on preserving topological features in their correct spatial locations, not merely obtaining the right overall topological counts.

The authors introduce induced matchings from persistent homology to match persistence barcodes in a spatially appropriate way. From these matches, they define the Betti matching error, an interpretable metric that evaluates topology at the level of individual features. It addresses limitations of Betti number error, which does not provide the same feature-wise assessment.

The new error is differentiable and efficient enough to serve directly as a training loss. Across six datasets, using it significantly improves segmentation networks' topological performance while maintaining performance on traditional scores. This means the reported structural improvements do not come at the expense of those conventional measurements. The contribution connects a more spatially faithful evaluation metric with an objective that can guide learning.
summary.tldr: Betti matching provides a differentiable segmentation loss that preserves spatially corresponding topological features and improves structural accuracy.

title: Topologically Faithful Image Segmentation via Induced Matching of Persistence Barcodes

abstract: The distinguishing power of graph transformers is tied to the choice of positional encoding: features used to augment the base transformer with information about the graph. There are two primary types of positional encoding: absolute positional encodings (APEs) and relative positional encodings (RPEs). APEs assign features to each node and are given as input to the transformer. RPEs instead assign a feature to each pair of nodes, e.g., shortest-path distance, and are used to augment the attention block. A priori, it is unclear which method is better for maximizing the power of the resulting graph transformer. In this paper, we aim to understand the relationship between these different types of positional encodings. Interestingly, we show that graph transformers using APEs and RPEs are equivalent in their ability to distinguish non-isomorphic graphs. In particular, we demonstrate how to interchange APEs and RPEs while maintaining their distinguishing power in terms of graph transformers. However, in the case of graphs with node features, we show that RPEs may have an advantage over APEs. Based on our theoretical results, we provide a study of different APEs and RPEs—including the shortest-path and resistance distance and the recently introduced stable and expressive positional encoding (SPE)—and compare their distinguishing power in terms of transformers. We believe our work will help navigate the vast number of positional encoding choices and provide guidance on the future design of positional encodings for graph transformers.

paragraphs: Graph transformers need structural information to distinguish graphs. Absolute positional encodings provide features for individual nodes, while relative positional encodings describe pairs of nodes and modify attention. Using the theoretical results, the paper compares specific choices, including shortest-path distance, resistance distance, and stable and expressive positional encoding. The findings provide a basis for evaluating encoding choices according to the structural distinctions they enable and for designing future graph transformer encodings.
summary.tldr: Absolute and relative graph encodings can preserve equivalent distinguishing power, although relative encodings may offer an advantage with node features.

title: Comparing Graph Transformers via Positional Encodings

abstract: Counterfactual explanations (CEs) based on concepts are explanations that consider alternative scenarios to understand which high-level semantic features contributed to particular model predictions. In this work, we propose CEs based on the semantic graphs accompanying input data to achieve more descriptive, accurate, and human-aligned explanations. Building upon state-of-the-art (SotA) conceptual attempts, we adopt a model-agnostic edit-based approach and introduce leveraging GNNs for efficient Graph Edit Distance (GED) computation. With a focus on the visual domain, we represent images as scene graphs and obtain their GNN embeddings to bypass solving the NP-hard graph similarity problem for all input pairs, an integral part of CE computation process. We apply our method to benchmark and real-world datasets with varying difficulty and availability of semantic annotations. Testing on diverse classifiers, we find that our CEs outperform previous SotA explanation models based on semantics, including both white and black-box as well as conceptual and pixel-level approaches. Their superiority is proven quantitatively and qualitatively, as validated by human subjects, highlighting the significance of leveraging semantic edges in the presence of intricate relationships. Our model-agnostic graph-based approach is widely applicable and easily extensible, producing actionable explanations across different contexts. The code is available at https://github.com/aggeliki-dimitriou/SGCE.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe alternative scenarios that help reveal which features contributed to a prediction. This paper builds such explanations from semantic graphs accompanying the input, so that relationships between meaningful concepts can enter the explanation. In the visual setting, images are represented as scene graphs rather than only as pixels or isolated concepts.

The method uses a model-agnostic, edit-based approach. To make graph comparisons efficient, it obtains graph-neural-network embeddings for the scene graphs, avoiding the need to solve the NP-hard graph-similarity problem for every input pair. This makes structured semantic information usable within the counterfactual computation while addressing an otherwise expensive comparison step.

Evaluations span benchmark and real-world datasets, different levels of semantic annotation, and diverse classifiers. The explanations outperform previous semantic explanation approaches in quantitative and qualitative comparisons, including human-subject validation. The findings especially emphasize the value of semantic edges when relationships are intricate. The resulting graph-based explanations offer actionable changes while retaining information about how concepts relate to one another.
summary.tldr: Semantic-graph counterfactuals use efficient learned graph comparisons to produce explanations that better capture meaningful relationships and perform well in human evaluations.

title: Structure Your Data: Towards Semantic Graph Counterfactuals

abstract: This paper studies the theoretical guarantees of the classical projected gradient and conditional gradient methods applied to constrained optimization problems with biased relative-error gradient oracles. These oracles are used in various settings, such as distributed optimization systems or derivative-free optimization, and are particularly common when gradients are compressed, quantized, or estimated via finite differences computations. Several settings are investigated: Optimization over the box with a coordinate-wise erroneous gradient oracle, optimization over a general compact convex set, and three more specific scenarios. Convergence guarantees are established with respect to the relative-error magnitude, and in particular, we show that the conditional gradient is invariant to relative-error when applied over the box with a coordinate-wise erroneous gradient oracle, and the projected gradient maintains its convergence guarantees when optimizing a nonconvex objective function.

These oracles are used in various settings, such as distributed optimization systems or derivative-free optimization, and are particularly common when gradients are compressed, quantized, or estimated via finite differences computations. Several settings are investigated: Optimization over the box with a coordinate-wise erroneous gradient oracle, optimization over a general compact convex set, and three more specific scenarios. Convergence guarantees are established with respect to the relative-error magnitude, and in particular, we show that the conditional gradient is invariant to relative-error when applied over the box with a coordinate-wise erroneous gradient oracle, and the projected gradient maintains its convergence guarantees when optimizing a nonconvex objective function.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms often rely on gradients to decide how to improve a solution, but those gradients may be inaccurate. This paper studies errors that are biased and measured relative to the gradient itself. Such errors arise when gradients are compressed, represented with reduced numerical precision, or estimated using finite differences. The central question is how these inaccuracies affect established methods for constrained optimization.

The authors analyze projected gradient and conditional gradient methods across several settings. These include optimization within a box, where each variable has bounds and gradient errors are specified coordinate by coordinate, and optimization over a general compact convex set. Their guarantees explicitly account for the size of the relative error, connecting the quality of gradient information to algorithmic convergence.

Two results stand out within the settings studied. Conditional gradient is invariant to relative error in the box-constrained, coordinate-wise error setting, while projected gradient retains convergence guarantees for nonconvex objectives. These findings identify circumstances in which approximate gradients remain compatible with reliable optimization, with conclusions tied to the particular constraints and error models analyzed.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes convergence guarantees for constrained optimization with biased relative-error gradients, including robustness results for specific methods and settings.

title: A Study of First-Order Methods with a Deterministic Relative-Error Gradient Oracle

abstract: Despite the recent successes of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms, efficiently adapting to co-players in mixed-motive environments remains a significant challenge. One feasible approach is to hierarchically model co-players’ behavior based on inferring their characteristics. However, these methods often encounter difficulties in efficient reasoning and utilization of inferred information. To address these issues, we propose Hierarchical Opponent modeling and Planning (HOP), a novel multi-agent decision-making algorithm that enables few-shot adaptation to unseen policies in mixed-motive environments. HOP is hierarchically composed of two modules: an opponent modeling module that infers others’ goals and learns corresponding goal-conditioned policies, and a planning module that employs Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to identify the best response. Our approach improves efficiency by updating beliefs about others’ goals both across and within episodes and by using information from the opponent modeling module to guide planning. Experimental results demonstrate that in mixed-motive environments, HOP exhibits superior few-shot adaptation capabilities when interacting with various unseen agents, and excels in self-play scenarios. Furthermore, the emergence of social intelligence during our experiments underscores the potential of our approach in complex multi-agent environments.

paragraphs: Agents in mixed-motive environments must adapt to other participants whose interests can involve both cooperation and competition. Predicting those participants is useful only if the agent can turn its predictions into effective decisions. HOP addresses both parts of this problem, aiming to adapt after relatively few interactions with previously unseen policies.

Its hierarchical structure contains an opponent-modeling module and a planning module. The first infers other agents’ goals and learns policies conditioned on those goals. The second uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to search for a best response. Beliefs about others’ goals are updated both during an episode and across episodes, while the learned opponent information guides planning.

Experiments show superior few-shot adaptation when HOP interacts with various unseen agents in mixed-motive environments, as well as strong performance in self-play. The authors also report the emergence of social intelligence in their experiments. Together, these results suggest that inferring goals can be especially useful when that inference directly shapes planning and is revised as interactions unfold.
summary.tldr: HOP combines goal-based opponent modeling with tree-search planning to adapt quickly to unfamiliar agents in mixed-motive environments.

title: Efficient Adaptation in Mixed-Motive Environments via Hierarchical Opponent Modeling and Planning

abstract: Classification models are expected to perform equally well for different classes, yet in practice, there are often large gaps in their performance. This issue of class bias is widely studied in cases of datasets with sample imbalance, but is relatively overlooked in balanced datasets. In this work, we introduce the concept of spectral imbalance in features as a potential source for class disparities and study the connections between spectral imbalance and class bias in both theory and practice. To build the connection between spectral imbalance and class gap, we develop a theoretical framework for studying class disparities and derive exact expressions for the per-class error in a high-dimensional mixture model setting. We then study this phenomenon in 11 different state-of-the-art pre-trained encoders, and show how our proposed framework can be used to compare the quality of encoders, as well as evaluate and combine data augmentation strategies to mitigate the issue. Our work sheds light on the class-dependent effects of learning, and provides new insights into how state-of-the-art pre-trained features may have unknown biases that can be diagnosed through their spectra.

paragraphs: Equal numbers of training examples per class do not necessarily produce equal classification performance. This paper investigates a possible explanation within the features themselves: spectral imbalance. The idea directs attention to differences in feature structure across classes, extending the study of class bias beyond unequal sample counts.

The authors develop a theoretical framework connecting spectral imbalance with differences in class error. Within a high-dimensional mixture model, they derive exact expressions for the error of each class. This gives a setting in which class disparities can be analyzed mathematically and related to feature spectra, rather than attributed only to how many examples each class contains.

The empirical study examines eleven pretrained encoders. The authors show how their framework can compare encoders and help evaluate and combine data augmentation strategies to reduce disparities. The findings identify spectra as a useful diagnostic for potential class-dependent biases in pretrained features. They support spectral imbalance as a possible source of unequal performance, including when the dataset is balanced.
summary.tldr: Feature spectra can reveal class performance disparities even in balanced datasets and help assess encoders and augmentation strategies.

title: Balanced Data, Imbalanced Spectra: Unveiling Class Disparities with Spectral Imbalance

abstract: Learning effective negotiation strategies poses two key challenges: the exploration-exploitation dilemma and dealing with large action spaces. However, there is an absence of learning-based approaches that effectively address these challenges in negotiation. This paper introduces a comprehensive formulation to tackle various negotiation problems. Our approach leverages contextual combinatorial multi-armed bandits, with the bandits resolving the exploration-exploitation dilemma, and the combinatorial nature handles large action spaces. Building upon this formulation, we introduce NegUCB, a novel method that also handles common issues such as partial observations and complex reward functions in negotiation. NegUCB is contextual and tailored for full-bandit feedback without constraints on the reward functions. Under mild assumptions, it ensures a sub-linear regret upper bound. Experiments conducted on three negotiation tasks demonstrate the superiority of our approach.

paragraphs: Learning to negotiate involves two linked difficulties: deciding when to try unfamiliar actions and handling a large number of possible offers. This paper brings both into a contextual combinatorial bandit formulation. Context lets decisions depend on the situation, while the combinatorial structure represents actions assembled from multiple choices.

The resulting method, NegUCB, addresses negotiation settings with partial observations and complex rewards. It is designed for full-bandit feedback, where feedback concerns the overall chosen action rather than separate rewards for its components. The formulation does not constrain the reward functions, allowing the method to accommodate varied ways of assessing negotiation outcomes.

Under assumptions described as mild, the authors establish a sublinear upper bound on regret. This means the bound on accumulated performance loss grows more slowly than the number of decisions, rather than maintaining a constant loss per decision. Experiments on three negotiation tasks report superior performance, supporting the usefulness of combining contextual learning with a structured treatment of large action spaces.
summary.tldr: NegUCB frames negotiation as a contextual combinatorial bandit problem, with a conditional sublinear regret guarantee and favorable results on three tasks.

title: A Contextual Combinatorial Bandit Approach to Negotiation

abstract: Adaptive gradient optimizers like Adam(W) are the default training algorithms for many deep learning architectures, such as transformers. Their diagonal preconditioner is based on the gradient outer product which is incorporated into the parameter update via a square root. While these methods are often motivated as approximate second-order methods, the square root represents a fundamental difference. In this work, we investigate how the behavior of adaptive methods changes when we remove the root, i.e. strengthen their second-order motivation. Surprisingly, we find that such square-root-free adaptive methods close the generalization gap to SGD on convolutional architectures, while maintaining their root-based counterpart’s performance on transformers. The second-order perspective also has practical benefits for the development of non-diagonal adaptive methods through the concept of preconditioner invariance. In contrast to root-based methods like Shampoo, the root-free counterparts do not require numerically unstable matrix root decompositions and inversions, thus work well in half precision. Our findings provide new insights into the development of adaptive methods and raise important questions regarding the currently overlooked role of adaptivity for their success.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adam and AdamW scale parameter updates using information derived from gradient outer products. Their usual update applies a square root to this information. Although these methods are often explained as approximations to second-order optimization, that square root creates a fundamental difference. The paper investigates what happens when it is removed.

The authors find that the resulting root-free methods close the generalization gap to stochastic gradient descent on convolutional architectures while retaining the performance of root-based counterparts on transformers. These findings connect a seemingly small change in the update rule to meaningful differences across architecture families. They also motivate reconsidering which aspects of adaptive optimization account for its success.

The second-order viewpoint further supports non-diagonal adaptive methods through preconditioner invariance. Compared with root-based methods such as Shampoo, the proposed counterparts avoid numerically unstable matrix root decompositions and inversions. The authors report that this lets them work well in half precision, making the theoretical perspective relevant to practical low-precision training.
summary.tldr: Removing square roots from adaptive updates improves reported convolutional-model generalization and supports numerically stable half-precision optimization.

title: Can We Remove the Square-Root in Adaptive Gradient Methods? A Second-Order Perspective

abstract: Semiparametric statistics play a pivotal role in a wide range of domains, including but not limited to missing data, causal inference, and transfer learning, to name a few. In many settings, semiparametric theory leads to (nearly) statistically optimal procedures that yet involve numerically solving Fredholm integral equations of the second kind. Traditional numerical methods, such as polynomial or spline approximations, are difficult to scale to multi-dimensional problems. Alternatively, statisticians may choose to approximate the original integral equations by ones with closed-form solutions, resulting in computationally more efficient, but statistically suboptimal or even incorrect procedures. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework by formulating the semiparametric estimation problem as a bi-level optimization problem; and then we propose a scalable algorithm called Deep Neural-Nets Assisted Semiparametric Estimation ($\mathsf{DNA\mbox{-}SE}$) by leveraging the universal approximation property of Deep Neural-Nets (DNN) to streamline semiparametric procedures. Through extensive numerical experiments and a real data analysis, we demonstrate the numerical and statistical advantages of $\mathsf{DNA\mbox{-}SE}$ over traditional methods. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to bring DNN into semiparametric statistics as a numerical solver of integral equations in our proposed general framework.
originalAbstract: Semiparametric statistics play a pivotal role in a wide range of domains, including but not limited to missing data, causal inference, and transfer learning, to name a few. Traditional numerical methods, such as polynomial or spline approximations, are difficult to scale to multi-dimensional problems. Alternatively, statisticians may choose to approximate the original integral equations by ones with closed-form solutions, resulting in computationally more efficient, but statistically suboptimal or even incorrect procedures. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework by formulating the semiparametric estimation problem as a bi-level optimization problem; and then we propose a scalable algorithm called Deep Neural-Nets Assisted Semiparametric Estimation ($\mathsf{DNA\mbox{-}SE}$) by leveraging the universal approximation property of Deep Neural-Nets (DNN) to streamline semiparametric procedures. Through extensive numerical experiments and a real data analysis, we demonstrate the numerical and statistical advantages of $\mathsf{DNA\mbox{-}SE}$ over traditional methods. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to bring DNN into semiparametric statistics as a numerical solver of integral equations in our proposed general framework.

paragraphs: Semiparametric theory can produce statistically strong estimation procedures for problems such as missing data, causal inference, and transfer learning. Making those procedures practical can require solving Fredholm integral equations of the second kind. Traditional polynomial or spline approximations become difficult to scale when the problem involves multiple dimensions.

A computational shortcut is to replace the original equation with an easier one that has a closed-form solution. The paper explains that this can sacrifice statistical quality or even produce an incorrect procedure. DNA-SE instead formulates semiparametric estimation as a bi-level optimization problem and uses deep neural networks as numerical solvers within that framework.

The method draws on neural networks’ universal approximation property to support a scalable algorithm for these integral-equation problems. Numerical experiments and a real-data analysis show numerical and statistical advantages over traditional methods. The contribution places neural networks inside the computational machinery of semiparametric estimation, aiming to make its theoretically motivated procedures more practical without relying on the same equation-simplification shortcuts.
summary.tldr: DNA-SE uses neural networks to solve integral equations within semiparametric estimation, showing computational and statistical advantages in the reported evaluations.

title: DNA-SE: Towards Deep Neural-Nets Assisted Semiparametric Estimation

abstract: Recent work has shown that deep reinforcement learning agents have difficulty in effectively using their network parameters. We leverage prior insights into the advantages of sparse training techniques and demonstrate that gradual magnitude pruning enables value-based agents to maximize parameter effectiveness. This results in networks that yield dramatic performance improvements over traditional networks, using only a small fraction of the full network parameters. Our code is publicly available, see Appendix A for details.

Our code is publicly available, see Appendix A for details.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a parameter-efficiency problem in deep reinforcement learning: agents can struggle to make effective use of the networks they already have. The authors investigate whether sparse training techniques can improve that use of capacity. Their focus is value-based agents, so the central question concerns the networks supporting value-based learning.

The proposed approach uses gradual magnitude pruning to make those networks sparse. This brings a parameter-reduction technique into the effort to improve learning performance itself. The paper frames pruning as a way to maximize parameter effectiveness, connecting earlier insights about sparse training with the particular difficulty of using neural-network capacity in reinforcement learning.

The reported result is a substantial performance improvement over traditional networks while retaining only a small fraction of the full parameter count. These findings make model size and agent performance separate considerations in the studied setting: keeping more parameters did not deliver the stronger result. The contribution is empirical evidence that gradual magnitude pruning can improve both parameter economy and the performance of value-based agents.
summary.tldr: Gradual magnitude pruning substantially improves the reported performance of value-based reinforcement-learning agents while retaining only a small fraction of their parameters.

title: In value-based deep reinforcement learning, a pruned network is a good network

abstract: The advancement toward deeper graph neural networks is currently obscured by two inherent issues in message passing, oversmoothing and oversquashing. We identify the root cause of these issues as information loss due to heterophily mixing in aggregation, where messages of diverse category semantics are mixed. We propose a novel multi-track graph convolutional network to address oversmoothing and oversquashing effectively. Our basic idea is intuitive: if messages are separated and independently propagated according to their category semantics, heterophilic mixing can be prevented. Consequently, we present a novel multi-track message passing scheme capable of preventing heterophilic mixing, enhancing long-distance information flow, and improving separation condition. Empirical validations show that our model achieved state-of-the-art performance on several graph datasets and effectively tackled oversmoothing and oversquashing, setting a new benchmark of $86.4$% accuracy on Cora.

paragraphs: Deeper graph neural networks face oversmoothing and oversquashing: useful distinctions can fade, and information traveling across the graph can become difficult to preserve. This paper identifies information loss from heterophily mixing as the root cause of these issues. In the authors’ account, aggregation mixes messages carrying different category meanings and loses useful semantic distinctions.

The proposed multi-track graph convolutional network separates messages according to their category semantics and propagates them independently. Keeping these information streams apart is intended to prevent heterophilic mixing during message passing. The resulting scheme is designed to improve long-distance information flow and the conditions for maintaining separation between categories.

Empirical evaluations report state-of-the-art performance on several graph datasets and effective mitigation of both oversmoothing and oversquashing. The model reaches 86.4% accuracy on Cora, which the paper presents as a new benchmark. These results support the proposed connection between semantic separation during aggregation and stronger graph learning, with the multi-track architecture translating that explanation into a concrete message-passing method.
summary.tldr: Multi-track message passing separates category-specific information to address oversmoothing and oversquashing, reporting strong graph-learning results.

title: Multi-Track Message Passing: Tackling Oversmoothing and Oversquashing in Graph Learning via Preventing Heterophily Mixing

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable proficiency in comprehending and handling text-based tasks. Many efforts are being made to transfer these attributes to video modality, which are termed Video-LLMs. However, existing Video-LLMs can only capture the coarse-grained semantics and are unable to effectively handle tasks related to comprehension or localization of specific video segments. In light of these challenges, we propose Momentor, a Video-LLM capable of accomplishing fine-grained temporal understanding tasks. To support the training of Momentor, we design an automatic data generation engine to construct Moment-10M, a large-scale video instruction dataset with segment-level instruction data. We train Momentor on Moment-10M, enabling it to perform segment-level reasoning and localization. Zero-shot evaluations on several tasks demonstrate that Momentor excels in fine-grained temporally grounded comprehension and localization.

paragraphs: Understanding a video's broad subject differs from understanding a particular segment or finding where it occurs. The paper identifies this gap in existing video language models, which capture coarse meaning but struggle with fine-grained temporal comprehension and localization. Momentor is designed to address these segment-level tasks.

The authors build an automatic data-generation engine to create Moment-10M, a large video instruction dataset containing segment-level supervision. They train Momentor on this dataset so that its instruction learning includes reasoning about specific portions of a video and locating them in time. The training data therefore directly targets the temporal granularity that the model is intended to handle.

Zero-shot evaluations across several tasks show strong fine-grained, temporally grounded comprehension and localization. These results support the combination of a video language model with automatically generated segment-level instruction data. The contribution includes both the model and a way to construct training material for understanding particular moments, extending evaluation beyond broad descriptions of entire videos.
summary.tldr: Momentor uses automatically generated segment-level instructions to learn fine-grained video comprehension and temporal localization.

title: Momentor: Advancing Video Large Language Model with Fine-Grained Temporal Reasoning

abstract: Discovering causal relationships from time series data is significant in fields such as finance, climate science, and neuroscience. However, contemporary techniques rely on the simplifying assumption that data originates from the same causal model, while in practice, data is heterogeneous and can stem from different causal models. In this work, we relax this assumption and perform causal discovery from time series data originating from a mixture of causal models. We propose a general variational inference-based framework called MCD to infer the underlying causal models as well as the mixing probability of each sample. Our approach employs an end-to-end training process that maximizes an evidence-lower bound for the data likelihood. We present two variants: MCD-Linear for linear relationships and independent noise, and MCD-Nonlinear for nonlinear causal relationships and history-dependent noise. We demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks in causal discovery tasks through extensive experimentation on synthetic and real-world datasets, particularly when the data emanates from diverse underlying causal graphs. Theoretically, we prove the identifiability of such a model under some mild assumptions. Implementation is available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/MCD.

paragraphs: Time-series causal discovery often assumes that all observations arise from one underlying causal model. Heterogeneous data can violate that assumption: different samples may reflect different relationships between variables. This paper develops MCD, a framework for discovering a mixture of causal models instead of forcing every sample into a shared causal structure.

MCD uses variational inference to learn the underlying models together with each sample's mixing probabilities. Training proceeds jointly by maximizing a lower bound on the data likelihood. The authors provide two versions with different modeling choices. MCD-Linear handles linear causal relationships and independent noise, while MCD-Nonlinear allows nonlinear relationships and noise that depends on the preceding history.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show improvements over state-of-the-art causal discovery benchmarks, particularly when samples originate from different causal graphs. The authors also prove identifiability under stated mild assumptions, giving theoretical support for recovering the mixture structure. The contribution connects heterogeneous time-series modeling with causal discovery while retaining explicit assumptions about when the model can be identified.
summary.tldr: MCD jointly learns multiple causal models and sample mixing probabilities from heterogeneous time series, with conditional identifiability guarantees.

title: Discovering Mixtures of Structural Causal Models from Time Series Data

abstract: The existing graph neural architecture search (GNAS) methods assume that the graph tasks are static during the search process, ignoring the ubiquitous scenarios where sequential graph tasks come in a continual fashion. Moreover, existing GNAS works resort to entangled graph factors during the architecture search process, resulting in the catastrophic forgetting problems. In this paper, we study the problem of continual graph neural architecture search that is expected to continually search the architecture to learn new graph tasks without forgetting the past, which remains largely unexplored in the literature. However, this problem poses the challenge of architecture conflicts, i.e., the optimal architecture for the new graph task may have performance deterioration and thus sub-optimal for past tasks. To address the challenge, we propose a novel Disentangled Continual Graph Neural Architecture Search with Invariant Modularization (GASIM) method, which is able to continually search the optimal architectures without forgetting past knowledge. Specifically, we first design a modular graph architecture super-network incorporating multiple modules to enable searching architecture with factor expertise. Second, we propose a factor-based task-module router that discovers the latent graph factors and routes the incoming task to the best suitable architecture module to alleviate the forgetting problem induced by architecture conflicts. Finally, we propose an invariant architecture search mechanism to capture the shared knowledge among tasks. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance against baselines in continual graph neural architecture search.

paragraphs: Graph neural architecture search usually assumes that the task remains fixed while a suitable network is found. This paper considers tasks arriving sequentially. An architecture that works well for a new task may perform worse on earlier ones, creating conflicts between adaptation and preservation of previously learned knowledge.

GASIM addresses these conflicts through a modular super-network. Different modules can develop expertise in different underlying graph factors. A task-module router discovers those factors and directs an incoming task toward a suitable module. An additional invariant architecture search mechanism seeks knowledge shared across tasks, allowing specialization and reuse to contribute to the same search process.

These components target forgetting at the architecture level: changes in which structures serve a task can matter alongside changes in learned knowledge. Experiments on real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance against continual graph architecture search baselines. The results support organizing architecture search around both task-specific factors and shared information as a way to learn new graph tasks while retaining useful past knowledge.
summary.tldr: GASIM combines specialized architecture modules, task routing, and shared-knowledge search to reduce forgetting across sequential graph tasks.

title: Disentangled Continual Graph Neural Architecture Search with Invariant Modular Supernet

abstract: Model regularization requires extensive manual tuning to balance complexity against overfitting. Cross-regularization resolves this tradeoff by computing validation gradients that directly adapt regularization parameters during training. The method splits parameter optimization - training data guides feature learning while validation data shapes complexity controls - converging provably to cross-validation optima with computational cost scaling only in regularization dimension. When implemented through noise injection in neural networks, this approach reveals striking patterns: unexpectedly high noise tolerance and architecture-specific regularization that emerges organically during training. Beyond complexity control, the framework integrates seamlessly with data augmentation and uncertainty calibration while maintaining single-run efficiency through a simple gradient-based approach.

paragraphs: Regularization controls how much complexity a model can use, but selecting its strength often requires extensive manual tuning. Cross-regularization makes those controls part of the training process. It uses gradients from validation data to adjust regularization parameters as the model learns, turning complexity selection into an ongoing optimization problem.

The method assigns distinct responsibilities to the two data sources: training data guides feature learning, while validation data guides complexity controls. The authors establish convergence to cross-validation optima and report that the relevant computational cost scales only with the dimension of the regularization parameters. This makes the number of adjustable controls central to the method's computational requirements.

When implemented by injecting noise into neural networks, the method reveals unexpectedly high tolerance for noise and regularization patterns that depend on the architecture. These patterns emerge during training rather than being specified individually beforehand. The framework also accommodates data augmentation and uncertainty calibration. Its practical contribution is a simple gradient-based route to adapting these choices within one training run.
summary.tldr: Cross-regularization uses validation gradients to adapt complexity controls during training, with convergence guarantees and single-run efficiency.

title: Cross-regularization: Adaptive Model Complexity through Validation Gradients

abstract: Automation of analog topology design is crucial due to customized requirements of modern applications with heavily manual engineering efforts. The state-of-the-art work applies a sequence-to-sequence approach and supervised finetuning on language models to generate topologies given user specifications. However, its circuit formulation is inefficient due to $O(|V|^2)$ token length and suffers from low precision sensitivity to numeric inputs. In this work, we introduce LaMAGIC2, a succinct float-input canonical formulation with identifier (SFCI) for language model-based analog topology generation. SFCI addresses these challenges by improving component-type recognition through identifier-based representations, reducing token length complexity to $O(|V|)$, and enhancing numeric precision sensitivity for better performance under tight tolerances. Our experiments demonstrate that LaMAGIC2 achieves 34% higher success rates under a tight tolerance 0.01 and 10X lower MSEs compared to a prior method. LaMAGIC2 also exhibits better transferability for circuits with more vertices with up to 58.5% improvement. These advancements establish LaMAGIC2 as a robust framework for analog topology generation.

paragraphs: Analog circuit topology design requires substantial manual work to meet application-specific requirements. Language models can generate circuit structures from specifications, but the prior formulation discussed here has two weaknesses: its token count grows quadratically with the number of vertices, and it responds inadequately to precise numerical inputs.

LaMAGIC2 introduces a succinct float-input canonical formulation with identifiers, called SFCI. Identifiers improve recognition of component types, while the new representation reduces token-length growth from quadratic to linear in the number of vertices. These results connect representation design with both efficiency and specification matching: a shorter encoding can also communicate component identity and numerical requirements more effectively in the evaluated circuit-generation tasks.
summary.tldr: LaMAGIC2 improves circuit-generation accuracy and transferability with a linear-length representation that better conveys component identities and numerical specifications.

title: LaMAGIC2: Advanced Circuit Formulations for Language Model-Based Analog Topology Generation

abstract: Tool-augmented large language models (LLMs) may need to forget learned tools due to security concerns, privacy restrictions, or deprecated tools. However, “tool unlearning” has not been investigated in machine unlearning literature. We introduce this novel task, which requires addressing distinct challenges compared to traditional unlearning: knowledge removal rather than forgetting individual samples, the high cost of optimizing LLMs, and the need for principled evaluation metrics. To bridge these gaps, we propose ToolDelete , the first approach for unlearning tools from tool-augmented LLMs which implements three properties for effective tool unlearning, and a new membership inference attack (MIA) model for evaluation. Experiments on three tool learning datasets and tool-augmented LLMs show that ToolDelete effectively unlearns both randomly selected and category-specific tools, while preserving the LLM’s knowledge on non-deleted tools and maintaining performance on general tasks.

paragraphs: Language models that have learned to use tools may need to forget particular tools because of security concerns, privacy restrictions, or deprecation. This paper introduces tool unlearning as a distinct task. The target is removal of tool-related knowledge, which creates different demands from forgetting individual training examples.

The authors identify optimization cost and principled evaluation as additional challenges for this setting. Their proposed method, ToolDelete, implements three properties intended to support effective tool unlearning. They also introduce a membership-inference attack model for evaluation, pairing the removal method with a dedicated way to assess unlearning behavior.

Experiments on three tool-learning datasets and tool-augmented language models evaluate both randomly selected tools and entire tool categories. The reported results show effective removal while preserving knowledge of tools outside the deletion target and maintaining performance on general tasks. The contribution is therefore both a task formulation and an evaluated approach to selective forgetting, where success includes retaining useful capabilities alongside removing the specified tool knowledge.
summary.tldr: ToolDelete selectively removes learned tool knowledge while preserving other tools and general-task performance in reported experiments.

title: Tool Unlearning for Tool-Augmented LLMs

abstract: Monte-Carlo tree search (MCTS) has driven many recent breakthroughs in deep reinforcement learning (RL). However, scaling MCTS to parallel compute has proven challenging in practice which has motivated alternative planners like sequential Monte-Carlo (SMC). Many of these SMC methods adopt particle filters for smoothing through a reformulation of RL as a policy inference problem. Yet, persisting design choices of these particle filters often conflict with the aim of online planning in RL, which is to obtain a policy improvement at the start of planning. Drawing inspiration from MCTS, we tailor SMC planners specifically to RL by improving data generation within the planner through constrained action sampling and explicit terminal state handling, as well as improving policy and value target estimation. This leads to our Trust-Region Twisted SMC (TRT-SMC), which shows improved runtime and sample-efficiency over baseline MCTS and SMC methods in both discrete and continuous domains.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo tree search is an effective reinforcement-learning planner, but scaling it across parallel computation is challenging. Sequential Monte Carlo offers an alternative based on particles. This paper argues that design choices inherited from particle-filter smoothing can conflict with online planning’s immediate objective: improving the policy at the point where planning begins.

Trust-Region Twisted SMC adapts the planner to that objective. Inspired by tree search, it changes how planning data are generated through constrained action sampling and explicit treatment of terminal states. It also improves the estimation of policy and value targets, addressing both the experiences produced inside planning and the information extracted from them.

The resulting TRT-SMC method improves runtime and sample efficiency relative to the evaluated tree-search and SMC baselines in both discrete and continuous domains. The findings support tailoring particle-based planning to reinforcement learning’s policy-improvement goal. The contribution is therefore a coordinated redesign of the planner, rather than only a change to how many particles or simulations it uses.
summary.tldr: TRT-SMC tailors particle-based planning to immediate policy improvement, achieving better runtime and sample efficiency than evaluated MCTS and SMC baselines.

title: Trust-Region Twisted Policy Improvement

abstract: We study the task of Multiclass Linear Classification (MLC) in the distribution-free PAC model with Random Classification Noise (RCN). Specifically, the learner is given a set of labeled examples $(x, y)$, where $x$ is drawn from an unknown distribution on $R^d$ and the labels are generated by a multiclass linear classifier corrupted with RCN. That is, the label $y$ is flipped from $i$ to $j$ with probability $H_{ij}$ according to a known noise matrix $H$ with non-negative separation $\sigma: = \min_{i \neq j} H_{ii}-H_{ij}$. The goal is to compute a hypothesis with small 0-1 error. For the special case of two labels, prior work has given polynomial-time algorithms achieving the optimal error. Surprisingly, little is known about the complexity of this task even for three labels. As our main contribution, we show that the complexity of MLC with RCN becomes drastically different in the presence of three or more labels. Specifically, we prove super-polynomial Statistical Query (SQ) lower bounds for this problem. In more detail, even for three labels and constant separation, we give a super-polynomial lower bound on the complexity of any SQ algorithm achieving optimal error. For a larger number of labels and smaller separation, we show a super-polynomial SQ lower bound even for the weaker goal of achieving any constant factor approximation to the optimal loss or even beating the trivial hypothesis.

As our main contribution, we show that the complexity of MLC with RCN becomes drastically different in the presence of three or more labels. paragraphs: This paper studies linear classification when there are multiple labels and random label corruption follows a known matrix. Inputs come from an unknown distribution. The noise matrix specifies how likely each true class is to become another observed class, and its separation parameter compares keeping the correct label with individual incorrect alternatives.

For two labels, earlier algorithms can achieve optimal error in polynomial time. The authors show a sharp change within the Statistical Query model once there are three labels. Even with constant noise separation, achieving optimal error requires super-polynomial Statistical Query complexity. Knowing the corruption matrix therefore does not remove this computational barrier.

With more labels and smaller separation, the lower bounds become stronger: they also obstruct obtaining any constant-factor approximation to optimal loss, or even improving on a trivial hypothesis. These are lower bounds for Statistical Query algorithms, so their scope is a specified computational model. The findings show why efficient methods for noisy binary classification cannot automatically be expected to extend to the multiclass setting.
summary.tldr: Statistical Query lower bounds reveal a sharp increase in noisy linear-classification difficulty when moving from two labels to three or more.

title: Statistical Query Hardness of Multiclass Linear Classification with Random Classification Noise

abstract: Effectively modeling and utilizing spatiotemporal features from RGB and other modalities (e.g., depth, thermal, and event data, denoted as X) is the core of RGB-X tracker design. Existing methods often employ two parallel branches to separately process the RGB and X input streams, requiring the model to simultaneously handle two dispersed feature spaces, which complicates both the model structure and computation process. More critically, intra-modality spatial modeling within each dispersed space incurs substantial computational overhead, limiting resources for inter-modality spatial modeling and temporal modeling. To address this, we propose a novel tracker, CSTrack, which focuses on modeling Compact Spatiotemporal features to achieve simple yet effective tracking. Specifically, we first introduce an innovative Spatial Compact Module that integrates the RGB-X dual input streams into a compact spatial feature, enabling thorough intra- and inter-modality spatial modeling. Additionally, we design an efficient Temporal Compact Module that compactly represents temporal features by constructing the refined target distribution heatmap. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our compact spatiotemporal modeling method, with CSTrack achieving new SOTA results on mainstream RGB-X benchmarks. The code and models will be released at: https://github.com/XiaokunFeng/CSTrack.
originalAbstract: Effectively modeling and utilizing spatiotemporal features from RGB and other modalities (e.g., depth, thermal, and event data, denoted as X) is the core of RGB-X tracker design. Existing methods often employ two parallel branches to separately process the RGB and X input streams, requiring the model to simultaneously handle two dispersed feature spaces, which complicates both the model structure and computation process. More critically, intra-modality spatial modeling within each dispersed space incurs substantial computational overhead, limiting resources for inter-modality spatial modeling and temporal modeling. To address this, we propose a novel tracker, CSTrack, which focuses on modeling Compact Spatiotemporal features to achieve simple yet effective tracking. Specifically, we first introduce an innovative Spatial Compact Module that integrates the RGB-X dual input streams into a compact spatial feature, enabling thorough intra- and inter-modality spatial modeling. Additionally, we design an efficient Temporal Compact Module that compactly represents temporal features by constructing the refined target distribution heatmap. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our compact spatiotemporal modeling method, with CSTrack achieving new SOTA results on mainstream RGB-X benchmarks. The code and models will be released at: https://github.com/XiaokunFeng/CSTrack.

The paper argues that maintaining these separate feature spaces complicates computation, while modeling spatial relationships within each stream consumes resources that could support interaction between modalities and tracking over time.

CSTrack brings the streams into a compact representation. Its Spatial Compact Module integrates RGB and the additional input into a shared spatial feature, supporting relationships both within each modality and across modalities. Its Temporal Compact Module represents information over time through a refined heatmap describing the target distribution.

The two modules address complementary parts of tracking: combining spatial evidence from different sensors and retaining useful temporal information. The authors report that extensive experiments validate this compact approach and produce new state-of-the-art results on mainstream RGB-X benchmarks. The findings support compact spatiotemporal representation as an effective way to organize multimodal tracking, with the claimed gains demonstrated on those benchmarks.
summary.tldr: CSTrack combines multimodal spatial features and compact temporal heatmaps to achieve state-of-the-art results on RGB-X tracking benchmarks.

title: CSTrack: Enhancing RGB-X Tracking via Compact Spatiotemporal Features

abstract: In this work, we take the first exploration of the recently popular foundation model, i.e., State Space Model/Mamba, in image quality assessment (IQA), aiming at observing and excavating the perception potential in vision Mamba. A series of works on Mamba has shown its significant potential in various fields, e.g., segmentation and classification. However, the perception capability of Mamba remains under-explored. Consequently, we propose QMamba by revisiting and adapting the Mamba model for three crucial IQA tasks, i.e., task-specific, universal, and transferable IQA, which reveals its clear advantages over existing foundational models, e.g., Swin Transformer, ViT, and CNNs, in terms of perception and computational cost. To improve the transferability of QMamba, we propose the StylePrompt tuning paradigm, where lightweight mean and variance prompts are injected to assist task-adaptive transfer learning of pre-trained QMamba for different downstream IQA tasks. Compared with existing prompt tuning strategies, our StylePrompt enables better perceptual transfer with lower computational cost. Extensive experiments on multiple synthetic, authentic IQA datasets, and cross IQA datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed QMamba.

paragraphs: Image quality assessment asks models to judge visual quality, making perceptual capability central to the task. This paper investigates that capability in vision Mamba, a state-space model architecture whose use in other vision tasks had received more attention. The authors adapt it into QMamba for task-specific, universal, and transferable quality assessment.

A second contribution, StylePrompt, supports adapting a pretrained QMamba model to downstream quality-assessment tasks. It introduces lightweight prompts based on means and variances to guide task-adaptive transfer learning. The authors report better perceptual transfer with lower computational cost than existing prompt-tuning strategies.

The reported results show advantages over Swin Transformer, ViT, and convolutional models in perception and computational cost. The contribution therefore combines an assessment of Mamba's suitability for visual-quality judgments with a lightweight adaptation method, addressing both the quality of those judgments and the cost of transferring them to different tasks.
summary.tldr: QMamba adapts vision Mamba for image quality assessment, while StylePrompt improves perceptual transfer at lower reported computational cost.

title: QMamba: On First Exploration of Vision Mamba for Image Quality Assessment

abstract: Aligning language models with human preferences relies on pairwise preference datasets. While some studies suggest that on-policy data consistently outperforms off-policy data for preference learning, others indicate that the advantages of on-policy data are task-dependent, highlighting the need for a systematic exploration of their interplay. In this work, we show that on-policy and off-policy data offer complementary strengths: on-policy data is particularly effective for reasoning tasks like math and coding, while off-policy data performs better on subjective tasks such as creative writing and making personal recommendations. Guided by these findings, we introduce SimpleMix, an approach to combine the complementary strengths of on-policy and off-policy preference learning by simply mixing these two data sources. Our empirical results across diverse tasks and benchmarks demonstrate that SimpleMix substantially improves language model alignment. Specifically, SimpleMix improves upon on-policy DPO and off-policy DPO by an average of 6.03 on Alpaca Eval 2.0. Moreover, it surpasses prior approaches that are much more complex in combining on- and off-policy data, such as HyPO and DPO-Mix-P, by an average of 3.05. These findings validate the effectiveness and efficiency of SimpleMix for enhancing preference-based alignment.

paragraphs: Preference learning trains language models using comparisons between candidate responses. This paper investigates the choice between on-policy and off-policy preference data, motivated by conflicting findings about which works better. Its experiments find complementary strengths: on-policy data helps particularly with mathematical and coding reasoning, while off-policy data performs better on subjective tasks such as creative writing and recommendations.

SimpleMix uses these findings to motivate directly mixing the two data sources. The approach aims to combine their benefits across tasks without introducing a complicated method for coordinating them. The key contribution is the empirical case that the choice of data source should reflect complementary task strengths rather than a single preferred source.

Across diverse tasks and benchmarks, SimpleMix improves alignment. On Alpaca Eval 2.0, it reports an average gain of 6.03 over on-policy and off-policy DPO, and an average gain of 3.05 over the more complex HyPO and DPO-Mix-P approaches. These results support simple data mixing as an effective and efficient preference-learning strategy in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SimpleMix combines on-policy and off-policy preference data to exploit their complementary strengths across reasoning and subjective tasks.

title: SIMPLEMIX: Frustratingly Simple Mixing of Off- and On-policy Data in Language Model Preference Learning

abstract: The Fourier transform is a fundamental tool in computer science and signal processing. In particular, when the signal is sparse in the frequency domain—having only $k$ distinct frequencies—sparse Fourier transform (SFT) algorithms can recover the signal in a sublinear time (proportional to the sparsity $k$). Most prior research focused on SFT for discrete signals, designing both randomized and deterministic algorithms for one-dimensional and high-dimensional discrete signals. However, SFT for continuous signals (i.e., $x^*(t)=\sum_{j=1}^k v_j e^{2\pi \mathbf{i} f_j t}$ for $t\in [0,T]$) is a more challenging task. The discrete SFT algorithms are not directly applicable to continuous signals due to the sparsity blow-up from the discretization. Prior to this work, there is a randomized algorithm that achieves an $\ell_2$ recovery guarantee in $\widetilde{O}(k\cdot \mathrm{polylog}(F/\eta))$ time, where $F$ is the band-limit of the frequencies and $\eta$ is the frequency gap. Nevertheless, whether we can solve this problem without using randomness remains open. In this work, we address this gap and introduce the first sublinear-time deterministic sparse Fourier transform algorithm in the continuous setting. Specifically, our algorithm uses $\widetilde{O}(k^2 \cdot \mathrm{polylog}(F/\eta))$ samples and $\widetilde{O}(k^2 \cdot \mathrm{polylog}(F/\eta))$ time to reconstruct the on-grid signal with arbitrary noise that satisfies a mild condition. This is the optimal recovery guarantee that can be achieved by any deterministic approach.

paragraphs: A sparse Fourier transform recovers a signal using the fact that it contains only a small number of distinct frequencies. Its stated reconstruction result applies to an on-grid signal with arbitrary noise satisfying a mild condition. Both sample use and running time scale roughly quadratically with the number of frequencies, multiplied by polylogarithmic factors involving the frequency band limit and the gap between frequencies, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed.

The authors characterize the recovery guarantee as optimal among deterministic approaches. That optimality concerns the recovery guarantee, rather than asserting optimal running time. The contribution establishes deterministic recovery under the stated signal and noise conditions, complementing the earlier randomized result.
summary.tldr: A deterministic algorithm achieves sublinear-time continuous sparse Fourier recovery for on-grid signals under a stated noise condition.

title: Deterministic Sparse Fourier Transform for Continuous Signals with Frequency Gap

abstract: Unlike its vanilla counterpart with i.i.d. samples, stochastic optimization with Markovian sampling allows the sampling scheme following a Markov chain. This problem encompasses various applications that range from asynchronous distributed optimization to reinforcement learning. In this work, we lower bound the sample complexity of finding $\epsilon$-approximate critical solutions for any first-order methods when sampling is Markovian. We show that for samples drawn from stationary Markov processes with countable state space, any algorithm that accesses smooth, non-convex functions through queries to a stochastic gradient oracle, requires at least $\Omega(\epsilon^{-4})$ samples. Moreover, for finite Markov chains, we show a $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2})$ lower bound and propose a new algorithm, called MaC-SAGE, that is proven to (nearly) match our lower bound.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization often assumes that each sampled observation is independent of the others. This paper studies sampling governed by a Markov chain, where observations can depend on preceding states. Such sampling appears in settings including reinforcement learning and asynchronous distributed optimization, making its effect on optimization complexity practically relevant.

The authors establish lower bounds on the samples needed by first-order methods to find approximately critical solutions of smooth, non-convex functions. These methods obtain information through stochastic gradient queries. For stationary Markov processes with countable state spaces, the stated lower bound scales as ε to the power of −4, where ε specifies the desired approximation accuracy.

For finite Markov chains, the paper gives a lower bound scaling as ε to the power of −2 and introduces MaC-SAGE, an algorithm proven to nearly match that bound. A lower bound identifies a fundamental difficulty of the specified problem class; a nearly matching algorithm shows that the finite-chain benchmark is almost attainable. The results distinguish these sampling settings rather than assigning one complexity rate to all Markovian sampling.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes sample-complexity lower bounds under Markov sampling and introduces an algorithm that nearly matches its finite-chain bound.

title: Improved Lower Bounds for First-order Stochastic Non-convex Optimization under Markov Sampling

abstract: Neural networks capable of accurate, input-conditional uncertainty representation are essential for real-world AI systems. Deep ensembles of Gaussian networks have proven highly effective for continuous regression due to their ability to flexibly represent aleatoric uncertainty via unrestricted heteroscedastic variance, which in turn enables accurate epistemic uncertainty estimation. However, no analogous approach exists for $\textit{count}$ regression, despite many important applications. To address this gap, we propose the Deep Double Poisson Network (DDPN), a novel neural discrete count regression model that outputs the parameters of the Double Poisson distribution, enabling arbitrarily high or low predictive aleatoric uncertainty for count data and improving epistemic uncertainty estimation when ensembled. We formalize and prove that DDPN exhibits robust regression properties similar to heteroscedastic Gaussian models via learnable loss attenuation, and introduce a simple loss modification to control this behavior. Experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that DDPN outperforms current baselines in accuracy, calibration, and out-of-distribution detection, establishing a new state-of-the-art in deep count regression.
