paragraphs: Predicting counts requires representing uncertainty as well as estimating a numerical outcome. For continuous outcomes, Gaussian neural networks can let uncertainty vary flexibly with the input. This paper develops an analogous approach for discrete counts, where the desired uncertainty representation must remain compatible with count-valued predictions.

The Deep Double Poisson Network, or DDPN, predicts parameters of a Double Poisson distribution. This lets it represent very high or very low aleatoric uncertainty: variability inherent in the outcome for a given input. Combining multiple DDPNs into an ensemble also improves the estimation of epistemic uncertainty, which concerns uncertainty in the learned model.

The authors prove that DDPN has robust regression properties through learnable loss attenuation, a mechanism that adjusts how strongly prediction errors affect training, and introduce a loss modification to control it. Experiments on diverse datasets report improvements over existing baselines in prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and detection of out-of-distribution inputs. These results connect flexible count uncertainty to benefits in both prediction and reliability assessment.
summary.tldr: DDPN gives count-prediction networks flexible input-dependent uncertainty, improving reported accuracy, calibration, and out-of-distribution detection.

title: Fully Heteroscedastic Count Regression with Deep Double Poisson Networks

abstract: This paper considers a canonical problem in kernel regression: how good are the model performances when it is trained by the popular online first-order algorithms, compared to the offline ones, such as ridge and ridgeless regression? In this paper, we analyze the foundational single-pass Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in kernel regression under source condition where the optimal predictor can even not belong to the RKHS, i.e. the model is misspecified. Specifically, we focus on the inner product kernel over the sphere and characterize the exact orders of the excess risk curves under different scales of sample sizes $n$ concerning the input dimension $d$. Surprisingly, we show that SGD achieves min-max optimal rates up to constants among all the scales, $without$ suffering the saturation, a prevalent phenomenon observed in (ridge) regression, except when the model is highly misspecified and the learning is in a final stage where $n\gg d^\gamma$ with any constant $\gamma >0$. The main reason for SGD to overcome the curse of saturation is the exponentially decaying step size schedule, a common practice in deep neural network training. As a byproduct, we provide the $first$ provable advantage of the scheme over the iterative averaging method in the common setting.

paragraphs: This paper asks how single-pass stochastic gradient descent compares with offline kernel regression methods as data increases. The analysis covers an inner-product kernel on the sphere under a source condition, including misspecified cases where the optimal predictor lies outside the kernel's function space. It characterizes excess-risk scaling across sample sizes relative to input dimension.

The result therefore retains a meaningful boundary rather than claiming unrestricted optimality. The analysis additionally establishes what the authors describe as the first provable advantage of this schedule over iterative averaging in the common setting they study.
summary.tldr: For the analyzed kernel regression setting, exponentially decaying step sizes let single-pass SGD attain optimal rates across most sample-size regimes without saturation.

title: Learning Curves of Stochastic Gradient Descent in Kernel Regression

abstract: We study the problem of neural logistic bandits, where the main task is to learn an unknown reward function within a logistic link function using a neural network. Existing approaches either exhibit unfavorable dependencies on $\kappa$, where $1/\kappa$ represents the minimum variance of reward distributions, or suffer from direct dependence on the feature dimension $d$, which can be huge in neural network–based settings. In this work, we introduce a novel Bernstein-type inequality for self-normalized vector-valued martingales that is designed to bypass a direct dependence on the ambient dimension. This lets us deduce a regret upper bound that grows with the effective dimension $\widetilde{d}$, not the feature dimension, while keeping a minimal dependence on $\kappa$. Based on the concentration inequality, we propose two algorithms, NeuralLog-UCB-1 and NeuralLog-UCB-2, that guarantee regret upper bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(\widetilde{d}\sqrt{\kappa T})$ and $\widetilde{O}(\widetilde{d}\sqrt{T/\kappa})$, respectively, improving on the existing results. Lastly, we report numerical results on both synthetic and real datasets to validate our theoretical findings.

In this work, we introduce a novel Bernstein-type inequality for self-normalized vector-valued martingales that is designed to bypass a direct dependence on the ambient dimension. paragraphs: Neural logistic bandits learn an unknown reward function represented by a neural network within a logistic link. The paper addresses theoretical bounds that become unfavorable when they depend directly on a large feature dimension or strongly on kappa, a parameter whose reciprocal represents the minimum reward variance.

Its main technical contribution is a Bernstein-type concentration inequality for self-normalized vector-valued martingales. This avoids direct dependence on the ambient feature dimension. The resulting regret analysis instead uses an effective dimension, allowing the bound to reflect that quantity while maintaining a small dependence on the reward-variance parameter.

The authors derive two algorithms from this inequality. NeuralLog-UCB-1 has a regret upper bound of order d-tilde times sqrt(kappa T), while NeuralLog-UCB-2 has a bound of order d-tilde times sqrt(T/kappa), with logarithmic factors suppressed. These improve on existing results. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the theoretical findings. The advance is a more favorable account of learning difficulty in neural settings with potentially huge feature spaces.
summary.tldr: A new concentration inequality enables neural logistic bandit algorithms with improved regret bounds based on effective rather than ambient dimension.

title: Neural Logistic Bandits

abstract: Scaling autoregressive large language models (LLMs) has driven unprecedented progress but comes with vast computational costs. In this work, we tackle these costs by leveraging unstructured sparsity within an LLM’s feedforward layers, the components accounting for most of the model parameters and execution FLOPs. To achieve this, we introduce a new sparse packing format and a set of CUDA kernels designed to seamlessly integrate with the optimized execution pipelines of modern GPUs, enabling efficient sparse computation during LLM inference and training. To substantiate our gains, we provide a quantitative study of LLM sparsity, demonstrating that simple L1 regularization can induce over 99% sparsity with negligible impact on downstream performance. When paired with our kernels, we show that these sparsity levels translate into substantial throughput, energy efficiency, and memory usage benefits that increase with model scale. We will release all code and kernels under an open-source license to promote adoption and accelerate research toward establishing sparsity as a practical axis for improving the efficiency and scalability of modern foundation models.

paragraphs: Large language models devote much of their parameter count and computation to feedforward layers. This paper targets those costs using unstructured sparsity, where many individual entries can be zero without following a fixed block pattern. The work combines a study of how much sparsity models tolerate with GPU machinery designed to make that sparsity computationally useful.

The authors introduce a sparse packing format and CUDA kernels that fit into optimized modern GPU execution pipelines. These support sparse computation during both training and inference. Their quantitative study finds that simple L1 regularization can induce more than 99% sparsity with negligible effects on downstream performance in the reported setting.

When paired with the proposed kernels, these sparse models show substantial improvements in throughput, energy efficiency, and memory use. The benefits increase with model scale. The result connects two necessary pieces of the proposed efficiency strategy: learning highly sparse feedforward layers while retaining performance, and executing those layers efficiently enough for the sparsity to deliver practical resource savings.
summary.tldr: Highly sparse feedforward layers and specialized GPU kernels deliver reported language-model speed, energy, and memory benefits with negligible performance impact.

title: Sparser, Faster, Lighter Transformer Language Models

abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have produced many specialized multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) that share common foundational LLMs, forming distinct model lineages. It remains unclear whether a fundamental behavioral link exists between the foundational LLMs and downstream variants. We investigate this question by quantifying head-level context-truthfulness scores. Across diverse LLM and MLLM lineages, including Vicuna-, Qwen2.5-, LLaMA2-, and Mistral-based models, we find that Truth Scores are strongly preserved within model families, even after instruction tuning or multimodal adaptation. We further show that this inheritance is consistent with attention-head weight preservation, and that context-truthful heads attend to query-relevant evidence. Building on this finding, we propose TruthProbe, a soft-gating strategy that amplifies context-truthful heads while preserving other head contributions. TruthProbe improves contextual truthfulness on HaluEval and reduces multimodal hallucination on POPE and CHAIR, with base-LLM Truth Scores transferring effectively to their fine-tuned LLM and MLLM descendants. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/TruthProbe.

paragraphs: Many specialized language and multimodal models descend from the same foundational language model. This paper investigates whether those family relationships preserve internal behavior relevant to contextual truthfulness. It assigns attention heads context-truthfulness scores and compares those scores across foundational models and their instruction-tuned or multimodally adapted descendants.

Across Vicuna-, Qwen2.5-, LLaMA2-, and Mistral-based families, the authors find strong preservation of these scores. That inheritance is consistent with preservation of attention-head weights, and heads with strong contextual-truthfulness scores attend to evidence relevant to the query. The findings connect model lineage with a measurable internal tendency to use supplied context.

TruthProbe builds on this pattern through soft gating: it amplifies context-truthful heads while retaining contributions from other heads. The method improves contextual truthfulness on HaluEval and reduces multimodal hallucination on POPE and CHAIR. Scores obtained from base language models also transfer effectively to their descendants. This suggests that measurements made on a foundational model can guide useful interventions in related specialized models, as demonstrated in the evaluated families.
summary.tldr: TruthProbe amplifies context-truthful attention heads whose scores persist across model families, improving contextual truthfulness and reducing evaluated multimodal hallucinations.

title: The Truth Stays in the Family: Enhancing Contextual Truthfulness via Inherited Heads in Model Lineages

abstract: This paper proposes a synergy of amortised and particle-based methods for sampling from distributions defined by unnormalised density functions. We state a connection between sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) and neural sequential samplers trained by maximum-entropy reinforcement learning (MaxEnt RL), wherein learnt sampling policies and value functions define proposal kernels and twist functions. Exploiting this connection, we introduce an off-policy RL training procedure for the sampler that uses samples from SMC – using the learnt sampler as a proposal – as a behaviour policy that better explores the target distribution. We describe techniques for stable joint training of proposals and twist functions and an adaptive weight tempering scheme to reduce training signal variance. Furthermore, building upon past attempts to use experience replay to guide the training of neural samplers, we derive a way to combine historical samples with annealed importance sampling weights within a replay buffer. On synthetic multi-modal targets (in both continuous and discrete spaces) and the Boltzmann distribution of alanine dipeptide conformations, we demonstrate improvements in approximating the true distribution as well as training stability compared to both amortised and Monte Carlo methods.

Exploiting this connection, we introduce an off-policy RL training procedure for the sampler that uses samples from SMC – using the learnt sampler as a proposal – as a behaviour policy that better explores the target distribution. We describe techniques for stable joint training of proposals and twist functions and an adaptive weight tempering scheme to reduce training signal variance. Furthermore, building upon past attempts to use experience replay to guide the training of neural samplers, we derive a way to combine historical samples with annealed importance sampling weights within a replay buffer. On synthetic multi-modal targets (in both continuous and discrete spaces) and the Boltzmann distribution of alanine dipeptide conformations, we demonstrate improvements in approximating the true distribution as well as training stability compared to both amortised and Monte Carlo methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies sampling from distributions specified by unnormalized densities, combining learned samplers with particle-based methods. A learned sampler can reuse what training has taught it, while sequential Monte Carlo maintains and updates a collection of candidate samples. The proposed approach connects these methods through maximum-entropy reinforcement learning.

In this connection, the learned sampling policy supplies proposal kernels, while value functions supply twist functions that guide sequential Monte Carlo. Samples generated by this particle procedure then train the neural sampler through off-policy reinforcement learning. Because the procedure itself uses the learned sampler as its proposal, the two components form a training loop intended to improve exploration of the target distribution.

Tests cover synthetic multimodal targets in continuous and discrete spaces and alanine dipeptide conformations. Compared with both amortized and Monte Carlo methods, the approach improves approximation of the target distribution and training stability in these evaluations.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement-learning and sequential-Monte-Carlo training loop improves learned sampling accuracy and stability on evaluated multimodal and molecular distributions.

title: Reinforced Sequential Monte Carlo for Amortised Sampling

abstract: Consumer-level applications require fast optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with high-fidelity novel view rendering. However, existing 3DGS acceleration approaches still incur substantial computation on redundant pixels while sacrificing fine details. In this paper, we present TurboGS, an error-guided training framework that accelerates 3DGS by concentrating optimization on perceptually informative pixels. TurboGS is built upon four core components: (1) a tile-wise sparse pixel sampling, which, driven by multi-view reconstruction errors during training, prioritizes challenging regions and skips well-reconstructed ones to avoid redundant gradient computation; (2) a tile-wise structure-aware loss with sparse Normalized Cross-Correlation, which provides sparse yet effective supervision to preserve fine details and stabilize training; (3) an error-driven Gaussian density control strategy, which dynamically allocates model capacity and removes redundant primitives; and (4) a tailored hybrid optimizer that couples Hessian-informed updates with Adam moment damping to stabilize and improve convergence under sparse supervision. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that TurboGS can deliver on par or superior rendering quality within 100 seconds (up to 10x training speedup over vanilla 3DGS).

paragraphs: TurboGS accelerates training for 3D Gaussian Splatting by concentrating computation on pixels that still need improvement. Existing acceleration approaches can spend substantial effort on redundant pixels while losing fine detail. The proposed framework uses reconstruction errors across views to identify challenging regions and skip regions that are already reconstructed well.

These are the reported experimental outcomes rather than fixed speed guarantees. The approach’s significance is coordinating pixel selection, structural supervision, model capacity, and optimization so that reducing computation does not require sacrificing fine reconstruction detail.
summary.tldr: TurboGS targets difficult pixels and adapts Gaussian capacity and optimization, reporting up to tenfold faster training with comparable or better rendering quality.

title: TurboGS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting via Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling and Optimization

abstract: Mathematical search problems present a unique challenge for Reinforcement Learning (RL) due to vast search spaces and sparse rewards. In previous works, the Andrews-Curtis (AC) conjecture was established as an illustrative example of such problems. In this work, we identify a critical structural barrier in the AC landscape: a "Two Hump" distribution, where problem instances are either trivially solvable or effectively impossible, with a scarcity of intermediate "hard-but-solvable" instances required for effective learning. We tackle this challenge through two primary avenues: novel data generation techniques to populate the difficulty gap, and significant algorithmic enhancements including the introduction of supermoves and Transformer-based architectures. We demonstrate substantial performance improvements over previous baselines, and release new comprehensive benchmark datasets including AC-19 (125,192 AC-trivial presentations of varying difficulty with length at most 19) and AC-1M (1,136,154 hard AC-trivial presentations of length at most 30), the first large-scale, publicly available datasets of this kind.

paragraphs: Mathematical search can be difficult for reinforcement learning because possible action sequences are numerous and successful outcomes are rare. Studying problems associated with the Andrews-Curtis conjecture, the authors identify an additional obstacle: available instances cluster into trivially solvable and effectively impossible groups, leaving few challenging but solvable examples between them.

This gap matters because intermediate problems provide opportunities for a learner to improve beyond easy behavior while still encountering success. The paper addresses it through new data-generation techniques that populate the missing difficulty range. It also introduces algorithmic changes, including supermoves and Transformer-based architectures, to improve the search process.

The resulting methods substantially improve performance over previous baselines. The authors also release AC-19, containing 125,192 AC-trivial presentations of varying difficulty and length at most 19, and AC-1M, containing 1,136,154 hard AC-trivial presentations of length at most 30. These datasets make the difficulty distribution itself a concrete research resource. The work links better learning to both the search algorithm and the availability of appropriately challenging training problems.
summary.tldr: New intermediate-difficulty data, supermoves, and Transformer architectures improve reinforcement learning for Andrews-Curtis mathematical search.

title: The Two-Hump Problem: Bridging the Difficulty Gap in Mathematical Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning rate configuration is a fundamental aspect of modern deep learning. The prevailing practice of applying a uniform learning rate across all layers overlooks the structural heterogeneity of Transformers, potentially limiting their effectiveness as the backbone of Large Language Models (LLMs). In this paper, we introduce Layerwise Learning Rate (LLR), an adaptive scheme that assigns distinct learning rates to individual Transformer layers. Our method is grounded in Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HT-SR) theory, which characterizes the empirical spectral density (ESD) of weight correlation matrices to quantify heavy-tailedness. Layers with weaker heavy-tailedness are assigned larger learning rates to accelerate their training, while layers with stronger heavy-tailedness receive smaller learning rates. By tailoring learning rates in this manner, LLR promotes balanced training across layers, leading to faster convergence and improved generalization. Extensive experiments across architectures (from LLaMa to GPT-nano), optimizers (AdamW and Muon), and parameter scales (60M–3B, up to 100B tokens) demonstrate that LLR achieves up to 1.5$\times$ training speedup and outperforms baselines, notably raising average zero-shot accuracy from 47.09% to 49.02% for 1B models and from 48.58% to 50.61% for 3B models. A key advantage of LLR is its low tuning overhead: it transfers nearly optimal LR settings directly from the uniform baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/hed-ucas/Layer-wise-Learning-Rate.

paragraphs: Transformer layers have different internal structures, yet training commonly applies the same learning rate to all of them. Layerwise Learning Rate, or LLR, uses properties of each layer’s weights to choose separate update rates. The aim is to balance progress across layers and improve training speed and generalization.

The method draws on Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization theory, examining the spectral distribution of weight correlation matrices. Layers with weaker heavy-tailedness receive larger learning rates, while those with stronger heavy-tailedness receive smaller ones. This turns a measured property of the weights into a rule for distributing learning effort across the network.

summary.tldr: LLR assigns layer-specific learning rates from weight spectral properties, improving training speed and zero-shot accuracy with low tuning overhead.

title: One LR Doesn’t Fit All: Heavy-Tail Guided Layerwise Learning Rates for LLMs

abstract: Despite the high accuracy of EEG-based emotion recognition, existing models remain opaque "black boxes", lacking semantic grounding between abstract neural features and human-interpretable states. In this paper, we reframe EEG explainability as a cross-modal generation task, shifting the paradigm from feature attribution to behavioral visualization. We introduce Facial Emoji Proxy Modeling, a novel framework that translates high-dimensional EEG signals into identity-anonymized facial emojis. Guided by the neuroscientific inspiration of neural-facial association, this approach grounds neural representations in the manifold of observable facial dynamics. Technically, our framework integrates FMENet, a specialized backbone modeling expression-relevant spatial synergies, and the Facial Emoji Learning Branch (FELB), which treats emoji reconstruction as a structured semantic regularizer. Extensive experiments on EAV and MMER benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among EEG-only models. Crucially, it generates semantically faithful facial animations that provide a transparent, privacy-preserving window into the brain’s emotional evolution, effectively allowing users to “see the emotion” directly from neural signals. Code is available at https://github.com/xian-sh/SeeEmotion

This paper makes those representations more accessible by translating EEG signals into identity-anonymized facial emojis. It treats explanation as cross-modal generation, giving an observable behavioral form to the model’s representation of emotional change.

Reconstructing emojis acts as a structured semantic regularizer: the learned EEG representation must support meaningful facial dynamics as well as emotion recognition. The design draws inspiration from associations between neural activity and facial behavior, using animated expressions as an interpretable proxy.

Experiments on EAV and MMER report state-of-the-art accuracy among models using EEG alone. The generated facial animations are described as semantically faithful and provide a visual account of emotional evolution without reproducing personal identity. The findings support combining recognition with an interpretable generation task, so the same framework produces both emotion predictions and a privacy-preserving visual representation of the signals.
summary.tldr: The framework translates EEG into anonymized facial animations, pairing interpretable emotional visualization with strong EEG-only recognition accuracy.

title: See the Emotion: A Facial Emoji Proxy Modeling for EEG Emotion Recognition

abstract: Algorithmic fairness is often studied in static or single-agent settings, yet many real-world decision-making systems involve multiple interacting entities whose multi-stage actions jointly influence long-term outcomes. Existing fairness methods applied at isolated decision points frequently fail to mitigate disparities that accumulate over time. Although recent work has modeled fairness as a sequential decision-making problem, it typically assumes centralized agents or simplified dynamics, limiting its applicability to complex social systems. We introduce MAFE, a suite of Multi-Agent Fair Environments designed to simulate realistic, modular, and dynamic systems in which fairness emerges from the interplay of multiple agents. We demonstrate MAFEs in three domains—loan processing, healthcare, and higher education—supporting heterogeneous agents, configurable interventions, and fairness metrics. The environments are open-source and compatible with standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) libraries, enabling reproducible evaluation of fairness-aware policies. Through extensive experiments on cooperative use cases, we demonstrate how MAFE facilitates the design of equitable multi-agent algorithms and reveals critical trade-offs between fairness, performance, and coordination. MAFE provides a foundation for systematic progress in dynamic, multi-agent fairness research.

paragraphs: Fairness in a social decision system can depend on the combined actions of several entities over time. Addressing disparities at one isolated decision point may leave accumulated inequalities unresolved. MAFE provides simulation environments for studying this interaction, extending evaluation beyond static decisions or a single centralized agent.

The suite covers loan processing, healthcare, and higher education. Its environments support different kinds of agents, configurable interventions, and fairness metrics within modular, dynamic systems. They are open source and compatible with standard multi-agent reinforcement learning libraries, providing a common basis for reproducible experiments with policies intended to improve equity.

The contribution is a research platform for observing how those objectives interact across multiple stages. It makes the consequences of coordinated decisions part of fairness evaluation, rather than assessing each agent’s choices solely in isolation.
summary.tldr: MAFE supplies multi-agent simulations for studying how sequential decisions create fairness, performance, and coordination trade-offs.

title: MAFE: Enabling Equitable Algorithm Design in Multi-Agent Multi-Stage Decision-Making Systems

abstract: Encoder-only language models are frequently used for a variety of language tasks, including classification and retrieval. However, there has been a lack of recent research efforts for encoder models, especially with respect to multilingual models. We introduce mmBERT, an encoder-only language model pretrained on 3T tokens of multilingual text in over 1800 languages. To build mmBERT we introduce several novel elements to massively multilingual encoder training, including phased data curation and scheduled language inclusion. We add over 1700 low-resource languages to the data mix only during the decay phase, showing that it boosts performance dramatically and maximizes the gains from the relatively small amount of training data without excessive repetition. The model uses recent advances in architecture and training schemes to be faster and more multilingual than other models and we release weights, data, and code. We show that mmBERT significantly outperforms the previous generation, on various tasks, for both high and low-resource languages.

This paper introduces mmBERT, pretrained on three trillion tokens covering more than 1,800 languages. Its contribution includes both a multilingual model and a training strategy for making effective use of unevenly available language data.

The strategy combines phased data curation with scheduled language inclusion. More than 1,700 low-resource languages enter the training mixture only during the decay phase. The authors report that this timing substantially improves performance while obtaining more value from limited data without excessive repetition. Thus, when a language enters training is an important part of the approach.

The model also incorporates recent architectural and training advances to improve speed and multilingual coverage. Evaluations show significant gains over the previous generation across multiple tasks for both high-resource and low-resource languages. Released weights, data, and code accompany the model. The findings highlight training schedules as a useful tool for extending language coverage while improving performance.
summary.tldr: mmBERT improves multilingual encoder performance using phased training that introduces over 1,700 low-resource languages during the decay phase.

title: mmBERT: A Modern Multilingual Encoder with Annealed Language Learning

abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models based on next-scale prediction are rapidly emerging as a powerful tool for image generation, but they face a critical weakness: information inconsistencies between patches across timesteps introduced by progressive resolution scaling. These inconsistencies scatter guidance signals, causing them to drift away from conditioning information and leaving behind ambiguous, unfaithful features. We tackle this challenge with Information-Grounding Guidance (IGG), a novel mechanism that anchors guidance to semantically important regions through attention. By adaptively reinforcing informative patches during sampling, IGG ensures that guidance and content remain tightly aligned. Across both class-conditioned and text-to-image generation tasks, IGG delivers sharper, more coherent, and semantically grounded images, setting a new benchmark for AR-based methods.

paragraphs: Some autoregressive image generators build an image by predicting progressively finer scales. The paper identifies a problem in this process: information in different patches can become inconsistent across generation steps as resolution increases. Guidance then becomes scattered, weakening the connection between the generated content and its conditioning information.

Information-Grounding Guidance, or IGG, uses attention to anchor guidance to semantically important image regions. During sampling, it adaptively reinforces informative patches so that the guidance remains aligned with the content being generated. This directly targets the drift associated with progressive scaling and the ambiguous or unfaithful features that can result.

The authors evaluate IGG on both class-conditioned generation and text-to-image generation. They report sharper images, greater coherence, and stronger semantic grounding, describing the results as a new benchmark for autoregressive methods. The contribution emphasizes where guidance is applied during sampling: preserving its connection to informative regions can improve how faithfully the evolving image follows its condition.
summary.tldr: IGG uses attention to keep autoregressive image-generation guidance focused on informative regions, improving coherence and semantic fidelity.

title: Rethinking Visual Autoregressive Sampling with Information-Grounding Guidance

abstract: Deep sequence models are said to store atomic facts predominantly in the form of associative memory: a brute-force lookup of co-occurring entities. We identify a dramatically different form of storage of atomic facts that we term as geometric memory. Here, the model has synthesized embeddings encoding novel global relationships between all entities, including ones that do not co-occur in training. Such storage is powerful: for instance, we show how it transforms a hard reasoning task involving an $\ell$-fold composition into an easy-to-learn $1$-step navigation task. From this phenomenon, we extract fundamental aspects of neural embedding geometries that are hard to explain. We argue that the rise of such a geometry, as against a lookup of local associations, cannot be straightforwardly attributed to typical supervisory, architectural, or optimizational pressures. Counterintuitively, a geometry is learned even when it is more complex than the brute-force lookup. Then, by analyzing a connection to Node2Vec, we demonstrate how the geometry stems from a spectral bias that—in contrast to prevailing theories—indeed arises naturally despite the lack of various pressures. This analysis also points out to practitioners a visible headroom to make Transformer memory more strongly geometric. We hope the geometric view of parametric memory encourages revisiting the default intuitions that guide researchers in areas like knowledge acquisition, capacity, discovery, and unlearning.

paragraphs: Atomic facts in sequence models are often understood as associations between entities that appeared together during training. This paper identifies another form of storage: embeddings that encode global relationships across entities, including pairs never observed together. The authors call this geometric memory because relationships are organized through the structure of the embedding space.

That organization can simplify reasoning. The paper demonstrates how a task requiring repeated composition can become a learnable single navigation step when the relevant relationships are represented geometrically. It also finds that this geometry can emerge even when it is more complex than storing local associations, challenging a straightforward explanation based on simpler memorization.

The authors argue that familiar supervisory, architectural, and optimization pressures do not readily account for the phenomenon. Through a connection to Node2Vec, they identify a spectral bias that can generate geometry despite the absence of several such pressures. The analysis also points to room for making Transformer memory more geometric, motivating a reconsideration of how stored facts support knowledge acquisition and reasoning.
summary.tldr: Sequence models can organize facts into global embedding geometries that simplify reasoning, with a Node2Vec connection revealing a possible underlying spectral bias.

title: Deep sequence models tend to memorize geometrically; it is unclear why

abstract: We investigate why deep neural networks suffer from loss of plasticity in continual learning, and thus fail to learn new tasks without reinitializing parameters. We show that this failure is preceded by Hessian spectral collapse at new-task initialization, where meaningful curvature directions vanish and gradient descent becomes ineffective. Analyzing a linearized ReLU network, we derive explicit $\epsilon$-rank conditions for successful training and prove that the loss-weighted Gram matrix is spectrally equivalent to the Generalized Gauss-Newton approximation, thereby relating NTK dynamics to Hessian curvature. Targeting spectral collapse directly, we then discuss the Kronecker factored approximation of the Hessian, which motivates two regularization enhancements: maintaining high effective feature rank and applying L2 penalties. Experiments on continual supervised and reinforcement learning tasks confirm that combining these two regularizers effectively preserves plasticity.

We show that this failure is preceded by Hessian spectral collapse at new-task initialization, where meaningful curvature directions vanish and gradient descent becomes ineffective. Targeting spectral collapse directly, we then discuss the Kronecker factored approximation of the Hessian, which motivates two regularization enhancements: maintaining high effective feature rank and applying L2 penalties. paragraphs: A network trained across successive tasks can lose plasticity: its ability to learn new tasks without resetting its parameters. This paper links that failure to a collapse in the Hessian spectrum when a new task begins. Meaningful curvature directions disappear, leaving gradient descent ineffective at adapting the network.

The authors analyze a linearized ReLU network and derive explicit epsilon-rank conditions for successful training. They also prove a spectral equivalence between a loss-weighted Gram matrix and the Generalized Gauss–Newton approximation. This connects a description of learning through neural tangent kernel dynamics with a description based on the curvature of the loss.

To address the identified collapse, the paper examines a Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation and motivates two regularization enhancements: preserving high effective feature rank and adding L2 penalties. Experiments in continual supervised learning and reinforcement learning find that combining them effectively preserves plasticity. The contribution links a mathematical account of lost learning capacity with a practical intervention aimed at maintaining the directions needed for future adaptation.
summary.tldr: Hessian spectral collapse precedes lost learning capacity, and combining feature-rank preservation with L2 regularization preserves plasticity in experiments.

title: Spectral Collapse Drives Loss of Plasticity in Deep Continual Learning

abstract: Crystal modeling spans a family of conditional and unconditional generation tasks, including crystal structure prediction (CSP) and de novo generation (DNG). While recent deep generative models have shown promising performance, they remain largely task-specific, lacking a unified framework that shares crystal representations across tasks. To address this limitation, we propose Multimodal Crystal Flow (MCFlow), a unified multimodal flow model that realizes multiple crystal generation tasks as distinct inference trajectories via independent time variables for atom types and crystal structures. To enable multimodal flow in a standard transformer model, we introduce a composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering with hierarchical permutation augmentation, injecting compositional and crystallographic priors without explicit structural templates. Experiments on the MP-20 and MPTS-52 benchmarks show that a single MCFlow model is competitive with task-specific baselines across CSP, DNG, and structure-conditioned atom type generation.

paragraphs: Crystal modeling includes predicting a structure, generating a new crystal, and selecting atom types for a given structure. Existing generative models often specialize in individual tasks, limiting how their representations are shared. MCFlow brings these tasks into one multimodal flow model, treating atom types and crystal structures as connected generation targets.

The model assigns independent time variables to those two modalities. Different generation tasks then correspond to different inference trajectories through the same model. To support this approach in a standard transformer, the authors introduce atom ordering that reflects composition and symmetry, together with hierarchical permutation augmentation. This incorporates compositional and crystallographic knowledge without explicit structural templates.

On the MP-20 and MPTS-52 benchmarks, a single MCFlow model is competitive with task-specific baselines for structure prediction, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom type generation. The stated result demonstrates breadth within one model rather than superiority on every task. Its significance is that shared crystal representations can support several conditional and unconditional generation problems through different inference procedures.
summary.tldr: MCFlow uses one multimodal flow model for several crystal generation tasks and achieves competitive results against task-specific baselines.

title: Multimodal Crystal Flow: Any-to-Any Modality Generation for Unified Crystal Modeling

abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) learns policies from human trajectory-level comparisons, avoiding explicit reward design and expert demonstrations. Existing methods typically train utility functions on trajectory or segment-level preferences while relying on per-step utility estimates during policy optimization. This training and inference mismatch induces a distribution shift that severely degrades temporal credit assignment and limits policy learning. We analyze this issue and propose PAWS, a segment-based preference learning method that performs policy updates directly using segment-level advantage functions. By aligning utility training with policy optimization, PAWS preserves trajectory-level preference information and avoids unreliable per-step learning signals. Experiments on simulated robotic manipulation and locomotion tasks demonstrate that PAWS consistently outperforms existing PbRL approaches, highlighting the importance of distribution-consistent preference learning.

A person can prefer one trajectory or segment over another, providing information about behavior across time. The paper identifies a mismatch when a utility model trained on those comparisons is then asked to supply individual-step signals for policy optimization.

According to the authors' analysis, this change in granularity creates a distribution shift that harms temporal credit assignment: deciding which parts of a behavior deserve credit becomes unreliable. PAWS keeps policy learning at the segment level. It updates the policy directly using segment-level advantage functions, aligning the units used for preference learning with those used to improve behavior.

In simulated robotic manipulation and locomotion experiments, PAWS consistently outperforms existing preference-based reinforcement-learning methods. The findings support preserving the temporal information contained in comparisons instead of relying on unreliable per-step utility estimates. More broadly, the work shows that the level at which feedback is learned can materially affect how effectively that feedback guides a policy.
summary.tldr: PAWS improves preference-based policy learning by keeping utility training and policy updates aligned at the segment level.

title: PAWS: Preference Learning with Advantage-Weighted Segments

abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) merging can efficiently combine diverse generative capabilities from multiple trained LoRAs for a diffusion model. However, existing LoRA merging techniques often suffer from severe parameter interference, causing destructive collisions in the shared parameter space. To address this, we propose Subspace Signal Routing (SSR), which resolves interference by routing internal signals instead of performing parameter-space merge. Specifically, SSR first constructs a unified subspace by concatenating candidate LoRAs along the rank dimension. Next, SSR employs an inverse correlation matrix to decorrelate mixed signals within this space. Finally, a directional guide matrix steers these purified signals into their respective task-specific subspaces. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis proving that SSR aligns with the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) solution, thereby ensuring mathematical optimality. We utilize the additivity of sufficient statistics to design a streaming algorithm. This enables on-the-fly updates that significantly reduce memory overhead and computation time. Extensive experiments validate that SSR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable efficiency. The source code will be made publicly available.

SSR-Merge addresses this by controlling how internal signals move through the combined adapters. Its central proposal is to resolve conflicting contributions through signal routing instead of merging parameters directly.

The method first concatenates candidate adapters along their rank dimension to construct a shared subspace. An inverse correlation matrix then separates correlated contributions within that space. A directional guide matrix routes the resulting signals toward their corresponding task-specific subspaces. These stages aim to preserve distinct capabilities while allowing the adapters to operate together.

The authors prove that SSR aligns with an Ordinary Least Squares solution, establishing mathematical optimality in that formulation. They also exploit additive sufficient statistics to create a streaming algorithm that supports on-the-fly updates with reduced memory and computation. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art merging methods while maintaining comparable efficiency, supporting signal routing as an effective way to manage adapter interference.
summary.tldr: SSR-Merge combines diffusion-model LoRAs through decorrelated signal routing, reducing interference with an Ordinary Least Squares foundation and streaming updates.

title: SSR-Merge: Subspace Signal Routing for Training-Free LoRA Merging in Diffusion Models

abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation, language models can generate incorrect responses if they fail to utilize query-relevant content from the retrieved evidence. This shifts the focus of uncertainty quantification (UQ) toward assessing contextual grounding, i.e., whether predictions are supported by query-relevant tokens. Recent UQ methods unpack language models to characterize how inputs are processed. Nevertheless, these methods focus on a few layers and overlook the whole progressive propagation within the model, thereby failing to fully capture the grounding dynamics essential for reliable uncertainty estimation. We use information flow to build a layer-wise trace that reveals each context token’s contribution to the output, providing an interpretable basis for assessing reliability. From this analysis, we introduce two measures to calibrate prediction confidence. The first, simulatability, posits that a prediction is more likely to be correct when context token contributions align closely with their true relevance. The second, concentration, asserts that a response is more likely to be correct when it is derived from a narrow, focused subset of tokens. Experiments show that our method achieves an average AUROC of 0.709, exceeding the runner-up performance of 0.676, while maintaining moderate computational cost.

paragraphs: Retrieved evidence helps a language model only if the model uses the parts relevant to the question. This paper studies uncertainty through contextual grounding: whether an answer draws on appropriate evidence tokens. It argues that inspecting only a few layers misses how those contributions develop as information moves through the model.

The method builds a layer-by-layer information-flow trace of each context token’s contribution to the output. It derives two confidence measures from that trace. Simulatability captures the idea that answers are more likely to be correct when influential tokens match genuinely relevant evidence. Concentration captures the idea that reliance on a focused subset of tokens is associated with greater correctness.

These measures turn the pattern of evidence use into an interpretable basis for estimating reliability. In the reported experiments, the method reaches an average AUROC of 0.709, compared with 0.676 for the runner-up, with moderate computational cost. The result supports improved discrimination between correct and incorrect responses, without making either grounding measure a guarantee of correctness.
summary.tldr: Tracing context-token influence across model layers improves confidence estimates by measuring how answers use relevant evidence.

title: Information Flow Reveals When to Trust Language Models

abstract: 3D open-world environments with adversarial opponents remain a core challenge for reinforcement learning due to their vast state spaces. Effective reasoning representations are essential in such settings. While existing self-supervised visual foresight reasoning approaches often suffer from multi-step error accumulation, many recent studies resort to injecting domain-specific knowledge for more stable guidance. Our key insight is that the photorealistic fidelity of visual reasoning representations is secondary; what truly matters is providing informative, task-relevant signals. To this end, we propose ResDreamer, a hierarchical world model in which each higher-level layer is trained to reconstruct the residuals of the layer below. This design enables progressive abstraction of increasingly sophisticated world dynamics and fosters the emergence of richer latent representations. Drawing inspiration from the “Bitter Lesson,” ResDreamer trains its reasoning representations in a purely self-supervised manner. The higher-level residual representations are used to modulate lower-level predictions, allowing the world model to scale effectively with only linearly increasing cross-layer communication costs. Experiments show that ResDreamer achieves state-of-the-art sample efficiency and parameter efficiency. This scalable hierarchical visual foresight reasoning architecture paves the way for more capable online RL agents in open-ended, dynamic environments.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents in open 3D worlds must reason about large, changing environments and adversarial opponents. Predicting future visual states can help, but errors can accumulate across prediction steps. ResDreamer focuses on learning representations that carry useful task information, with photorealistic reconstruction treated as secondary to that reasoning role.

This gives higher levels a learning signal based on what lower levels have not captured. Experiments report state-of-the-art sample efficiency and parameter efficiency. These findings support hierarchical residual modeling as a scalable route to visual foresight, with useful reasoning representations learned from the prediction process itself rather than supplied through domain-specific guidance.
summary.tldr: ResDreamer learns hierarchical residual world models that improve the reported sample and parameter efficiency of visual reinforcement learning.

title: Self-supervised Hierarchical Visual Reasoning with World Model

abstract: Self-evolving memory serves as the trainable parameters for Large Language Models (LLMs)-based agents, where extraction (distilling insights from experience) and management (updating the memory bank) must be tightly coordinated. Existing methods predominantly optimize memory management while treating memory extraction as a static process, resulting in poor generalization, where agents accumulate instance-specific noise rather than robust memories. To address this, we propose Unified Memory Extraction and Management (UMEM), a self-evolving agent framework that jointly optimizes a LLM to simultaneously extract and manage memories. To mitigate overfitting to specific instances, we introduce Semantic Neighborhood Modeling and optimize the model with a neighborhood-level marginal utility reward via GRPO. This approach ensures memory generalizability by evaluating memory utility across clusters of semantically related queries. Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that UMEM significantly outperforms highly competitive baselines, achieving up to 11.49 points improvement in multi-turn interactive tasks. Furthermore, UMEM maintains a stable improvement trend during continuous evolution.

paragraphs: An agent's memory improves future behavior only if it captures useful lessons from experience. That requires both extracting the right information and deciding how to update the memory bank. UMEM addresses the problem that optimizing memory management while leaving extraction fixed can accumulate details tied to individual cases instead of reusable knowledge.

The framework jointly optimizes a language model to perform extraction and management. Its Semantic Neighborhood Modeling groups semantically related queries and evaluates the marginal usefulness of memory across those neighborhoods. A neighborhood-level reward, optimized with GRPO, encourages memories whose benefits extend beyond the particular interaction from which they were extracted.

Across five benchmarks, the authors report significant improvements over highly competitive baselines, including gains of up to 11.49 points on multi-turn interactive tasks. Performance also maintains a stable improvement trend during continued evolution. The findings support coordinating what gets remembered with how memory is maintained, and judging memory through its usefulness to related queries rather than a single isolated instance.
summary.tldr: UMEM jointly learns memory extraction and management, rewarding memories that help groups of related queries rather than only individual cases.

title: UMEM: Unified Memory Extraction and Management Framework for Generalizable Memory

abstract: Multi-tenant multi-LoRA serving multiplexes many LoRA adapters on a single GPU under high utilization, where most device memory is reserved for the KV cache, leaving only a small residency budget $K$ for adapters. In this regime, adapter readiness is atomic: if an adapter is not device-resident, the engine must perform a mandatory fetch, stalling shared execution and amplifying tail latency system-wide. With only $K$ residency slots, we identify a LoRA residency cliff: once the active adapter working set exceeds $K$, time-to-first-token (TTFT) tail latency can exhibit a congestion collapse rather than smooth degradation. To tame this cliff, we propose CLIMB, a minimal ingress controller that enforces feasibility-first admission by queueing non-resident adapters outside the engine, prioritizing critical (VIP) traffic, and rotating background adapters via round-robin. On a cliff-inducing workload, CLIMB averts collapse, reducing VIP TTFT p99 from 38.7 s to 13.1 s at matched throughput (10.66 rps) by keeping VIP engine latency near 0.13 s and shifting the residual tail into explicit ingress queueing. Overall, CLIMB shifts fetch-induced stalls from inside the engine to managed ingress queues, mitigating tail amplification without throughput loss in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Serving many LoRA adapters on one heavily used GPU creates competition for a small amount of adapter memory. Most memory is reserved for the attention cache. When a requested adapter is absent from the GPU, fetching it stalls shared execution. The paper identifies a regime where exceeding the available adapter slots can cause a sharp collapse in response latency.

CLIMB manages requests before they enter the serving engine. It queues requests for nonresident adapters outside the engine, gives priority to critical VIP traffic, and rotates background adapters in round-robin order. VIP latency inside the engine stayed near 0.13 seconds; remaining delay largely moved to ingress queueing. The evaluated benefit is controlled waiting and reduced system-wide amplification, without a throughput loss in those settings.
summary.tldr: CLIMB reduces severe multi-LoRA serving delays by managing adapter availability and request priorities before requests enter the engine.

title: CLIMB: Taming the LoRA Residency Cliff in Multi-LoRA Serving

abstract: The deployment of quantized neural networks on edge devices, combined with privacy regulations like GDPR, creates an urgent need for machine unlearning in quantized models. However, existing methods face critical challenges: they induce forgetting by training models to memorize incorrect labels, conflating forgetting with misremembering, and employ scalar gradient reweighting that cannot resolve directional conflicts between gradients. We propose $\textbf{OEU}$, a novel Orthogonal Entropy Unlearning framework with two key innovations: 1) Entropy-guided unlearning provides an unbiased forgetting direction by maximizing prediction uncertainty on forgotten data, avoiding confident misprediction toward any specific class, and 2) Gradient orthogonal projection eliminates interference by projecting forgetting gradients onto the orthogonal complement of retain gradients, providing theoretical guarantees for utility preservation under first-order approximation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OEU outperforms existing methods in both forgetting effectiveness and retain accuracy.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training data while preserving useful behavior on retained data. This paper addresses that task for quantized neural networks. It identifies a problem with methods that teach incorrect labels: the model can become confidently wrong about the forgotten examples, which conflates forgetting with learning a replacement mistake.

Orthogonal Entropy Unlearning, or OEU, instead increases prediction uncertainty on the data to be forgotten. Maximizing entropy avoids directing the model toward a particular incorrect class. A second component handles conflicts between forgetting and retention updates. It projects the forgetting gradient onto directions orthogonal to the retain gradient, addressing directional interference that scalar gradient reweighting cannot resolve.

The utility-preservation guarantee applies under a first-order approximation, which is the stated scope of the theoretical result. Experiments show better forgetting effectiveness and retained-data accuracy than existing methods. Together, the two components frame unlearning as reducing confidence in selected information while controlling how that change affects knowledge the model should keep.
summary.tldr: OEU forgets selected data by increasing uncertainty and projects forgetting updates away from directions that interfere with retained knowledge.

title: Forget by Uncertainty: Orthogonal Entropy Unlearning for Quantized Neural Networks

abstract: The Policy-Space Response Oracles (PSRO) framework scales equilibrium computation to large zero-sum games by iteratively expanding a restricted strategy set using deep reinforcement learning (DRL). A central challenge is to construct, under limited computational budgets, a small strategy population whose induced game well approximates the full game. Existing PSRO variants typically expand the population using best responses to meta-strategies computed from restricted-game payoffs, which can lead to inefficient expansions that provide limited global improvement. We propose to guide population expansion by directly evaluating the post-expansion population quality. Specifically, we adopt Population Exploitability (PE) to measure how well a restricted strategy set represents the full game, and introduce a two-phase exploration–selection framework that explicitly minimizes PE during expansion. We instantiate this framework as Global PSRO, a practical DRL-based algorithm that efficiently generates candidate responses and estimates PE via parameter-sharing conditional neural networks. Experiments across multiple two-player zero-sum games show that Global PSRO achieves lower exploitability and approximates Nash equilibria with significantly fewer policy iterations than prior PSRO methods. The experimental code is available at https://github.com/Zhangjy1997/GlobalPSRO.

paragraphs: Solving large two-player zero-sum games often requires working with a manageable population of strategies. Policy-Space Response Oracles expands such a population through reinforcement learning. The challenge is to select additions that make the restricted game represent the full game well, especially when the available computation limits how many strategies can be trained.

Global PSRO evaluates the quality of the population that would result from an addition. It uses Population Exploitability to measure representation quality and organizes expansion into exploration and selection phases that explicitly seek to minimize that measure. Parameter-sharing conditional neural networks help generate candidate responses and estimate their resulting population quality efficiently.

Across multiple games, Global PSRO achieves lower exploitability and approaches Nash equilibria with significantly fewer policy iterations than earlier PSRO methods. The results support evaluating new strategies through their contribution to the whole population. This connects the expansion decision more directly to the ultimate objective of constructing a small strategy set that approximates the full game.
summary.tldr: Global PSRO selects strategy additions by their effect on population exploitability, reaching stronger game approximations with fewer policy iterations.

title: Global Policy-Space Response Oracles for Two-Player Zero-Sum Games

abstract: Incomplete Multi-View Clustering (IMVC) is affected not only by missing feature values, but also by the degradation of relational structure induced by missing views. Many graph-based approaches either rely on costly data imputation or adopt first-order fusion mechanisms, which can be viewed as shallow low-pass filters with limited spectral selectivity. As a result, they may be insufficient to distinguish latent consensus structure from view-specific structural variations. To address this limitation, we reformulate IMVC from a spectral filtering perspective and propose Contractive Anchor Resolvent Diffusion (CARD), a scalable framework for structural refinement without explicit view imputation. CARD constructs a unified anchor-induced hypergraph from observed sample–anchor relations and derives a high-order resolvent diffusion operator that acts as a rational spectral filter. This operator enhances the relative response of consensus-dominant modes while attenuating view-specific variations. We further derive a compact implicit solver that couples similarity learning and clustering without materializing dense matrices, and provide a conditional local refinement analysis under spectral-gap and local-stability assumptions. Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks, including large-scale datasets, show that CARD achieves competitive performance while scaling linearly in $N$ for a fixed anchor budget. The code for our method is publicly available at https://github.com/Whale-Waves/CARD.

paragraphs: When objects have several views or feature sets, missing views damage both their available features and the relationships used to cluster them. Existing graph approaches may fill in missing data at substantial cost or combine relationships with shallow filters that struggle to separate shared structure from view-specific variation.

CARD instead builds a unified hypergraph from observed relationships between samples and representative anchors. A higher-order resolvent diffusion operator then filters this structure, strengthening the relative contribution of modes dominated by agreement across views while suppressing view-specific variations. Together, these results support structural refinement as a scalable way to handle incomplete views without a separate imputation stage.
summary.tldr: CARD refines shared relationships for incomplete multi-view clustering without filling in missing views, scaling linearly with sample count at a fixed anchor budget.

title: Contractive Anchor Resolvent Diffusion for Incomplete Multi-View Clustering

abstract: The essence of video lies in pixel dynamics: motion, state transitions, and the flow of visual information across frames. Video Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become the dominant paradigm for video understanding in computer vision, sophisticated multimodal reasoning over complex, long-form visual streams. In this position paper, we argue that recent progress in video understanding is measured by benchmarks and protocols that can be solved without reliably perceiving spatiotemporal evidence, rewarding language-driven plausibility over video-grounded inference. We identify two coupled failure modes that consistently emerge across recent Video LLM evaluations: (i) static-cue dominance, where appearance and context outweigh spatiotemporal evidence, and (ii) prior-driven temporal hallucination, where learned regularities fill in temporal and causal structure when dynamics are subtle or counterintuitive. We synthesize recent diagnostic probes that expose these failure modes into a call to action for the community: to re-center video understanding on what a video uniquely contains, namely, dynamic evidence that unfolds over time, by enforcing spatiotemporal grounding in both models and benchmarks, before the pixel dynamics are lost in plain sight.

paragraphs: Video contains motion, changing states, and information that unfolds across frames. This paper argues that current video-language-model benchmarks can sometimes be solved without reliably perceiving those dynamics. As a result, measured progress can reward answers that sound plausible from language and context without demonstrating that the model used the relevant visual evidence over time.

The authors identify two connected failure modes across recent evaluations. Static-cue dominance occurs when appearance and context outweigh evidence about change. Prior-driven temporal hallucination occurs when learned regularities supply an account of timing or causation, especially when the actual dynamics are subtle or counterintuitive. Both can obscure whether a model follows what happens in the video.

The paper synthesizes diagnostic probes that expose these problems and calls for stronger spatiotemporal grounding in models and benchmarks. The goal is to make evaluation depend on the evidence that video uniquely provides. Its contribution is a diagnosis of how existing assessments can miss dynamic understanding and a research priority centered on motion and state transitions.
summary.tldr: Video models and benchmarks should require evidence of motion and change, because plausible answers can conceal failures to perceive dynamics.

abstract: A new hierarchical nonparametric Bayesian model is proposed for the problem of multitask learning (MTL) with sequential data. Sequential data are typically modeled with a hidden Markov model (HMM), for which one often must choose an appropriate model structure (number of states) before learning. Here we model sequential data from each task with an infinite hidden Markov model (iHMM), avoiding the problem of model selection. The MTL for iHMMs is implemented by imposing a nested Dirichlet process (nDP) prior on the base distributions of the iHMMs. The nDP-iHMM MTL method allows us to perform task-level clustering and data-level clustering simultaneously, with which the learning for individual iHMMs is enhanced and between-task similarities are learned. Learning and inference for the nDP-iHMM MTL are based on a Gibbs sampler. The effectiveness of the framework is demonstrated using synthetic data as well as real music data.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a Bayesian framework for learning several related sequential-data tasks together. Standard hidden Markov models often require choosing the number of hidden states before learning. The authors instead assign each task an infinite hidden Markov model, avoiding that advance choice of a fixed state count.

To connect the tasks, the framework places a nested Dirichlet process prior on the base distributions of their models. This allows clustering at two levels simultaneously: among tasks and within their data. The shared hierarchy supports learning individual sequence models while also discovering similarities between tasks.

Learning and inference use a Gibbs sampler. The framework is demonstrated on synthetic sequences and real music data. Its significance is the joint treatment of model structure and relationships across tasks: the method can learn how tasks group together while fitting their sequential patterns. The reported demonstrations support the effectiveness of this combined nonparametric approach for the data considered.
summary.tldr: A nested Dirichlet process connects infinite HMMs to learn sequential tasks jointly while discovering task similarities and data clusters.

title: Multi-task learning for sequential data via iHMMs and the nested Dirichlet process

abstract: In ranking with the pairwise classification approach, the loss associated to a predicted ranked list is the mean of the pairwise classification losses. This loss is inadequate for tasks such as information retrieval where we prefer ranked lists with high precision on the top of the list. We propose to optimize a larger class of loss functions for ranking, based on an ordered weighted average (OWA) (Yager, 88} of the classification losses. Convex OWA aggregation operators range from the max to the mean depending on their weights, and can be used to focus on the top ranked elements as they give more weight to the largest losses. When aggregating hinge losses, the optimization problem is similar to the SVM for interdependent output spaces. Moreover, we show that an OWA aggregation of margin-based classification losses has good generalization properties. Experiments on the Letor 3.0 benchmark dataset for information retrieval validate our approach.

paragraphs: Pairwise ranking approaches often evaluate a predicted list by averaging losses over document pairs. That average can be poorly aligned with information retrieval, where correct results near the top matter especially strongly. This paper broadens the ranking objective by changing how pairwise classification losses are combined.

The proposed combination is an ordered weighted average: losses receive weights according to their order. Convex versions range from the maximum loss to the ordinary mean, depending on the weights. Emphasizing larger losses can focus learning on top-ranked elements. When the component losses are hinge losses, the resulting optimization resembles an SVM formulation for interdependent outputs.

The authors also establish good generalization properties for ordered weighted aggregation of margin-based classification losses. Experiments on the Letor 3.0 information-retrieval benchmark validate the approach. The contribution offers a flexible alternative to treating every pairwise loss equally, with both theoretical support and empirical evidence for making the training objective more responsive to the priorities of ranking tasks.
summary.tldr: Ordered weighting of pairwise losses lets ranking objectives emphasize larger errors and better address performance near the top of a list.

title: Ranking with ordered weighted pairwise classification

abstract: In this paper, we present a robust feature extraction framework based on information-theoretic learning. Its formulated objective aims at dual targets, motivated by the Renyi's quadratic entropy of the features and the Renyi's cross entropy between features and class labels, respectively. This objective function reaps the advantages in robustness from both redescending M-estimator and manifold regularization, and can be efficiently optimized via half-quadratic optimization in an iterative manner. In addition, the popular algorithms LPP, SRDA and LapRLS for feature extraction are all justified to be the special cases within this framework. Extensive comparison experiments on several real-world data sets, with contaminated features or labels, well validate the encouraging gain in algorithmic robustness from this proposed framework.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a feature-extraction framework designed to remain useful when features or class labels are contaminated. Its objective has two parts, motivated by Rényi's quadratic entropy of the features and Rényi's cross entropy between features and labels. These give the framework an information-theoretic basis for constructing its feature representation.

The objective combines robustness benefits associated with a redescending M-estimator and manifold regularization. The authors show that it can be optimized efficiently through an iterative half-quadratic procedure. They also place the existing feature-extraction algorithms LPP, SRDA, and LapRLS within the framework as special cases, linking the proposed method to several established approaches.

Comparative experiments on multiple real-world datasets include contamination in either features or labels. The results support encouraging improvements in robustness for the proposed framework. The contribution is thus both a unified formulation and an empirically supported way to handle corrupted information during feature extraction. The experimental claim concerns robustness in the tested contaminated-data settings, rather than immunity to all forms of corruption.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic feature-extraction framework unifies several existing methods and shows improved robustness to contaminated features or labels.

title: Robust feature extraction via information theoretic learning

abstract: In this paper we propose a novel clustering algorithm based on maximizing the mutual information between data points and clusters. Unlike previous methods, we neitherassume the data are given in terms of distributions nor impose any parametric model on the within-cluster distribution. Instead, we utilize a non-parametric estimation of the average cluster entropies and search for a clustering that maximizes the estimated mutual information between data points and clusters. The improved performance of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated on several standard datasets.
originalAbstract: In this paper we propose a novel clustering algorithm based on maximizing the mutual information between data points and clusters. Unlike previous methods, we neitherassume the data are given in terms of distributions nor impose any parametric model on the within-cluster distribution. Instead, we utilize a non-parametric estimation of the average cluster entropies and search for a clustering that maximizes the estimated mutual information between data points and clusters. The improved performance of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated on several standard datasets.

paragraphs: Clustering groups data points according to a chosen criterion of useful organization. This paper uses mutual information between data points and clusters as that criterion. The aim is to find an assignment in which cluster membership carries substantial information about the data, giving the clustering problem an explicit information-theoretic objective.

The proposed algorithm does not require the input data to be supplied as probability distributions. It also avoids specifying a parametric form for the distribution inside each cluster. Instead, it estimates average cluster entropies nonparametrically and searches for a grouping that maximizes the resulting estimate of mutual information.

This approach matters because the clustering objective can be pursued without imposing a predetermined within-cluster distribution family. The authors demonstrate improved performance on several standard datasets, providing empirical support for this combination of estimation and search. The reported improvement concerns the evaluated datasets, while the methodological contribution is the use of nonparametric entropy estimates to make an information-based clustering objective operational.
summary.tldr: A clustering algorithm maximizes estimated mutual information using nonparametric cluster-entropy estimates, with improved performance on standard datasets.

title: Nonparametric Information Theoretic Clustering Algorithm

abstract: We develop several predictive models linking legislative sentiment to legislative text. Our models, which draw on ideas from ideal point estimation and topic models, predict voting patterns based on the contents of bills and infer the political leanings of legislators. With supervised topics, we provide an exploratory window into how the language of the law is correlated with political support. We also derive approximate posterior inference algorithms based on variational methods. Across 12 years of legislative data, we predict specific voting patterns with high accuracy.
originalAbstract: We develop several predictive models linking legislative sentiment to legislative text.
