With supervised topics, we provide an exploratory window into how the language of the law is correlated with political support. We also derive approximate posterior inference algorithms based on variational methods. Across 12 years of legislative data, we predict specific voting patterns with high accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper develops models that connect the text of legislative bills with how legislators vote. The models use ideas from ideal point estimation and topic modeling to predict voting patterns from bill content while inferring legislators' political leanings. This links textual subject matter and political preferences within the same predictive task.

Supervised topics provide a way to explore which patterns in legislative language correlate with political support. That makes the models useful for examining associations as well as making predictions. The stated interpretation is correlational: the learned topics offer a view of how language and support align, rather than demonstrating that particular wording causes legislators to vote a certain way.

The authors derive variational algorithms for approximate posterior inference, supplying a computational approach for fitting the models. Across 12 years of legislative data, they report high accuracy in predicting specific voting patterns. The findings indicate that bill text contains useful predictive information about legislative support, while the inferred leanings and supervised topics offer complementary ways to examine those predictions.
summary.tldr: Models combining bill text, topics, and political leanings predict legislative voting patterns with reported high accuracy across 12 years of data.

title: Predicting Legislative Roll Calls from Text

abstract: Bayesian Optimization aims at optimizing an unknown non-convex/concave function that is costly to evaluate. We are interested in application scenarios where concurrent function evaluations are possible. Under such a setting, BO could choose to either sequentially evaluate the function, one input at a time and wait for the output of the function before making the next selection, or evaluate the function at a batch of multiple inputs at once. These two different settings are commonly referred to as the sequential and batch settings of Bayesian Optimization. In general, the sequential setting leads to better optimization performance as each function evaluation is selected with more information, whereas the batch setting has an advantage in terms of the total experimental time (the number of iterations). In this work, our goal is to combine the strength of both settings. Specifically, we systematically analyze Bayesian optimization using Gaussian process as the posterior estimator and provide a hybrid algorithm that, based on the current state, dynamically switches between a sequential policy and a batch policy with variable batch sizes. We provide theoretical justification for our algorithm and present experimental results on eight benchmark BO problems. The results show that our method achieves substantial speedup (up to % 78 ) compared to a pure sequential policy, without suffering any significant performance loss.

Specifically, we systematically analyze Bayesian optimization using Gaussian process as the posterior estimator and provide a hybrid algorithm that, based on the current state, dynamically switches between a sequential policy and a batch policy with variable batch sizes. paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to an unknown function that is expensive to evaluate. Sequential selection can use every completed evaluation to inform the next choice. Batch selection allows evaluations to run concurrently, reducing experimental time, but choices within a batch are made without all the feedback that sequential selection would have received.

The paper combines these modes using a Gaussian process as the posterior estimator. Its hybrid algorithm examines the current state and switches dynamically between sequential evaluation and batches of variable size. The central idea is to let the available information determine how much evaluation work to launch together, balancing informative choices with the opportunity for parallel execution.

The authors provide theoretical justification and evaluate the method on eight benchmark optimization problems. They report speedups of up to 78 percent relative to a purely sequential policy, without significant optimization-performance loss in those experiments. The result supports adaptive batching as a way to capture substantial time savings while preserving much of the benefit of feedback-informed selection.
summary.tldr: A hybrid Bayesian optimizer dynamically chooses sequential or batch evaluation, achieving reported speedups of up to 78 percent without significant performance loss.

title: Hybrid Batch Bayesian Optimization

abstract: We present a hybrid algorithm for Bayesian topic models that combines the efficiency of sparse Gibbs sampling with the scalability of online stochastic inference. The resulting method scales to a corpus of 1.2 million books comprising 33 billion words with thousands of topics on one CPU. This approach reduces the bias of variational inference and generalizes to many Bayesian hidden-variable models.
originalAbstract: We present a hybrid algorithm for Bayesian topic models that combines the efficiency of sparse Gibbs sampling with the scalability of online stochastic inference. The resulting method scales to a corpus of 1.2 million books comprising 33 billion words with thousands of topics on one CPU. This approach reduces the bias of variational inference and generalizes to many Bayesian hidden-variable models.

paragraphs: Bayesian topic models need inference methods that remain practical as both text collections and the number of topics grow. This paper introduces a hybrid algorithm for latent Dirichlet allocation that combines two useful properties: the efficiency of sparse Gibbs sampling and the scalability of online stochastic inference. The contribution centers on bringing those properties into one inference method.

The reported scale is substantial: the algorithm handles 1.2 million books containing 33 billion words, with thousands of topics, on one CPU. This result demonstrates that the combined approach can operate on a very large corpus without requiring multiple CPUs in the reported application. It also addresses a setting with a large topic collection, not merely a large amount of text.

The authors state that the method reduces variational-inference bias and extends to many Bayesian models with hidden variables. The broader significance is a combination of scalable computation and improved inference behavior. The claim is a reduction in bias, rather than its complete elimination, and generalization to many such models rather than every Bayesian model.
summary.tldr: Combining sparse Gibbs sampling with online stochastic inference scales topic modeling to 33 billion words on one CPU while reducing variational bias.

title: Sparse stochastic inference for latent Dirichlet allocation
